14	# Concentration of Training Workloads Is the Cornerstone Principle of Block Periodization
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin states the Block Periodization Concept (BPC) rests on one
17	foundational principle, concentration of training workloads, from which two others follow:
18	(1) a minimal number of targeted abilities per block, because highly concentrated loads
19	"only provide sufficient training stimuli to improve the targeted ability," and (2)
20	consecutive (not simultaneous) development of abilities, because "the number of decisive
21	abilities exceeds the number of abilities that can be developed simultaneously" (PDF p. 37,
22	printed p. 26, Figure 1.7). The rationale is laid out as a table of contradictions in the
23	traditional, simultaneous-development model for high-level athletes (Table 1.4, PDF p. 20,
24	printed p. 9): concurrent workloads compete for limited energy supply, differing
25	physiological-system restoration times leave athletes under-recovered for all targets at
26	once, workloads interact negatively (energy deficits, technical complexity, neuromuscular
27	fatigue), mental concentration cannot be split across many targets, and the training
28	stimulus needed for a high-level athlete's progress cannot be reached when it is divided
29	among many abilities.
30	
31	**Why it works** — Issurin's own explanation is that above a threshold of athletic level,
32	a quality only responds to a training stimulus concentrated enough to exceed that
33	threshold; splitting the same total training time across many qualities keeps each one's
34	stimulus below that threshold. He does not give a quantitative mechanism for where that
35	threshold sits or how "concentrated enough" is defined for a given ability or athlete — the
36	principle is argued from coaches' and scientists' collective experience (Table 1.4) rather
37	than derived from a stated dose-response model.
38	
39	**When to apply** — Designing training blocks for advanced, high-level athletes juggling
40	more qualities than can be trained well at once (the explicit target population, per
41	Issurin). **Eric's baseline:** this converges with the department's own compatibility rule,
42	"you can't ride two horses with one saddle" — incompatible qualities are not both trained at
43	full intensity in the same block (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
44	citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29). It also converges with
45	[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]], which independently
46	describes concentrated, saturated loading on one quality with a delayed 4-12 week rebound.
47	
48	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin's own text (PDF p. 44, printed p. 33) states the
49	traditional, complex (simultaneous multi-ability) model "has visible benefits for the
50	preparation of low- and mid-level athletes": it is "more diversified, attractive and
51	lively," and medium-level concentration is "sufficient stimulation" at that level — the
52	concentration principle is explicitly scoped to high-performance athletes, not a universal
53	programming rule. **Contested:** Issurin's blanket claim elsewhere in the same chapter that
54	the traditional model "does not work well for high-performance athletes" (PDF p. 19,
55	printed p. 8) is disputed by this library's own Bompa & Haff 5th-edition material
56	(`periodization--bompa`), which is a current (not 1984-vintage) textbook still teaching and
57	defending a form of the traditional/complex periodization model for high-level athletes.
58	Issurin's critique in this chapter names Bompa's *1984* edition specifically (PDF p. 13,
59	printed p. 2) as one of the texts that propagated the traditional model he is arguing
60	against — it is not a critique of the Bompa & Haff 5th edition already in this library,
61	which incorporates concentrated-loading and conjugated-sequence ideas closer to Issurin's
62	own. **Inference:** Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review (2016, *Sports Medicine*,
63	"Benefits and Limitations of Block Periodized Training Approaches," Zotero item
64	`PT9QTQ2I`, not yet full-text-cached in this ingest) is titled around limitations as well as
65	benefits and likely narrows this 2008 book's confident framing; treat the frontmatter
66	`confidence: contested` as applying specifically to the universal "traditional doesn't work
67	for high performers" claim, not to the narrower, self-limited concentration principle.
68	
69	**Example** — A collegiate football strength staff trying to develop max strength,
70	aerobic capacity, alactic power, and technical skill acquisition all at full intensity in
71	the same 4-week block, per Table 1.4's logic, risks under-stimulating all four rather than
72	meaningfully improving any one; concentrating the block on 1-2 of them (with the rest held
73	at a retention dose) is the alternative Issurin argues for.
74	
75	**Related** — [[framework--block-periodization-mesocycle-taxonomy]] — the three-block
76	structure this principle produces. [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]

79	check for overlap on why generalized simultaneous training under-delivers for advanced

# Concentration of Training Workloads Is the Cornerstone Principle of Block Periodization

**What it is** — Issurin states the Block Periodization Concept (BPC) rests on one
foundational principle, concentration of training workloads, from which two others follow:
(1) a minimal number of targeted abilities per block, because highly concentrated loads
"only provide sufficient training stimuli to improve the targeted ability," and (2)
consecutive (not simultaneous) development of abilities, because "the number of decisive
abilities exceeds the number of abilities that can be developed simultaneously" (PDF p. 37,
printed p. 26, Figure 1.7). The rationale is laid out as a table of contradictions in the
traditional, simultaneous-development model for high-level athletes (Table 1.4, PDF p. 20,
printed p. 9): concurrent workloads compete for limited energy supply, differing
physiological-system restoration times leave athletes under-recovered for all targets at
once, workloads interact negatively (energy deficits, technical complexity, neuromuscular
fatigue), mental concentration cannot be split across many targets, and the training
stimulus needed for a high-level athlete's progress cannot be reached when it is divided
among many abilities.

**Why it works** — Issurin's own explanation is that above a threshold of athletic level,
a quality only responds to a training stimulus concentrated enough to exceed that
threshold; splitting the same total training time across many qualities keeps each one's
stimulus below that threshold. He does not give a quantitative mechanism for where that
threshold sits or how "concentrated enough" is defined for a given ability or athlete — the
principle is argued from coaches' and scientists' collective experience (Table 1.4) rather
than derived from a stated dose-response model.

**When to apply** — Designing training blocks for advanced, high-level athletes juggling
more qualities than can be trained well at once (the explicit target population, per
Issurin). **Eric's baseline:** this converges with the department's own compatibility rule,
"you can't ride two horses with one saddle" — incompatible qualities are not both trained at
full intensity in the same block (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29). It also converges with
[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]], which independently
describes concentrated, saturated loading on one quality with a delayed 4-12 week rebound.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin's own text (PDF p. 44, printed p. 33) states the
traditional, complex (simultaneous multi-ability) model "has visible benefits for the
preparation of low- and mid-level athletes": it is "more diversified, attractive and
lively," and medium-level concentration is "sufficient stimulation" at that level — the
concentration principle is explicitly scoped to high-performance athletes, not a universal
programming rule. **Contested:** Issurin's blanket claim elsewhere in the same chapter that
the traditional model "does not work well for high-performance athletes" (PDF p. 19,
printed p. 8) is disputed by this library's own Bompa & Haff 5th-edition material
(`periodization--bompa`), which is a current (not 1984-vintage) textbook still teaching and
defending a form of the traditional/complex periodization model for high-level athletes.
Issurin's critique in this chapter names Bompa's *1984* edition specifically (PDF p. 13,
printed p. 2) as one of the texts that propagated the traditional model he is arguing
against — it is not a critique of the Bompa & Haff 5th edition already in this library,
which incorporates concentrated-loading and conjugated-sequence ideas closer to Issurin's
own. **Inference:** Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review (2016, *Sports Medicine*,
"Benefits and Limitations of Block Periodized Training Approaches," Zotero item
`PT9QTQ2I`, not yet full-text-cached in this ingest) is titled around limitations as well as
benefits and likely narrows this 2008 book's confident framing; treat the frontmatter
`confidence: contested` as applying specifically to the universal "traditional doesn't work
for high performers" claim, not to the narrower, self-limited concentration principle.

**Example** — A collegiate football strength staff trying to develop max strength,
aerobic capacity, alactic power, and technical skill acquisition all at full intensity in
the same 4-week block, per Table 1.4's logic, risks under-stimulating all four rather than
meaningfully improving any one; concentrating the block on 1-2 of them (with the rest held
at a retention dose) is the alternative Issurin argues for.

**Related** — [[framework--block-periodization-mesocycle-taxonomy]] — the three-block
structure this principle produces. [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]
and [[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]] — converging concentrated-load
ideas already in this library. [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (staging) —
check for overlap on why generalized simultaneous training under-delivers for advanced
athletes.

13	
14	# No More Than Three Training Modalities Per Workout, With 65-70% of Time on One or Two
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin extends the concentration principle to single-session design
17	(Figure 2.4, PDF p. 75, printed p. 63; Table 2.12, PDF p. 76, printed p. 65) with five
18	stated rules (PDF p. 75, printed p. 64): (1) a workout should contain **no more than three
19	training modalities** — typically one dominant, one compatible with the main purpose, and
20	one for technique/tactics improvement or restoration; (2) **65-70% of total training time**
21	in a development workout should go to one or two selected modalities, to preserve workload
22	concentration; (3) after a key-workout, the following session should show a significant
23	load reduction — running two consecutive key-workouts is possible but risks excessive load
24	concentration; (4) hypertrophy-focused sessions require workload to be "substantially
25	reduced" for **at least 20 hours** afterward to protect the anabolic phase of muscle
26	restoration; (5) limiting modality count matters most in high-performance training —
27	junior/developmental athletes' programs can be more diverse and multilateral. Figure 2.4
28	maps which modalities are compatible as secondary/tertiary additions to five dominant ones:
29	aerobic endurance pairs with alactic sprint, strength-endurance-aerobic, and
30	hypertrophy-strength (placed after); anaerobic glycolytic endurance pairs with
31	strength-endurance-anaerobic, aerobic restoration, and mixed aerobic-anaerobic endurance;
32	alactic sprint pairs with aerobic endurance, explosive strength, hypertrophy-strength
33	(after), and aerobic restoration; hypertrophy-strength pairs with neural-strength, flexibility,
34	and aerobic restoration; new-technical-skill learning pairs with any modality, but only
35	*after* the dominant task. Table 2.12 gives the physiological/psychological rationale for
36	several of the strongest pairings (e.g., aerobic endurance + strength endurance: increased
37	oxidation supports the resistance work; alactic sprint + aerobic endurance: brief sprints
38	break monotony and keep a wide muscle-fiber pool activated for the subsequent aerobic work).
39	
40	**Why it works — the specific numeric thresholds are asserted, not derived** — The
41	underlying logic is the same concentration principle from Chapter 1
42	([[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]): splitting a session across too many
43	modalities dilutes the stimulus for all of them. **Inference:** Issurin gives no stated
44	derivation for why the cutoff is exactly three modalities rather than two or four, why the
45	time-share threshold is 65-70% rather than some other range, or why 20 hours is the specific
46	reduced-load window after hypertrophy work (versus, e.g., 24 or 48 hours) — these read as
47	the author's own practical rules of thumb built from coaching experience rather than
48	citations to a dose-response study.
49	
50	**When to apply** — Auditing whether a practice plan or lift is trying to do too much:
51	count distinct training modalities in a session and check whether one or two of them
52	actually receive the majority of training time, per the 65-70% rule. Use Figure 2.4/Table
53	2.12 to check whether a planned secondary modality is a known-compatible pairing or an
54	unaddressed combination. **Eric's baseline** independently states a directionally identical
55	rule for compatibility, though at the block level rather than the single-session level:
56	"incompatible qualities... are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block"
57	(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
58	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29, "you can't ride two horses with one
59	saddle") — this Issurin entry gives that same instinct a specific numeric structure (≤3
60	modalities, 65-70% time-share) that the baseline material does not currently specify at
61	either the block or session level.
62	
63	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Treat the ≤3-modality, 65-70%, and 20-hour figures as
64	Issurin's own heuristics rather than established constants — no citation or underlying data
65	is given for any of the three in this chapter. Issurin explicitly narrows the number
66	constraints to high-performance training; junior/developmental programming is stated to
67	reasonably need more variety, not fewer modalities. Figure 2.4's compatibility map is not
68	exhaustive (it covers five dominant modalities, not every possible combination) — an
69	untested pairing should not be assumed incompatible or compatible by default; Issurin gives
70	no guidance for modalities not shown in the figure.
71	
72	**Example** — A practice plan combining strength-endurance, aerobic-anaerobic conditioning,
73	maximal-speed sprint work, and new-install technical work in one session would have four
74	distinct modalities, exceeding the stated ≤3 rule; per Figure 2.4, glycolytic endurance
75	pairs well with strength-endurance-anaerobic and aerobic restoration, but maximal speed and
76	new technical skill acquisition would need to be reduced to secondary/tertiary roles or
77	moved to a separate session to keep the session within the concentration guideline.
78	
79	**Related** — [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]],
80	[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
81	[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]].
82

14	# Accumulation, Transmutation (Transformation), and Realization: the Three Mesocycle-Blocks
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin's core structural unit is the mesocycle-block, one of three types
17	(Table 1.7, PDF p. 37, printed p. 26): **Accumulation** targets basic abilities (aerobic
18	endurance, muscular strength, basic coordination) with high volume/reduced intensity and
19	"reasonable restoration"; **Transmutation** targets sport-specific abilities (special
20	endurance, strength endurance, proper technique) with reduced volume/increased intensity,
21	and explicitly does *not* provide full restoration — fatigue accumulates; **Realization**
22	targets integrative, competition-ready preparedness (model performances, maximum speed,
23	event-specific tactics) at low-medium volume/high intensity, with full restoration required
24	going in. Each type has its own monitoring focus: basic-ability tests for accumulation,
25	sport-specific-ability tests for transmutation, and maximum speed/strategy checks for
26	realization. **Locator note:** the 1985 origin paper (Issurin & Kaverin) and this book's

# Accumulation, Transmutation (Transformation), and Realization: the Three Mesocycle-Blocks

**What it is** — Issurin's core structural unit is the mesocycle-block, one of three types
(Table 1.7, PDF p. 37, printed p. 26): **Accumulation** targets basic abilities (aerobic
endurance, muscular strength, basic coordination) with high volume/reduced intensity and
"reasonable restoration"; **Transmutation** targets sport-specific abilities (special
endurance, strength endurance, proper technique) with reduced volume/increased intensity,
and explicitly does *not* provide full restoration — fatigue accumulates; **Realization**
targets integrative, competition-ready preparedness (model performances, maximum speed,
event-specific tactics) at low-medium volume/high intensity, with full restoration required
going in. Each type has its own monitoring focus: basic-ability tests for accumulation,
sport-specific-ability tests for transmutation, and maximum speed/strategy checks for
realization. **Locator note:** the 1985 origin paper (Issurin & Kaverin) and this book's
1.2.1 narrative (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22) use the term **transformation**; from section
1.2.2 onward (PDF p. 37+, printed p. 26+) and in the book's own tables, the term used is
**transmutation**. Both names refer to the same middle block; record both because a search
for either term should resolve to this entry.

**Why it works** — The sequencing is designed to exploit the fact that different motor
abilities have different **residual training effect** durations (see
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]): basic abilities (aerobic
endurance, max strength) decay slowest, so they can be built early and coast on their own
residual while transmutation and realization narrow the focus toward faster-decaying,
more specific and speed-dependent qualities close to competition. Issurin frames this as
superimposition of residual effects (Figure 1.8, PDF p. 39, printed p. 28) rather than
concurrent development of everything at once.

**When to apply** — Structuring a training stage (the accumulation-transmutation-realization
sequence, ending in competition) for advanced athletes who need multiple qualities peaked
together — see [[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]] for how these three
blocks compose into a full annual plan. **Eric's baseline** shows a structurally similar but
independently-arrived-at sequence: the department's own preparatory-period design goes
hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power
(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing week1-lecture.md pp.43-48) —
a general-to-specific progression that parallels accumulation-to-realization, though the
baseline's sequence is not explicitly framed with Issurin's residual-effect superimposition
logic or his restoration-status distinctions between blocks.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a three-way classification built for advanced
athletes who can tolerate the fatigue-accumulating transmutation block (see
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] for the low-/mid-level-athlete
carve-out). It presumes a training stage that ends in a real competition or test date to
absorb the realization block's tapering logic; without a fixed target date, there is no
clear trigger for when accumulation should end and transmutation begin. **Contested (partly):**
the vault's Bompa & Haff material (`periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching`)
independently describes a comparable saturated-load-then-restitution structure with a
4-12 week delayed rebound — a longer and less rigidly three-staged model than Issurin's
roughly two-month training stage (below); the two should be read as convergent but not
identical prescriptions, and a program note should say which model's timing a given plan
follows.

**Example** — A training stage built for a mid-season peak: 3-4 weeks of accumulation
(aerobic base, general strength), 3-4 weeks of transmutation (sport-specific conditioning,
strength-endurance, technique under fatigue), then 1-2 weeks of realization (tapered
volume, high-intensity model-speed work, full restoration) ending at the target competition
or test date.

**Related** — [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]],
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]] (a different three-block taxonomy
from the same era, worth distinguishing from this one),
[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]],
[[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]].

14	# World-Class Track and Field Athletes Compete and Peak Many Times Per Season, Not Once
15	
16	**What it is** — Table 1.5 (PDF p. 24, printed p. 13, based on Suslov, 2001, with Issurin's
17	modifications) reports three world-class athletes' single-season competition patterns:
18	**Marion Jones** (100-200m, long jump; 1998 season) had **10 peaks** (8 in running, 2 in
19	long jump, all at personal-best level) across a **200-day** competitive span, with typical
20	19-22 day intervals between peaks. **Sergei Bubka** (pole vault; 1991 season) had **7
21	peaks** (all within 3% of his personal best, 595-612 cm) across a **265-day** span,
22	23-43 day intervals. **Stefka Kostadinova** (high jump; 1998 season) had **11 peaks** (all
23	within 3% of her personal best, 200-205 cm) across a combined **155-day** span (winter ~20
24	days; spring/summer 135 days), 14-25 day intervals. Issurin's summary point: these athletes'
25	5-8 month competitive spans "can not be subdivided into traditional preparatory and
26	competitive periods," yet their basic abilities (max strength, aerobic regeneration
27	capacity) still had to be maintained across that entire span.
28	
29	**Why it works — this is observational, not interventional** — These are real competition
30	records for three specific, historically documented elite athletes (Olympic/World
31	champions), not an experiment; the "why" is a report of what elite competition calendars
32	actually looked like by 1991/1998, cited to Suslov's (2001) analysis rather than derived
33	from a controlled study of periodization models.
34	
35	**When to apply** — As direct evidence for the strength-and-conditioning miss-log's
36	"peaking phase structure" gap: this table is the empirical case Issurin uses to argue that a
37	single annual peak (or even a two-/three-peak model) does not describe how modern elite
38	individual-sport athletes actually compete, which motivates the multi-stage annual model in
39	[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]]. Useful for framing the *problem*
40	(competition calendars now demand many peaks) to Baylor coaches even before the
41	*solution* (Chapter 3's microcycle-level guidance, not yet ingested) is available.
42	
43	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — All three examples are individual, non-contact,
44	technique/power sports (sprinting/jumping, pole vault, high jump) where "peak" can be defined
45	by a single measurable performance (time, height, distance) on a given day. **Inference:**
46	this evidence does not directly transfer to football, where "peak" is not a single
47	measurable output and the competitive calendar is fixed by a weekly game schedule rather
48	than a chosen sequence of meets — the multi-peak *problem* generalizes (a football season
49	also demands repeated high-level performance, not one), but the specific 19-43 day
50	inter-peak intervals shown here are specific to how often these particular athletes chose to
51	compete, not a transferable spacing rule for football practice or game weeks. Data source is

53	was defined or verified for each performance.

56	more than one readiness peak per season, this table is a citable, real-world existence proof
57	that elite athletes routinely peak 7-11 times in a season — useful for framing, not for
58	directly copying an inter-peak interval into a football in-season plan.

14	# Case Study: Bondarchuk's Developmental/Competitive/Restorative Blocks and the 1988 Hammer Throw Podium
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin credits Anatoly Bondarchuk, hammer-throw coach, with one of the
17	precursor systems to Block Periodization (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21). Based on his own
18	athletic career (1972 Olympic hammer-throw champion) and doctoral research on throwers'
19	training programs (1988), Bondarchuk built a periodization chart using three types of
20	specialized mesocycle-blocks: **developmental** (workload gradually increases to maximum),
21	**competitive** (load stabilizes, athletes focus on competitive performance), and
22	**restorative** (active recovery, preparing for the next developmental block). Stated
23	durations: developmental and competitive blocks are "usually four weeks," restorative "can
24	be shortened to two weeks." Sequencing depends on the competition schedule and individual
25	athlete response. The claimed outcome: Bondarchuk coached the gold, silver, and bronze
26	medalists in hammer throw at the 1988 Olympics — "the entire Olympic podium occupied by
27	athletes of the same coach" (Bondarchuk, 1986 and 1988, as cited by Issurin).
28	
29	**Why it works — the author gives no mechanism beyond the general BPC rationale** —
30	Issurin does not describe Bondarchuk's own stated reasoning for why these particular block
31	lengths (4/4/2 weeks) or this particular three-way split (by competitive readiness rather
32	than by ability type) were chosen; the mechanism offered is the same general BPC logic
33	(concentrated, sequenced blocks beat simultaneous multi-ability training) applied
34	retroactively to Bondarchuk's design.
35	
36	**When to apply — untested, use as a historical precedent, not as evidence** — Useful for
37	explaining the lineage of block-periodization thinking (Bondarchuk predates and directly
38	inspired Issurin's own accumulation/transmutation/realization taxonomy, per PDF p. 32-33)
39	and as an alternative three-block naming scheme organized around competitive readiness
40	(developmental/competitive/restorative) rather than ability type
41	(accumulation/transmutation/realization) — worth distinguishing the two schemes explicitly
42	when citing "Bondarchuk's blocks" versus "Issurin's blocks."
43	
44	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a single coach's single-event outcome (n = 1
45	coaching program, one Olympic final) with no comparison group, no report of what other
46	finalists' training looked like, and total reliance on the coach's and Issurin's own
47	secondary account rather than an independent case audit. A three-medal sweep at one Olympics
48	is a striking result but cannot isolate the training design's contribution from athlete
49	talent, competitor variance on the day, or other coaching factors. Do not cite this as
50	evidence that a 4/4/2-week block cadence "works" for hammer throw or any other event; it
51	illustrates a design, not a validated dose-response finding. This is distinct from and
52	should not be merged with Issurin's own accumulation/transmutation/realization taxonomy — see
53	[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] for that separate, though
54	historically related, three-block system.
55	
56	**Example** — A coach citing "block periodization has a track record" should specify
57	which system (Bondarchuk's competitive-readiness blocks or Issurin's ability-type blocks) and
58	should not present the 1988 podium sweep as generalizable evidence beyond "one documented
59	historical instance this concept coincided with a strong outcome."
60	
61	**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
62	[[case-study--issurin-kaverin-canoe-kayak-block-periodization]] — a comparable single-coach
63	case from the same era; consider also cross-referencing
64	`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
65	(vault) — the *same* coach (Bondarchuk), but a completely different, unrelated framework
66	of his (an exercise-classification taxonomy by movement similarity, not a mesocycle-timing
67	system). The two should never be conflated when either is cited.

14	# Two Studies Issurin Cites Against Simultaneous Development: Swimmer Interference and Kayaker Decay
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin presents two data-backed examples as motivation for abandoning
17	simultaneous multi-ability training (traditional periodization) in favor of consecutive,
18	concentrated blocks.
19	
20	**(1) Swimmer concurrent-training interference (PDF pp. 21-22, printed pp. 10-11, Figure
21	1.3).** High-level male swimmers were studied over an 8-week early-season program combining
22	extensive swimming with resistive/power dry-land work aimed at swim-specific strength
23	(9-11 workouts/week; sample size not stated in this text). Measured: maximal force of
24	tethered swimming (Ftsw), dry-land explosive strength (Fexp), and dry-land strength
25	endurance (SE). Result: strength endurance improved markedly; swim-specific strength did not
26	improve; explosive strength *decreased* — despite about 30% of dry-land program time devoted
27	to maximal/explosive strength work. Issurin's mechanistic explanation: extensive endurance
28	work captures the metabolic (anabolic) energy needed for the hypertrophy and neural-drive
29	adaptations that explosive/maximal strength require, and the resulting chronic fatigue keeps
30	central and peripheral neural factors from the state needed for strength gains
31	(citing Klausen, 1990, for the neural-mechanism point).
32	
33	**(2) Kayaker decay under traditional periodization (PDF p. 25-26, printed pp. 14-15,
34	Figure 1.4 — the in-text citation reads "Fig.1.3," which appears to be a labeling error in
35	the source; the described variables match Figure 1.4's caption, not Figure 1.3's).** A group
36	of highly qualified kayakers were tracked across a full annual cycle built on the classical
37	model (Issurin et al., 1986). Measured: mean distance velocity (Vd), velocity at anaerobic
38	threshold (V-AT), peak paddle force (PF), stroke rate (SR), muscle mass (MM). Result: the
39	long general-preparatory period raised V-AT, muscle mass and peak force substantially; but
40	during the extended, highly specialized competitive period, extensive aerobic work and
41	maximum-strength work were reduced or dropped as "harmful for racing technique," and V-AT,
42	peak force, and muscle mass all *declined* by the competitive period. Distance velocity
43	still reached its season maximum, but only via increased stroke rate compensating for
44	reduced force — i.e., technique/rate covered for a real loss in the underlying strength and
45	aerobic qualities. Issurin's summary: "the timing pattern for developing different abilities
46	was far from optimal."
47	
48	**Why it works** — For the swimmer case, Issurin's own stated mechanism is that extensive
49	endurance work "captures the metabolic energy that is necessary for anabolism during
50	post-exercise recovery," suppressing the muscle hypertrophy and neural-drive adaptations
51	strength training requires, and that chronic fatigue from high-volume training keeps
52	"central and peripheral neural factors... far from optimum" (PDF pp. 21-22, printed pp.
53	10-11, citing Klausen, 1990, for the neural-mechanism point). For the kayaker case, Issurin
54	gives no physiological mechanism for the decline beyond narration of what happened (reduced
55	aerobic and strength work during the competitive period, PDF p. 25, printed p. 14) — treat
56	that case as a described pattern, not an explained one. **Inference:** labeling the two
57	cases as "concurrent interference" versus "sequential decay" is this entry's own
58	categorization for cross-referencing purposes, not language Issurin himself uses; both are
59	offered by Issurin as evidence for the same underlying argument against simultaneous,
60	non-block training (see [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]), which in turn
61	motivates the consecutive block sequencing in
62	[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] and
63	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]].
64	
65	**When to apply** — The swimmer study is the stronger evidence of the two: it is a
66	controlled, measured 8-week study with named outcome variables, giving concrete numbers
67	useful for illustrating concurrent-training interference to Baylor strength staff
68	programming for athletes who need both an aerobic base and explosive/max strength (e.g.,
69	many football positions in a fall-camp conditioning window). The kayaker case is useful
70	mainly as a cautionary illustration of "building a quality early in the year and then
71	letting it decay unaddressed."
72	
73	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The swimmer study's exact sample size is not given in
74	this text (only workout frequency, 9-11/week), so its statistical strength cannot be judged
75	from this source alone — treat the direction of the finding (interference occurred) as
76	`supported` but the specific numeric changes in Figure 1.3 as unverifiable without the
77	original 1986/whichever-year source Issurin drew Figure 1.3 from (not cited by name on this
78	page). **Untested:** the kayaker case is Issurin's own team's data (Issurin et al., 1986),
79	observational across one season with no control group — it demonstrates a plausible pattern,
80	not a controlled comparison against an alternative periodization model run on the same
81	athletes. Neither study is football-specific; football's in-season structure (weekly
82	competition, not one late-season peak) differs from both the swimmers' fixed 8-week block and
83	the kayakers' single annual peak design.
84	
85	**Example** — A Baylor position group with both an in-season conditioning demand and a
86	strength-maintenance demand should treat "just add more of both" as the swimmer study's
87	failure mode: without deliberate sequencing or volume management, the concurrent aerobic
88	load can blunt the intended strength/power adaptation even when strength work is
89	programmed.
90	
91	**Related** — [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (Table 1.4's rationale,
92	which these two studies are offered as concrete illustrations of),
93	[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

**Why it works** — For the swimmer case, Issurin's own stated mechanism is that extensive
endurance work "captures the metabolic energy that is necessary for anabolism during
post-exercise recovery," suppressing the muscle hypertrophy and neural-drive adaptations
strength training requires, and that chronic fatigue from high-volume training keeps
"central and peripheral neural factors... far from optimum" (PDF pp. 21-22, printed pp.
10-11, citing Klausen, 1990, for the neural-mechanism point). For the kayaker case, Issurin
gives no physiological mechanism for the decline beyond narration of what happened (reduced
aerobic and strength work during the competitive period, PDF p. 25, printed p. 14) — treat
that case as a described pattern, not an explained one. **Inference:** labeling the two
cases as "concurrent interference" versus "sequential decay" is this entry's own
categorization for cross-referencing purposes, not language Issurin himself uses; both are
offered by Issurin as evidence for the same underlying argument against simultaneous,
non-block training (see [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]), which in turn
motivates the consecutive block sequencing in
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] and
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]].

**When to apply** — The swimmer study is the stronger evidence of the two: it is a
controlled, measured 8-week study with named outcome variables, giving concrete numbers
useful for illustrating concurrent-training interference to Baylor strength staff
programming for athletes who need both an aerobic base and explosive/max strength (e.g.,
many football positions in a fall-camp conditioning window). The kayaker case is useful
mainly as a cautionary illustration of "building a quality early in the year and then
letting it decay unaddressed."

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The swimmer study's exact sample size is not given in
this text (only workout frequency, 9-11/week), so its statistical strength cannot be judged
from this source alone — treat the direction of the finding (interference occurred) as
`supported` but the specific numeric changes in Figure 1.3 as unverifiable without the
original 1986/whichever-year source Issurin drew Figure 1.3 from (not cited by name on this
page). **Untested:** the kayaker case is Issurin's own team's data (Issurin et al., 1986),
observational across one season with no control group — it demonstrates a plausible pattern,
not a controlled comparison against an alternative periodization model run on the same
athletes. Neither study is football-specific; football's in-season structure (weekly
competition, not one late-season peak) differs from both the swimmers' fixed 8-week block and
the kayakers' single annual peak design.

strength-maintenance demand should treat "just add more of both" as the swimmer study's

programmed.

which these two studies are offered as concrete illustrations of),
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

14	# Key-Workouts and Key-Exercises Apply the Concentration Principle Inside a Single Session
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin extends the BPC concentration principle (see
17	[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]) down to the level of a single session.
18	A **key-workout** is the most important development session in a training cycle, focused on
19	the current main training emphasis (Table 2.5, PDF p. 56, printed p. 45): it targets the
20	cycle's most relevant abilities (usually one motor-fitness and one technique/tactics
21	target), demands focused athlete motivation and coach support, is timed for the athlete's
22	"best time" (adjusted to prior load but not overly fatigued), is loaded at a
23	substantial/large/extreme level, favors partnership/team-spirit organizational forms, and
24	requires thorough objective monitoring (chronometry, HR, blood lactate, video). New,
25	unfamiliar training means should *not* be introduced during a key-workout, since novelty
26	diverts attention and motivation from load-specific execution. Within a workout, the
27	analogous concept is the **key-exercise** (or **key-task** in team/combat sports where a
28	scrimmage or sparring session plays the role) — the single most important exercise, given
29	priority placement, maximal self-motivation and support, "prime-time" timing, and careful
30	monitoring (Table 2.9, PDF p. 64, printed p. 53). Issurin gives typical prescriptive ranges
31	for key-exercises by targeted ability (Table 2.10, PDF p. 67, printed p. 55, based on Fox &
32	Mathews 1981 and Viru 1995, "with author's modification"): maximal speed, 7-15s work at a
33	1:10 work/rest ratio, maximal intensity, 5-8 reps, 2-5 series; anaerobic glycolytic power,
34	30-50s, 1:(4-5), submaximal, 4-6 reps, 2-4 series, blood lactate >8 mmol/L and HR >180;
35	anaerobic glycolytic endurance, 1-1.5 min, 1:3, high intensity, 8-12 reps, 1-3 series,
36	maximal lactate >8 and HR >180; aerobic power, 1-2 min, 1:(1-0.5), intermediate, 5-8 reps,
37	1-3 series, lactate 4-8 and HR 160-180; aerobic endurance, 1-8 min, 1:0.3, medium intensity,
38	4-16 reps, 1-3 series, lactate 2.5-4(5) and HR 140-160; restoration/fat oxidation, 20-90 min,
39	low intensity, 1-3 reps, HR 100-140.
40	
41	**Why it works** — Issurin states this connection directly, not just by analogy: "From the
42	viewpoint of block training, the emphasis on key-function exercises/drills is very
43	characteristic. Following the principle of training workload concentration (1.2.2) the
44	accentuation of a specially selected exercise is logical and desirable" (PDF p. 64, printed
45	p. 53). **Inference:** the further claim that this concentration "protects" the stimulus
46	from being diluted by fatigue or divided attention is this entry's own restatement of that
47	logic, not a sentence Issurin himself writes in those terms.
48	
49	**When to apply** — Programming a training cycle's hardest, most important session so it
50	actually gets the recovery state, attention, and monitoring it needs to produce the intended
51	adaptation, rather than treating every practice/lift as interchangeable. Table 2.10's
52	intervals give a concrete starting point for designing a key-exercise once the targeted
53	ability is chosen. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name an equivalent "key-workout"
54	concept explicitly, though the department's own metric-selection discipline (pick 1-2 output
55	metrics per force-plate report, per the Hawkin Dynamics ODSF framework,
56	`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring") reflects a similar
57	instinct toward concentrating monitoring attention rather than tracking everything equally.
58	
59	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin's own cautionary example (PDF p. 66, printed
60	p. 55) is that selecting the correct key-exercise is harder than it looks: at a national
61	coaching seminar of Olympic/World/Continental medalist-producing coaches, "more than 50%"
62	of proposed workouts confused exercises for maximal speed with exercises for speed endurance
63	(anaerobic glycolytic capacity), or aerobic endurance with aerobic power — i.e., experienced
64	coaches routinely mis-assign an exercise to the wrong physiological bucket. Table 2.10's
65	numeric ranges are themselves secondary citations (Fox & Mathews 1981; Viru 1995) filtered
66	through "author's modification" — the specific modification is not described, so treat the
67	exact numbers as Issurin's own adapted synthesis rather than a directly-reproduced published
68	table. This system also assumes a coach has the staff capacity for thorough, per-workout
69	objective monitoring (HR, blood lactate, video) — not always feasible outside individual/dual
70	sports with small rosters.
71	
72	**Example** — For a football skill player whose training cycle emphasizes maximal speed,
73	the key-exercise might be 6-8 reps of 7-15s maximal-intensity sprints at roughly a 1:10
74	work-rest ratio (per Table 2.10), placed early in the week's most-rested session, with
75	sprint times or GPS max-velocity data as the monitored variable — while other exercises in
76	that same session are deliberately treated as secondary, not co-equal priorities.
77	
78	**Related** — [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]],
79	[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
80	[[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]].

14	# Quantifying Workout Load on a 1-5 Scale, Mapped to Borg RPE Bands
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin presents a load-related workout classification built around three
17	functions: **development**, **retention**, and **restoration** (PDF p. 52, printed p. 41).
18	Table 2.3 (PDF p. 53, printed p. 42, based on Zatsiorsky 1995, modified by Issurin 2003)
19	quantifies this on a 1-5 scale using restoration time as the objective marker: restoration
20	level 1 (< 12 hours), retention level 2 (12-24 hours), development-substantial level 3
21	(24-48 hours), development-large level 4 (48-72 hours), development-extreme level 5
22	(> 72 hours). Because restoration-time-based classification does not fit every training type
23	well (Issurin notes coordination/neuro-emotional-stress workouts need less restoration time
24	than the scale implies), Table 2.4 (PDF p. 54, printed p. 43) offers a parallel mapping using
25	Borg's Rate of Perceived Exertion scale (Borg, 1973): RPE 6-11 (very-very-easy to
26	fairly-easy) = restoration; RPE 12-14 (slightly difficult) = retention; RPE 15-16
27	(difficult) = development-substantial; RPE 17-18 (very difficult) = development-large; RPE
28	19-20 (very-very difficult) = development-extreme.
29	
30	**Why it works — inference on the underlying logic** — Restoration time and perceived
31	exertion are both proxies for how disruptive a session was to homeostasis; using either (or
32	both together) lets a coach assign every workout a comparable numeric load value even in
33	non-measurable sports (team sports, gymnastics), which Issurin identifies as the practical
34	payoff: "the load level of each workout can be quantified and expressed numerically" (PDF
35	p. 54, printed p. 43), enabling load-dependent categorization (development vs. retention vs.
36	restoration) across an entire training plan, not just isolated hard/easy labeling.
37	
38	**When to apply** — Building a simple, athlete-reportable RPE-based load log for sports or
39	settings where objective physiological monitoring (HR, blood lactate) is not available for
40	every session; classifying a completed week of training after the fact into
41	development/retention/restoration proportions to check whether the intended block emphasis
42	(see [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]) was actually
43	delivered. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name Borg's RPE scale specifically, though
44	session-level subjective load tracking is philosophically consistent with the department's
45	general preference for practical, staff-sustainable monitoring tools over burdensome ones
46	(`method-baseline.md`, "Load monitoring and GPS," on why daily wellness surveys were
47	abandoned when athletes learned to game them) — RPE has its own well-documented gaming risk
48	that is not addressed anywhere in this Issurin chapter and should be treated as an open
49	question, not assumed solved.
50	
51	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — **The author gives no mechanism** for why these
52	specific RPE cut-points (11/12, 14/15, 16/17, 18/19) map to these specific restoration-time
53	bands rather than some other set of cut-points; both tables are presented as ready-made
54	scales without a validation study cited in this chapter. RPE is a subjective, athlete-reported
55	measure and is vulnerable to the same reporting-fatigue and gaming dynamics documented
56	elsewhere for subjective wellness tools; do not treat it as equivalent in reliability to the
57	objective HR/blood-lactate markers used in Table 2.10's key-exercise prescriptions
58	(see [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]]). The scale also does not
59	distinguish RPE driven by physical load from RPE driven by psychological/technical/cognitive
60	demand (e.g., a technically difficult but physically light session), a limitation Issurin
61	himself flags when noting coordination-heavy sessions need less restoration than their
62	subjective difficulty might imply.
63	
64	**Example** — A coach without force-plate or HR-monitor access for every practice can have
65	players self-report session RPE, multiply by session duration (an approach not itself stated
66	in this chapter but a standard extension of Borg RPE elsewhere in sport science, noted here
67	as an inference, not something Issurin describes), and classify the week's development
68	vs. retention vs. restoration balance against the intended training-stage emphasis.
69	
70	**Related** — [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]],
71	[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]].
72

14	# Squat-First vs. Squat-After-Hang-Pull Changes Whether You Get More Reps or More Power
15	
16	**What it is** — Spreuwenberg et al. (2006), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62):
17	**nine** resistance-trained male athletes performed the back squat (4 sets at 85% of 1RM) on
18	two separate days under two protocols. Protocol A: squat performed during the initial part
19	of the workout. Protocol B: squat performed after a whole-body resistance exercise (hang
20	pull). Results: Protocol A produced significantly more repetitions per set (8.0 ± 1.9 vs.
21	5.4 ± 2.7 in Protocol B), but average power per set was *higher* in Protocol B. Issurin
22	attributes the power difference to postactivation potentiation induced by the preceding
23	whole-body power exercise.
24	
25	**Why it works** — Issurin reports only the study authors' own attribution for the power
26	finding: they "attributed this phenomenon to postactivation potentiation induced by the
27	preceding whole-body power exercise" (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62). **Inference:** the
28	companion explanation for the rep-count finding, that fresh (unfatigued) muscle sustains
29	more total repetitions at a given relative load than muscle that has just performed a
30	preceding whole-body lift, is this entry's own reasoning to account for the Protocol A
31	result; Issurin does not state that explanation for the rep-count difference in this
32	passage.
33	
34	**When to apply** — Choosing exercise order based on the specific training goal for that
35	session: Issurin's stated takeaway (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62) is that a coach wanting maximum
36	hypertrophy stimulus should place the squat early in the session (more total volume/reps),
37	while a coach targeting maximum power output should place it after appropriate whole-body
38	resistance work, to exploit postactivation potentiation. Directly usable for Baylor
39	strength-staff session design when max-effort lower-body power output (not volume) is the
40	stated goal of a given lift.
41	
42	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a small (n = 9), single published study;
43	Issurin does not report effect sizes, statistical significance values, or the specific
44	whole-body exercise's loading in this citation beyond "hang pull" — treat the direction of
45	the finding as `supported` but do not treat the exact magnitude (8.0 vs. 5.4 reps) as
46	something to replicate precisely without reading the original study. It is unclear from this
47	text whether the postactivation-potentiation effect generalizes to different athlete
48	populations (this sample was resistance-trained males), different preceding exercises, or
49	different rest intervals between the potentiating exercise and the squat.
50	
51	**Example** — A power-focused lower-body day for football linemen might sequence a
52	moderate-load hang pull or clean pull before back squats at 85% 1RM, accepting fewer total
53	squat reps in exchange for higher power output per rep on the squats that follow — a
54	hypertrophy-focused day for the same lift would instead put the squat first.
55	
56	**Related** — [[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
57	[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

14	# A Structured Warm-Up/Cool-Down Program Cut Soccer Injuries Roughly Four-Fold Over Six Months
15	
16	**What it is** — Ekstrand et al. (1983), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 58, printed p. 47,
17	Figure 2.1): **twelve** national-division soccer teams (**180 players**) were split into two
18	groups. The intervention group (six teams) used a modified program with carefully structured
19	warm-ups (ball exercises plus a stretching program) and cool-downs (jogging plus hold-relax
20	stretching), supervised by doctors and physiotherapists. The control group (six teams)
21	trained traditionally. Over a six-month follow-up, the intervention group showed "highly
22	significant superiority": a roughly **four-fold reduction in the number of injuries** and a
23	"drastic decrease" in workouts and games missed to musculoskeletal disorders. Issurin
24	separately cites supporting single-factor findings: stretching in warm-up increases lower
25	extremity range of motion in soccer players (Moller et al., 1985); active warm-up *without*
26	stretching does not affect flexibility (Zakas et al., 2006); and intense prior exercise
27	meaningfully stimulates aerobic metabolism in working muscles during subsequent strenuous
28	performance (Bangsbo et al., 2001). A related study (Moller et al., 1985, PDF p. 68, printed
29	p. 57) tracked 48 adult soccer players across three warm-up/cool-down protocols and found
30	that inserting a stretching series into the *cool-down* (not just the warm-up) produced range-
31	of-motion benefits both immediately after the session and 24 hours later, while stretching
32	only in the warm-up helped immediately but not at 24 hours.
33	
34	**Why it works** — Issurin frames warm-up and cool-down as serving three functions each:
35	metabolic adjustment, technical/coordination adjustment, and mental readiness (warm-up,
36	Table 2.6, PDF p. 60, printed p. 49); and reduction of body temperature/HR/blood pressure,
37	removal of metabolic byproducts, endocrine-system recovery, and reduced emotional tension
38	(cool-down, Table 2.11, PDF p. 69, printed p. 58). **Contested — flag directly:** Issurin's
39	cool-down rationale explicitly frames blood lactate and "other acid metabolites" as "waste
40	products" to be "removed" from the muscles (PDF p. 68-69, printed pp. 57-58), citing a
41	specific clearance kinetic (blood lactate removal after a 4-minute exhausting time trial
42	takes about 20 minutes, Juel et al., 1990). This is in tension with a modern-physiology
43	claim already captured in this library's Verkhoshansky staging
44	([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]], `proven`): lactate is
45	not a toxin causing soreness or requiring active "removal," and it clears from the blood on
46	its own within about an hour of strenuous exercise regardless of cool-down activity, with
47	current research attributing post-exercise soreness to muscle/connective-tissue microtrauma
48	rather than residual lactate. The specific clearance-time citation (20 minutes for a 4-minute
49	time trial) may still be a real kinetic fact — that is not itself disputed here — but
50	Issurin's *framing* of this as evidence that cool-down actively "removes" a harmful waste
51	product reflects the outdated "lactic acid as toxin" model the Verkhoshansky entry corrects.
52	Cite this book's clearance-time number without repeating its waste-product framing.
53	
54	**When to apply** — The Ekstrand et al. (1983) result is directly relevant to Applied
55	Performance's collaboration with Athletic Medicine on injury reduction: a structured,
56	medically-supervised warm-up/cool-down protocol is associated with a large, measured
57	reduction in soft-tissue injury incidence in a team sport, over a real six-month season, not
58	an acute lab measure. The cool-down-stretching timing finding (Moller et al., 1985) suggests
59	cool-down, not just warm-up, is where a stretching series may do more for next-day range of
60	motion.
61	
62	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is an observational, non-randomized team-level
63	comparison (teams chose or were assigned to conditions; individual randomization is not
64	described), and the intervention bundled multiple changes at once (warm-up content, cool-down
65	content, and medical/physiotherapy supervision), so the four-fold injury reduction cannot be
66	attributed to warm-up or cool-down alone — Issurin himself flags this study as "atypical
67	because it refers to the complex effects of warming-up, cooling-down and medical supervision"
68	(PDF p. 58, printed p. 47). **Contested:** stretching's effect on preventing delayed-onset
69	muscle soreness specifically is described by Issurin himself as disputed within this same
70	chapter — "supported by several studies (Hartfield, 1985) and contradicted by others (High
71	et al., 1989)" (PDF p. 70, printed p. 59) — do not cite stretching-prevents-DOMS as settled.
72

74	with a stretching series (rather than stretching only in the pre-practice warm-up) has some
75	support here for next-day range-of-motion benefit, though the causal strength of the
76	underlying Moller et al. (1985) study for injury outcomes specifically (as opposed to ROM)
77	is not established by this citation.

13	
14	# Which Training Modalities Tolerate Fatigue, and Which Need a Fresh Athlete
15	
16	**What it is** — Figure 2.3 (PDF p. 72, printed p. 60) ranks eleven training modalities by
17	how much athlete fatigue they can tolerate before the acute training effect is compromised,
18	from "well rested" through "slightly fatigued," "moderately fatigued," to "fatigued":
19	**require well-rested or only slightly fatigued athletes** — maximal speed (least
20	fatigue-tolerant of all), acquisition of new technical skills, explosive strength, maximal
21	strength (neural mechanism, e.g. 1-3RM); **tolerate up to moderate fatigue** — anaerobic
22	glycolytic power, technique perfection, aerobic power, maximal strength (hypertrophy, e.g.
23	8-10RM); **tolerate fatigue through to the end of the session (most fatigue-tolerant)** —
24	anaerobic glycolytic capacity/endurance, aerobic endurance (long duration), strength
25	endurance, flexibility. Issurin's stated reasoning (PDF pp. 71-73, printed pp. 60-62):
26	exercises needing precise excitatory neural output (max speed, explosive strength, technical
27	skill acquisition, neural-mechanism strength) are blocked by inhibitory CNS output in
28	fatigued athletes, so they belong early; anaerobic glycolytic power needs available energy
29	reserves that are depleted in fatigued athletes; hypertrophy-strength work depends on total
30	mechanical work and post-exercise recovery conditions (not the athlete's pre-exercise
31	freshness), so it can be placed later or even after an endurance session; anaerobic

# Which Training Modalities Tolerate Fatigue, and Which Need a Fresh Athlete

**What it is** — Figure 2.3 (PDF p. 72, printed p. 60) ranks eleven training modalities by
how much athlete fatigue they can tolerate before the acute training effect is compromised,
from "well rested" through "slightly fatigued," "moderately fatigued," to "fatigued":
**require well-rested or only slightly fatigued athletes** — maximal speed (least
fatigue-tolerant of all), acquisition of new technical skills, explosive strength, maximal
strength (neural mechanism, e.g. 1-3RM); **tolerate up to moderate fatigue** — anaerobic
glycolytic power, technique perfection, aerobic power, maximal strength (hypertrophy, e.g.
8-10RM); **tolerate fatigue through to the end of the session (most fatigue-tolerant)** —
anaerobic glycolytic capacity/endurance, aerobic endurance (long duration), strength
endurance, flexibility. Issurin's stated reasoning (PDF pp. 71-73, printed pp. 60-62):
exercises needing precise excitatory neural output (max speed, explosive strength, technical
skill acquisition, neural-mechanism strength) are blocked by inhibitory CNS output in
fatigued athletes, so they belong early; anaerobic glycolytic power needs available energy
reserves that are depleted in fatigued athletes; hypertrophy-strength work depends on total
mechanical work and post-exercise recovery conditions (not the athlete's pre-exercise
freshness), so it can be placed later or even after an endurance session; anaerobic
glycolytic capacity and strength/aerobic endurance work are defined by sustained effort
*despite* accumulating fatigue, so some fatigue is expected and even required for the
intended stimulus.

**Why it works** — CNS-dependent, high-precision, high-velocity qualities are limited by
inhibitory neural output and available energy stores that both degrade with fatigue,
while volume/duration-dependent qualities (hypertrophy, strength/aerobic endurance) depend
on total accumulated work or post-session recovery rather than the athlete's moment-to-moment
freshness — so sequencing exists to protect the fatigue-sensitive qualities' window, not
because "harder exercises always go first."

**When to apply** — Ordering exercises within a single practice or lift: place max-speed
work, new skill acquisition, explosive strength, and low-rep neural-strength work at the
start of a session (or after only light warm-up fatigue); place hypertrophy work, technical
perfection under fatigue, and long-duration aerobic/strength-endurance work later, when some
accumulated fatigue is acceptable or even intended. Issurin gives a worked example (PDF
p. 72, printed p. 61): an endurance athlete needing to preserve muscle mass can have a
hypertrophy-focused strength session (8-10RM) placed *after* a medium-load endurance
session, because hypertrophy's driver is total mechanical work and post-workout recovery
conditions, not pre-workout freshness — this would be the wrong sequencing choice for a
neural-strength (1-3RM) session, which does need "prime time."

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — **The author gives no primary citation for Figure 2.3
itself** — it reads as the author's own synthesized ranking rather than a reproduced,
independently-sourced scale; treat the ordinal ranking (which modality is more or less
fatigue-tolerant than its neighbor) as a reasonable but unvalidated synthesis, not a measured
result. The figure gives no guidance on *how much* fatigue is "slight" vs. "moderate" in
objective terms (RPE, HR, or specific fatigue markers), so applying it requires a coach's own
judgment call about where an athlete currently sits on that continuum. It also does not
address multi-session days directly — see [[heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability]]
for cross-session sequencing.

**Example** — A football practice combining new install (technical skill acquisition) with
conditioning: install work belongs at the start of practice when players are fresh and can
attend to technical detail; conditioning work belongs at the end, where sustained effort
under fatigue is the intended stimulus rather than a limitation.

**Related** — [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]],
[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin describes how high-performance programs structure multiple same-day
17	sessions, most commonly two-a-days but up to four (routine in training-camp practice) or
18	occasionally six (an "exception," per anecdotal coach reports, PDF p. 76, printed p. 65). For
19	a four-session aerobic-development day (Figure 2.5, PDF p. 77, printed p. 66): session 1
20	(early morning) uses small load — warm-up, alactic bouts combined with medium-intensity
21	aerobic work, addressing morning stiffness/soreness; session 2 (mid-morning, after a
22	multi-hour break) uses medium/substantial load — aerobic interval series combined with
23	technical tasks, where sprint bouts interact positively with the aerobic work; session 3
24	(early afternoon, after a one-hour break) uses medium/substantial load — concentrated aerobic
25	work; session 4 (late afternoon, after a three-hour break) uses substantial load — continuous
26	aerobic exercise and aerobic-resistance work, with an emphasized, longer cool-down given
27	accumulated fatigue. For anaerobic-development days (Figure 2.6, PDF p. 78, printed p. 67):
28	session 2 uses substantial load for anaerobic glycolytic power (fast lactate/oxygen-debt
29	accumulation); the one-hour break before session 3 allows roughly 70-80% of accumulated
30	lactate to be oxidized (Volkov, 1986), so session 3's anaerobic glycolytic capacity work
31	still starts with an already-activated glycolytic/enzymatic system; session 4 (after a
32	three-hour break, athletes arriving fatigued) targets anaerobic strength endurance,
33	deliberately sustaining progressive fatigue. For the more common two-a-day structure, Table
34	2.13 (PDF p. 79, printed p. 68) gives compatible first/second-workout pairings by dominant
35	ability: aerobic power/capacity — fartlek (10-15s sprint, 3-6min at anaerobic threshold)
36	first, aerobic interval series second; anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity — anaerobic power
37	interval series first, anaerobic capacity interval series second; maximal speed — anaerobic
38	alactic interval series first, anaerobic alactic plus explosive strength exercises second;
39	techno-tactical abilities — techno-tactical simulation/maximum speed first, match/scrimmage
40	second.
41	
42	**Why it works** — The break length between sessions determines how much of the prior
43	session's fatigue and metabolic byproduct load has cleared before the next session begins,
44	and the daily plan deliberately exploits this: shorter breaks (one hour) leave residual
45	glycolytic activation that *helps* a subsequent glycolytic-capacity session, while longer
46	breaks (three hours) still leave athletes fatigued enough that only fatigue-tolerant
47	modalities (strength endurance, continuous aerobic work) are appropriate for the day's final
48	session.
49	
50	**When to apply** — Directly applicable to football fall-camp scheduling, where two-a-day
51	sessions are standard. **Eric's baseline** names a specific priority stack for fall camp —
52	"Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands" (`method-baseline.md`,
53	"Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` pp.34, 39) — and Table 2.13's
54	maximal-speed pairing (anaerobic alactic interval series both sessions, explosive strength
55	added to the second) is a directly relevant template for structuring a two-a-day built
56	around that same alactic/aerobic priority.
57	
58	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin gives no controlled-study citation for the
59	specific figures in this section (session load levels, the four-session structure, the
60	70-80% lactate-oxidation-in-one-hour figure attributed to Volkov, 1986, is the one sourced
61	number; the rest of the daily-series structure reads as the author's own applied synthesis).
62	The four-session model is explicitly noted as less common in practice than the two-a-day.
63	**Inference:** none of this section's examples are football-specific (they are framed around
64	individual/endurance-and-power sports generally); the specific break lengths (one hour,
65	three hours) and load progressions should be treated as a template to adapt, not a
66	prescription to copy directly into a football fall-camp schedule without accounting for
67	football-specific factors (equipment, heat, practice structure, position-group differences)
68	not addressed in this chapter.
69	
70	**Example** — A fall-camp two-a-day built around the department's stated alactic/aerobic
71	priority could pair a morning session of alactic interval sprint work with an afternoon
72	session combining more alactic work and explosive strength (per Table 2.13's maximal-speed
73	row), rather than defaulting to a generic "conditioning AM, lift PM" split that does not
74	target a specific dominant ability across the two sessions.

25	
26	This review distinguishes concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block models and provides a useful conceptual vocabulary for discussing concentrated workloads and sequencing.
27	
28	## Research question
29	
30	What benefits, limitations, and sport-context boundaries are reported for two versions of block-periodized athlete preparation?
31	
32	## Population and context
33	
34	- The review emphasizes elite, subelite, and well-trained athletes across endurance, team, combat, dual, jumping, and strength/power settings. [p. 11]
35	- It also discusses a smaller number of recreational-athlete studies.
36	- It is a training-theory review, not evidence specific to collegiate American football.
37	
38	## Study design and methods
39	
40	- Narrative review contrasting concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block-periodization models.
41	- The article summarizes prior studies in tables but does not report a systematic search, eligibility process, formal risk-of-bias appraisal, or meta-analysis.
42	- Consequently, the stated number and direction of supportive studies should be interpreted as an author-curated synthesis rather than a pooled comparative estimate.
43	
44	## Key findings
45	
46	- Concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance. [p. 6]
47	- In an elite-swimmer example, specific strength and anaerobic capacity improved but swimming performance improved in only two of three athletes. [p. 6]
48	- The author judged the concentrated-unidirectional evidence insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation. [p. 6]
49	- The review reports support from 28 studies for multi-targeted block programs, but the designs, populations, outcomes, and comparator quality varied. [p. 11]
50	- The concentrated-unidirectional model was presented as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality and as restricted when peak performance requires many interacting abilities. [p. 11]
51	
52	## Limitations and applicability
53	
54	- Non-systematic study selection and absent risk-of-bias assessment create a substantial risk of selective emphasis.
55	- Fitness improvements are not interchangeable with sport-specific performance, availability, or competitive outcomes. [p. 6]
56	- Training models were not consistently isolated from total volume, intensity, exercise choice, coaching, or athlete history.
57	- Evidence spans dissimilar sports and training levels; it does not supply validated block durations or effect estimates for collegiate American football.
58	- The strong conclusion favoring multi-targeted block periodization is the author's synthesis and should not be treated as settled comparative evidence. [p. 11]
59	
60	## Practitioner interpretation
61	
62	Use block periodization as a planning hypothesis: concentrate compatible emphases when competition structure and athlete needs justify it, while maintaining the qualities and technical exposure that cannot safely decay. Judge the plan by sport-specific performance, availability, and individual response—not by the periodization label. Compare it prospectively with the program's own prior practice where feasible.

# Issurin 2016 — Benefits and limitations of block-periodized preparation

> **Citation**
> Issurin, V. B. (2016). Benefits and limitations of block periodized training approaches to athletes' preparation: A review. *Sports Medicine, 46*(3), 329–338. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0425-5

## Why it was promoted

This review distinguishes concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block models and provides a useful conceptual vocabulary for discussing concentrated workloads and sequencing.

## Research question

What benefits, limitations, and sport-context boundaries are reported for two versions of block-periodized athlete preparation?

## Population and context

- The review emphasizes elite, subelite, and well-trained athletes across endurance, team, combat, dual, jumping, and strength/power settings. [p. 11]
- It also discusses a smaller number of recreational-athlete studies.
- It is a training-theory review, not evidence specific to collegiate American football.

## Study design and methods

- Narrative review contrasting concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block-periodization models.
- The article summarizes prior studies in tables but does not report a systematic search, eligibility process, formal risk-of-bias appraisal, or meta-analysis.
- Consequently, the stated number and direction of supportive studies should be interpreted as an author-curated synthesis rather than a pooled comparative estimate.

## Key findings

- Concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance. [p. 6]
- In an elite-swimmer example, specific strength and anaerobic capacity improved but swimming performance improved in only two of three athletes. [p. 6]
- The author judged the concentrated-unidirectional evidence insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation. [p. 6]
- The review reports support from 28 studies for multi-targeted block programs, but the designs, populations, outcomes, and comparator quality varied. [p. 11]
- The concentrated-unidirectional model was presented as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality and as restricted when peak performance requires many interacting abilities. [p. 11]

## Limitations and applicability

- Non-systematic study selection and absent risk-of-bias assessment create a substantial risk of selective emphasis.
- Fitness improvements are not interchangeable with sport-specific performance, availability, or competitive outcomes. [p. 6]
- Training models were not consistently isolated from total volume, intensity, exercise choice, coaching, or athlete history.
- Evidence spans dissimilar sports and training levels; it does not supply validated block durations or effect estimates for collegiate American football.
- The strong conclusion favoring multi-targeted block periodization is the author's synthesis and should not be treated as settled comparative evidence. [p. 11]

## Practitioner interpretation

Use block periodization as a planning hypothesis: concentrate compatible emphases when competition structure and athlete needs justify it, while maintaining the qualities and technical exposure that cannot safely decay. Judge the plan by sport-specific performance, availability, and individual response—not by the periodization label. Compare it prospectively with the program's own prior practice where feasible.

| Claim | Locator | Evidence type |
|---|---|---|
| Review scope and distinction between two models | p. 4 | narrative framing |
| Concentrated-unidirectional evidence and performance gaps | p. 6 | narrative synthesis |
| Multi-targeted evidence claim and applicability boundaries | p. 11 | narrative synthesis/limitation |

# Lactate Does Not "Poison" Muscle or Cause Soreness; "Oxygen Debt" Is an Outdated Concept

**What it is** — Two corrections to common misconceptions. (1) Muscle fatigue is not due
to "lactic acid poisoning"; lactate formation is accompanied by hydrogen ions that increase
acidity and can interfere with contraction and enzyme efficiency, but lactate itself is not
the toxin popularly described, and blood lactate returns to normal within about an hour of
strenuous interval training — well before delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) typically
peaks. The most pronounced soreness actually occurs after prolonged endurance efforts kept
below the lactate threshold, so current theory attributes soreness to transient muscle
cell or connective tissue damage, not lactic acid. (2) The classic "oxygen debt" concept
(the idea that post-exercise heavy breathing "repays" an oxygen deficit incurred during
anaerobic work) is now considered outdated; the post-exercise period instead reflects
recovery oxygen consumption used to regenerate ATP and CP and restore respiratory, ionic,
circulatory, hormonal, and thermal systems to baseline (McArdle, Katch & Katch, 1991). The
text says the former "anaerobic threshold" is now referred to as the "blood lactate
threshold (or turnpoint) or OBLA (Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation)" (printed 78). (PDF
pp. 87, 89, printed pp. 76, 78.)

**Why it works** — Both corrections reflect the same underlying update in exercise
physiology: lactate is a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not an anaerobic waste
product to be "cleared" or "repaid," and glycolysis runs alongside oxidative metabolism
rather than only replacing it when oxygen is absent (also noted in this book: glycolysis
dominates during sprinting even though muscles have adequate oxygen).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for correcting persistent coaching-room and
classroom misconceptions (e.g. in HHPR 5355 teaching) — "lactic acid causes the burn and
next-day soreness" and "you're paying back oxygen debt after a sprint" are both outdated
framings that this entry can directly correct with citable sources.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** correcting the mechanism does not mean lactate is
irrelevant to training; the blood lactate threshold (OBLA) remains a legitimate, useful
marker for endurance training intensity and athlete conditioning status — only the
"lactic acid as toxin/soreness cause" framing and the "oxygen debt" framing are being
corrected here, not the practical value of lactate-threshold-based training zones.
Inference: the H+/acidosis fatigue mechanism the authors give here (increased acidity
"can interfere with the muscle contraction process") is itself contested in modern work
(Westerblad, Allen & Lannergren 2002, News Physiol Sci 17:17; Allen, Lamb & Westerblad
2008, Physiol Rev 88:287); `proven` here covers only the two named corrections (lactate is
not the cause of DOMS; oxygen debt is replaced by recovery oxygen consumption and EPOC),
not the H+/acidosis fatigue mechanism.

**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete sore two days after a hard endurance session is
more likely dealing with muscle/connective tissue microtrauma than residual lactate, which
would have cleared within an hour; recovery guidance should be based on that, not on
"flushing out lactic acid."

**Related** — [[claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table]].
