content.text: Now I'll begin applying fixes. Starting with the sequencing heuristic (review priority 1).

input.old_string:
**What it is** — Figure 2.3 (PDF p. 72, printed p. 60) ranks eleven training modalities by
how much athlete fatigue they can tolerate before the acute training effect is compromised,
from "well rested" through "slightly fatigued," "moderately fatigued," to "fatigued":
**require well-rested or only slightly fatigued athletes** — maximal speed (least
fatigue-tolerant of all), acquisition of new technical skills, explosive strength, maximal
strength (neural mechanism, e.g. 1-3RM); **tolerate up to moderate fatigue** — anaerobic
glycolytic power, technique perfection, aerobic power, maximal strength (hypertrophy, e.g.
8-10RM); **tolerate fatigue through to the end of the session (most fatigue-tolerant)** —
anaerobic glycolytic capacity/endurance, aerobic endurance (long duration), strength
endurance, flexibility. Issurin's stated reasoning (PDF pp. 71-73, printed pp. 60-62):
exercises needing precise excitatory neural output (max speed, explosive strength, technical
skill acquisition, neural-mechanism strength) are blocked by inhibitory CNS output in
fatigued athletes, so they belong early; anaerobic glycolytic power needs available energy
reserves that are depleted in fatigued athletes; hypertrophy-strength work depends on total
mechanical work and post-exercise recovery conditions (not the athlete's pre-exercise
freshness), so it can be placed later or even after an endurance session; anaerobic
glycolytic capacity and strength/aerobic endurance work are defined by sustained effort
*despite* accumulating fatigue, so some fatigue is expected and even required for the
intended stimulus.

**Why it works** — CNS-dependent, high-precision, high-velocity qualities are limited by
inhibitory neural output and available energy stores that both degrade with fatigue,
while volume/duration-dependent qualities (hypertrophy, strength/aerobic endurance) depend
on total accumulated work or post-session recovery rather than the athlete's moment-to-moment
freshness — so sequencing exists to protect the fatigue-sensitive qualities' window, not
because "harder exercises always go first."

# Which Training Modalities Tolerate Fatigue, and Which Need a Fresh Athlete

**What it is** — Figure 2.3 (PDF p. 72, printed p. 60) ranks eleven training modalities by
how much athlete fatigue they can tolerate before the acute training effect is compromised,
from "well rested" through "slightly fatigued," "moderately fatigued," to "fatigued":
**require well-rested or only slightly fatigued athletes** — maximal speed (least
fatigue-tolerant of all), acquisition of new technical skills, explosive strength, maximal
strength (neural mechanism, e.g. 1-3RM); **tolerate up to moderate fatigue** — anaerobic
glycolytic power, technique perfection, aerobic power, maximal strength (hypertrophy, e.g.
8-10RM); **tolerate fatigue through to the end of the session (most fatigue-tolerant)** —
anaerobic glycolytic capacity/endurance, aerobic endurance (long duration), strength
endurance, flexibility. Issurin's stated reasoning (PDF pp. 71-73, printed pp. 60-62):
exercises needing precise excitatory neural output (max speed, explosive strength, technical
skill acquisition, neural-mechanism strength) are blocked by inhibitory CNS output in
fatigued athletes, so they belong early; anaerobic glycolytic power needs available energy
reserves that are depleted in fatigued athletes; hypertrophy-strength work depends on total
mechanical work and post-exercise recovery conditions (not the athlete's pre-exercise
freshness), so it can be placed later or even after an endurance session; anaerobic
glycolytic capacity and strength/aerobic endurance work are defined by sustained effort
*despite* accumulating fatigue, so some fatigue is expected and even required for the
intended stimulus.

**Why it works** — CNS-dependent, high-precision, high-velocity qualities are limited by
inhibitory neural output and available energy stores that both degrade with fatigue,
while volume/duration-dependent qualities (hypertrophy, strength/aerobic endurance) depend
on total accumulated work or post-session recovery rather than the athlete's moment-to-moment
freshness — so sequencing exists to protect the fatigue-sensitive qualities' window, not
because "harder exercises always go first."

**When to apply** — Ordering exercises within a single practice or lift: place max-speed
work, new skill acquisition, explosive strength, and low-rep neural-strength work at the
start of a session (or after only light warm-up fatigue); place hypertrophy work, technical
perfection under fatigue, and long-duration aerobic/strength-endurance work later, when some
accumulated fatigue is acceptable or even intended. Issurin gives a worked example (PDF
p. 72, printed p. 61): an endurance athlete needing to preserve muscle mass can have a
hypertrophy-focused strength session (8-10RM) placed *after* a medium-load endurance
session, because hypertrophy's driver is total mechanical work and post-workout recovery
conditions, not pre-workout freshness — this would be the wrong sequencing choice for a
neural-strength (1-3RM) session, which does need "prime time."

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — **The author gives no primary citation for Figure 2.3
itself** — it reads as the author's own synthesized ranking rather than a reproduced,
independently-sourced scale; treat the ordinal ranking (which modality is more or less
fatigue-tolerant than its neighbor) as a reasonable but unvalidated synthesis, not a measured
result. The figure gives no guidance on *how much* fatigue is "slight" vs. "moderate" in
objective terms (RPE, HR, or specific fatigue markers), so applying it requires a coach's own
judgment call about where an athlete currently sits on that continuum. It also does not
address multi-session days directly — see [[heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability]]
for cross-session sequencing.

**Example** — A football practice combining new install (technical skill acquisition) with
conditioning: install work belongs at the start of practice when players are fresh and can
attend to technical detail; conditioning work belongs at the end, where sustained effort
under fatigue is the intended stimulus rather than a limitation.

**Related** — [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]],
[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

# Structuring Two-a-Day (and Denser) Training Days by Dominant Ability and Rest Interval

**What it is** — Issurin describes how high-performance programs structure multiple same-day
sessions, most commonly two-a-days but up to four (routine in training-camp practice) or
occasionally six (an "exception," per anecdotal coach reports, PDF p. 76, printed p. 65). For
a four-session aerobic-development day (Figure 2.5, PDF p. 77, printed p. 66): session 1
(early morning) uses small load — warm-up, alactic bouts combined with medium-intensity
aerobic work, addressing morning stiffness/soreness; session 2 (mid-morning, after a
multi-hour break) uses medium/substantial load — aerobic interval series combined with
technical tasks, where sprint bouts interact positively with the aerobic work; session 3
(early afternoon, after a one-hour break) uses medium/substantial load — concentrated aerobic
work; session 4 (late afternoon, after a three-hour break) uses substantial load — continuous
aerobic exercise and aerobic-resistance work, with an emphasized, longer cool-down given
accumulated fatigue. For anaerobic-development days (Figure 2.6, PDF p. 78, printed p. 67):
session 2 uses substantial load for anaerobic glycolytic power (fast lactate/oxygen-debt
accumulation); the one-hour break before session 3 allows roughly 70-80% of accumulated
lactate to be oxidized (Volkov, 1986), so session 3's anaerobic glycolytic capacity work
still starts with an already-activated glycolytic/enzymatic system; session 4 (after a
three-hour break, athletes arriving fatigued) targets anaerobic strength endurance,
deliberately sustaining progressive fatigue. For the more common two-a-day structure, Table
2.13 (PDF p. 79, printed p. 68) gives compatible first/second-workout pairings by dominant
ability: aerobic power/capacity — fartlek (10-15s sprint, 3-6min at anaerobic threshold)
first, aerobic interval series second; anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity — anaerobic power
interval series first, anaerobic capacity interval series second; maximal speed — anaerobic
alactic interval series first, anaerobic alactic plus explosive strength exercises second;
techno-tactical abilities — techno-tactical simulation/maximum speed first, match/scrimmage
second.

**Why it works** — The break length between sessions determines how much of the prior
session's fatigue and metabolic byproduct load has cleared before the next session begins,
and the daily plan deliberately exploits this: shorter breaks (one hour) leave residual
glycolytic activation that *helps* a subsequent glycolytic-capacity session, while longer
breaks (three hours) still leave athletes fatigued enough that only fatigue-tolerant
modalities (strength endurance, continuous aerobic work) are appropriate for the day's final
session.

**When to apply** — Directly applicable to football fall-camp scheduling, where two-a-day
sessions are standard. **Eric's baseline** names a specific priority stack for fall camp —
"Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` pp.34, 39) — and Table 2.13's
maximal-speed pairing (anaerobic alactic interval series both sessions, explosive strength
added to the second) is a directly relevant template for structuring a two-a-day built
around that same alactic/aerobic priority.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin gives no controlled-study citation for the
specific figures in this section (session load levels, the four-session structure, the
70-80% lactate-oxidation-in-one-hour figure attributed to Volkov, 1986, is the one sourced
number; the rest of the daily-series structure reads as the author's own applied synthesis).
The four-session model is explicitly noted as less common in practice than the two-a-day.
**Inference:** none of this section's examples are football-specific (they are framed around
individual/endurance-and-power sports generally); the specific break lengths (one hour,
three hours) and load progressions should be treated as a template to adapt, not a
prescription to copy directly into a football fall-camp schedule without accounting for
football-specific factors (equipment, heat, practice structure, position-group differences)
not addressed in this chapter.

**Example** — A fall-camp two-a-day built around the department's stated alactic/aerobic
priority could pair a morning session of alactic interval sprint work with an afternoon
session combining more alactic work and explosive strength (per Table 2.13's maximal-speed
row), rather than defaulting to a generic "conditioning AM, lift PM" split that does not
target a specific dominant ability across the two sessions.

**Related** — [[claim--morning-resistance-training-no-decrement-after-6hr-rest]],
[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

sessions. Two- and three-workout days are routine in camp practice; four, five, and even six
daily workouts are reported anecdotally by prominent coaches, with six an exception (PDF p.
76, printed p. 65). For a four-session aerobic-development day (Figure 2.5, PDF p. 77,
printed p. 66): **session 1** (6:40-7:20 AM, small load) is warm-up, calisthenics,
stretching, and sport-specific technical elements; **session 2** (10:20-11:30 AM, medium or
substantial load, after a multi-hour break) is anaerobic alactic bouts combined with
aerobic medium-intensity exercises; **session 3** (12:30-13:30 PM, medium or substantial
load, after a one-hour break) is aerobic interval series combined with technical tasks, with
velocity-resisted regimes allowed; **session 4** (16:40-18:10 PM, substantial load, after a
three-hour break) is aerobic continuous exercising, strength-endurance aerobic exercises, and
stretching/relaxation, with an emphasized, longer cool-down given accumulated fatigue. For
anaerobic-development days (Figure 2.6, PDF p. 78, printed p. 67): session 2 is substantial
load for anaerobic glycolytic power (fast lactate/oxygen-debt accumulation); the one-hour
break before session 3 allows roughly 70-80% of accumulated lactate to be oxidized (Volkov,
1986), so session 3's anaerobic glycolytic capacity work still starts with an
already-activated glycolytic/enzymatic system; session 4 (after a three-hour break, athletes
arriving fatigued) targets anaerobic strength endurance, deliberately sustaining progressive
fatigue. **Source inconsistency:** the body text calls session 2 "highly intense aerobic
power exercises," but the Figure 2.6 box for that same session reads "anaerobic glycolitic
power series" (PDF p. 78, printed p. 67); this entry follows the figure's label, since that
is where the load level and content are specified. For the more common two-a-day structure, Table
2.13 (PDF p. 79, printed p. 68) gives compatible first/second-workout pairings by dominant
ability: aerobic power/capacity — fartlek (10-15s sprint, 3-6min at anaerobic threshold)
first, aerobic interval series second; anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity — anaerobic power
interval series first, anaerobic capacity interval series second; maximal speed — anaerobic
alactic interval series first, anaerobic alactic plus explosive strength exercises second;
techno-tactical abilities — techno-tactical simulation/maximum speed first, match/scrimmage
second.

**Why it works** — The break length between sessions determines how much of the prior
session's fatigue and metabolic byproduct load has cleared before the next session begins,
and the daily plan deliberately exploits this: shorter breaks (one hour) leave residual
glycolytic activation that *helps* a subsequent glycolytic-capacity session, while longer
breaks (three hours) still leave athletes fatigued enough that only fatigue-tolerant
modalities (strength endurance, continuous aerobic work) are appropriate for the day's final
session.

**When to apply** — Directly applicable to football fall-camp scheduling, where two-a-day
sessions are standard. **Eric's baseline** names a specific priority stack for fall camp —
"Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` pp.34, 39) — and Table 2.13's
maximal-speed pairing (anaerobic alactic interval series both sessions, explosive strength
added to the second) is a directly relevant template for structuring a two-a-day built
around that same alactic/aerobic priority.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin gives no controlled-study citation for the
specific figures in this section (session load levels, the four-session structure, the
70-80% lactate-oxidation-in-one-hour figure attributed to Volkov, 1986, is the one sourced
number; the rest of the daily-series structure reads as the author's own applied synthesis).
The four-session model is explicitly noted as less common in practice than the two-a-day.
**Inference:** none of this section's examples are football-specific (they are framed around
individual/endurance-and-power sports generally); the specific break lengths (one hour,
three hours) and load progressions should be treated as a template to adapt, not a
prescription to copy directly into a football fall-camp schedule without accounting for
football-specific factors (equipment, heat, practice structure, position-group differences)
not addressed in this chapter.

**Example** — A fall-camp two-a-day built around the department's stated alactic/aerobic
priority could pair a morning session of alactic interval sprint work with an afternoon
session combining more alactic work and explosive strength (per Table 2.13's maximal-speed
row), rather than defaulting to a generic "conditioning AM, lift PM" split that does not
target a specific dominant ability across the two sessions.

**Related** — [[claim--morning-resistance-training-no-decrement-after-6hr-rest]],
[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. The stated physiological basis: aerobic endurance's
long residual rests on morphological/biochemical changes (aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
capillaries, hemoglobin, glycogen storage) that increase 40-90% with training; maximum
strength's residual rests on comparably substantial morphological, biochemical and neural
changes (fiber cross-section, hyperplasia, motor-unit recruitment/synchronization,
motor-neuron discharge frequency, citing Zatsiorsky, 1995); maximum speed's short residual
reflects much smaller adaptations (phosphocreatine +2-5%, peak lactate +10-20%, anaerobic
enzymes +2-20%, citing Thorstensson, 1988) riding on delicate, unstable neuromuscular
patterns that decay quickly without continued training.

**Why it works — Inference** — Larger, more structural adaptations (aerobic
enzymatic/capillary changes, strength's neural and hypertrophic changes) persist longer
because the underlying tissue/enzyme changes take longer to reverse than the smaller,
more neurally-dependent changes behind peak speed. The author does not present this as an
experimentally isolated causal mechanism within this book — it is a physiological
rationale offered alongside the cited numbers, not derived from a controlled decay study
run on the same subjects who produced the durations.

**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. Table 1.6's own physiological-background column
lists aerobic endurance's residual as resting on increased aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
muscle capillaries, hemoglobin capacity, glycogen storage, and fat-metabolism rate, and
maximum strength's on improved neural mechanism and muscle hypertrophy from fiber
enlargement, with no percentages attached in the table itself. Later in the text (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), Issurin gives a specific figure for one of those table items: aerobic
enzymes increase by 40-90% with training (Volkov, 1986; Fox et al., 1993; Wilmore & Costill,
1993). He contrasts this with much smaller local adaptations from sprint training:
phosphocreatine storage (+2-5%), peak lactate accumulation (+10-20%), and anaerobic enzymes
(+2-20%), given without a citation on that page. On the following page (PDF p. 36, printed
p. 25), Thorstensson (1988) is cited specifically for "relatively small increases" in
quickly available energy sources, ATP and phosphocreatine, and enzymes such as creatine
kinase, from highly concentrated sprint training.

**Why it works** — Issurin states the mechanism directly (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp. 24-25):
aerobic ability, supported by pronounced morphological and biochemical changes, is retained
"for a number of weeks at near-peak level," while anaerobic abilities, particularly maximum
sprint speed, "retain near-peak levels for much shorter periods" because peak speed's gains
are smaller and rest on "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions, which
are relatively unstable and cannot be maintained at the highest level without specially
organized training." Maximum strength's comparably long residual is attributed to pronounced
morphological, biochemical, and neural changes: enlargement of muscle-fiber cross-sectional
area, hyperplasia, recruitment of previously inactive motor units, synchronization of their
activity, and increased motor-neuron discharge frequency (Zatsiorsky, 1995). Strength
endurance's residual is stated to depend on event duration and the degree of
anaerobic-resource mobilization; longer-duration strength endurance has a relatively longer
residual thanks to aerobic adaptation.

# Residual Training Effects Last Different Numbers of Days for Different Motor Abilities

**What it is** — The residual training effect is defined as "the retention of changes
induced by systematic workloads beyond a certain time period after the cessation of
training," a term Issurin attributes to Brian and James Counsilman (1991) (PDF p. 33,
printed p. 22). Issurin & Lustig (2004) is cited as the source of Table 1.6 (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), giving residual duration ± SD in days after cessation of training for each
motor ability: **aerobic endurance 30 ± 5 days**, **maximum strength 30 ± 5 days**,
**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. The stated physiological basis: aerobic endurance's
long residual rests on morphological/biochemical changes (aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
capillaries, hemoglobin, glycogen storage) that increase 40-90% with training; maximum
strength's residual rests on comparably substantial morphological, biochemical and neural
changes (fiber cross-section, hyperplasia, motor-unit recruitment/synchronization,
motor-neuron discharge frequency, citing Zatsiorsky, 1995); maximum speed's short residual
reflects much smaller adaptations (phosphocreatine +2-5%, peak lactate +10-20%, anaerobic
enzymes +2-20%, citing Thorstensson, 1988) riding on delicate, unstable neuromuscular
patterns that decay quickly without continued training.

**Why it works — Inference** — Larger, more structural adaptations (aerobic
enzymatic/capillary changes, strength's neural and hypertrophic changes) persist longer
because the underlying tissue/enzyme changes take longer to reverse than the smaller,
more neurally-dependent changes behind peak speed. The author does not present this as an
experimentally isolated causal mechanism within this book — it is a physiological
rationale offered alongside the cited numbers, not derived from a controlled decay study
run on the same subjects who produced the durations.

**When to apply** — Sequencing which ability to develop first in a training stage (see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]): an ability with a long
residual (aerobic endurance, max strength) can be built early in accumulation and largely
coast through transmutation/realization without a maintenance dose, while an ability with a
short residual (max speed) needs re-exposure close to competition or its gain will be lost
before it is used. **Eric's baseline directly echoes half of this table:** "Training
residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need
re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue
readiness for max-velocity work degrades" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` p.27) — this 30/30/5-day
pattern matches Issurin's 30±5 / 30±5 / 5±3 figures closely enough that it is very likely
this table (or a source repeating it) is the origin of that course-material claim, though
neither source cites the other directly, so this should be confirmed with Eric rather than
asserted as fact.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Treat the numbers as a synthesized rule of thumb
(±5, ±4, ±5, ±3 day spreads are themselves wide relative to the means), not a precise
per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig
(2004) in this text, so the table's evidentiary base cannot be checked further from this
source alone. **Contested — flag this directly to Eric:** a *different* part of the same
baseline corpus states the opposite ordering for detraining rate: "The traits easiest to
build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build
(alactic/speed) are lost slowest" (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems,"
citing `class-4-2026.md` p.47). This flatly contradicts both this table (aerobic residual
is the *longest*, tied with strength, at 30±5 days, while alactic speed is the *shortest*
at 5±3 days) and the baseline's own class-1-transcript-sourced claim quoted above. Do not

# Residual Training Effects Last Different Numbers of Days for Different Motor Abilities

**What it is** — The residual training effect is defined as "the retention of changes
induced by systematic workloads beyond a certain time period after the cessation of
training," a term Issurin attributes to Brian and James Counsilman (1991) (PDF p. 33,
printed p. 22). Issurin & Lustig (2004) is cited as the source of Table 1.6 (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), giving residual duration ± SD in days after cessation of training for each
motor ability: **aerobic endurance 30 ± 5 days**, **maximum strength 30 ± 5 days**,
**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. Table 1.6's own physiological-background column
lists aerobic endurance's residual as resting on increased aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
muscle capillaries, hemoglobin capacity, glycogen storage, and fat-metabolism rate, and
maximum strength's on improved neural mechanism and muscle hypertrophy from fiber
enlargement, with no percentages attached in the table itself. Later in the text (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), Issurin gives a specific figure for one of those table items: aerobic
enzymes increase by 40-90% with training (Volkov, 1986; Fox et al., 1993; Wilmore & Costill,
1993). He contrasts this with much smaller local adaptations from sprint training:
phosphocreatine storage (+2-5%), peak lactate accumulation (+10-20%), and anaerobic enzymes
(+2-20%), given without a citation on that page. On the following page (PDF p. 36, printed
p. 25), Thorstensson (1988) is cited specifically for "relatively small increases" in
quickly available energy sources, ATP and phosphocreatine, and enzymes such as creatine
kinase, from highly concentrated sprint training.

**Why it works** — Issurin states the mechanism directly (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp. 24-25):
aerobic ability, supported by pronounced morphological and biochemical changes, is retained
"for a number of weeks at near-peak level," while anaerobic abilities, particularly maximum
sprint speed, "retain near-peak levels for much shorter periods" because peak speed's gains
are smaller and rest on "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions, which
are relatively unstable and cannot be maintained at the highest level without specially
organized training." Maximum strength's comparably long residual is attributed to pronounced
morphological, biochemical, and neural changes: enlargement of muscle-fiber cross-sectional
area, hyperplasia, recruitment of previously inactive motor units, synchronization of their
activity, and increased motor-neuron discharge frequency (Zatsiorsky, 1995). Strength
endurance's residual is stated to depend on event duration and the degree of
anaerobic-resource mobilization; longer-duration strength endurance has a relatively longer
residual thanks to aerobic adaptation.

**When to apply** — Sequencing which ability to develop first in a training stage (see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]): an ability with a long
residual (aerobic endurance, max strength) can be built early in accumulation and largely
coast through transmutation/realization without a maintenance dose, while an ability with a
short residual (max speed) needs re-exposure close to competition or its gain will be lost
before it is used. **Eric's baseline directly echoes half of this table:** "Training
residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need
re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue
readiness for max-velocity work degrades" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` p.27) — this 30/30/5-day
pattern matches Issurin's 30±5 / 30±5 / 5±3 figures because it is this table:
week1-lecture.md (marker p.66) reproduces Table 1.6 directly, under a slide block that names
"Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source (marker p.64), and gives strength endurance as
~12 days against Issurin's 15±5, the one value where the course departs from the book.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Treat the numbers as a synthesized rule of thumb
(±5, ±4, ±5, ±3 day spreads are themselves wide relative to the means), not a precise
per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig
(2004) in this text, so the table's evidentiary base cannot be checked further from this
source alone. Issurin's own surrounding text also notes limits on how far residual-effect
thinking travels: maximum oxygen uptake in highly trained endurance athletes falls when
weekly training volume drops below a certain level (Steinacker, 1993; Steinacker et al.,
1998), and large volumes of highly intense exercise do not prevent detraining and loss of
aerobic endurance during a taper (Mujika, 1999) (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23).

**Contested, flag this directly to Eric:** a *different* part of the same baseline corpus
states the opposite ordering for detraining rate: "the traits easiest to build (aerobic) are
lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` p.47).
This conflicts with Table 1.6 (aerobic residual is the *longest*, tied with strength, at
30±5 days, while alactic speed is the *shortest* at 5±3 days). The class-1 transcript is
not a third, independent data point against class-4-2026.md: it also states that aerobic
capacity is gained and lost very quickly (marker pp.25, 28), gives its 30-day retention
windows as conditional on "a small retention load" continuing during that window (marker
p.28), a different construct from Issurin's residual *after cessation* of training, and
ties its 5-day speed figure to connective-tissue and nervous-system readiness ("otherwise
the nervous system doesn't change a whole lot," marker p.28) rather than to speed itself
decaying in 5 days. The course's own numbers come directly from this table (week1-lecture.md
marker pp.64, 66, strength endurance given there as ~12 days against Issurin's 15±5). Resolve
with Eric: this may be residual effect after cessation (Issurin, Table 1.6) versus rate of
loss without any retention dose (class-4-2026.md), two different constructs the corpus does
not itself reconcile. Do not harmonize these; record all three with their locators and keep
`contested`, with this as the stated reason.

**Inference:** this table also converges with, but is not identical to, the vault's
Verkhoshansky-staging entry on heterochronic adaptation
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]],
staging), which describes a *different* mechanism (order of biochemical sub-processes
gained/lost) rather than absolute day-counts per motor ability — both describe
heterochronicity in de-training, but at different levels of description; do not treat them
as restating the same specific claim.

**Example** — In a training stage that opens with 4 weeks of accumulation (building
aerobic base and max strength) followed by 3 weeks of transmutation and 2 weeks of
realization, the aerobic and strength gains from accumulation are still within their ~30-day
residual window when realization begins, so they need no further direct stimulus — but if
maximum speed work is not re-introduced within about 5 days of the target competition, its
residual will have already decayed below peak by competition day.

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],

fatigue-vs-fitness decay, distinct from this table's absolute per-ability day counts —
cross-reference, do not conflate),

stretching (Zakas et al., 2006); and intense prior exercise
meaningfully stimulates aerobic metabolism in working muscles during subsequent strenuous
performance (Bangsbo et al., 2001). A related study (Moller et al., 1985, PDF p. 68, printed
p. 57) tracked 48 adult soccer players across three warm-up/cool-down protocols and found
that inserting a stretching series into the *cool-down* (not just the warm-up) produced range-
of-motion benefits both immediately after the session and 24 hours later, while stretching
only in the warm-up helped immediately but not at 24 hours.

**Why it works** — Issurin frames warm-up and cool-down as serving three functions each:
metabolic adjustment, technical/coordination adjustment, and mental readiness (warm-up,
Table 2.6, PDF p. 60, printed p. 49); and reduction of body temperature/HR/blood pressure,
removal of metabolic byproducts, endocrine-system recovery, and reduced emotional tension
(cool-down, Table 2.11, PDF p. 69, printed p. 58). **Contested — flag directly:** Issurin's
cool-down rationale explicitly frames blood lactate and "other acid metabolites" as "waste
products" to be "removed" from the muscles (PDF p. 68-69, printed pp. 57-58), citing a
specific clearance kinetic (blood lactate removal after a 4-minute exhausting time trial
takes about 20 minutes, Juel et al., 1990). This is in tension with a modern-physiology
claim already captured in this library's Verkhoshansky staging
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]], `proven`): lactate is
not a toxin causing soreness or requiring active "removal," and it clears from the blood on
its own within about an hour of strenuous exercise regardless of cool-down activity, with
current research attributing post-exercise soreness to muscle/connective-tissue microtrauma
rather than residual lactate. The specific clearance-time citation (20 minutes for a 4-minute
time trial) may still be a real kinetic fact — that is not itself disputed here — but
Issurin's *framing* of this as evidence that cool-down actively "removes" a harmful waste
product reflects the outdated "lactic acid as toxin" model the Verkhoshansky entry corrects.
Cite this book's clearance-time number without repeating its waste-product framing.
input.new_string:
stretching (Zakas et al., 2006); and intense prior exercise
meaningfully stimulates aerobic metabolism in working muscles during subsequent strenuous
performance (Bangsbo et al., 2001). A related study (Moller et al., 1985, PDF p. 68, printed
p. 57) tracked 48 adult soccer players across three warm-up/cool-down protocols. The regular
soccer workout (no stretching) caused a significant decrease in all range-of-motion (ROM)
indices. A similar workout with a stretching series in the *warm-up* produced more favorable
ROM responses immediately after the session, with 24-hour ROM not reported for that arm. The
third version, with the stretching series inserted in the *cool-down*, produced significant
ROM benefits both immediately after the workout and 24 hours later.

**Why it works** — Issurin gives warm-up three stated functions: metabolic adjustment,
technical/coordination adjustment, and attainment of mental readiness (Table 2.6, PDF p. 60,
printed p. 49). Cool-down gets four stated objectives, given in prose rather than a table:
reduce body temperature, heart rate, and blood pressure to resting levels; remove acid
metabolites and other waste products from the muscles to the circulatory system for further
clearance; facilitate recovery of the endocrine system; and reduce emotional tension and
support positive mental recovery (PDF p. 67, printed p. 56).

**Contested, terminology only:** Issurin's cool-down rationale frames blood lactate and
"other acid metabolites" as "waste products" to be "removed" from the muscles (PDF pp.
67-69, printed pp. 56-58), and separately states that slow locomotion "causes faster lactate
removal" (Bonen & Belcastro, 1976, PDF p. 68, printed p. 57), with blood lactate removal
after a 4-minute exhausting time trial taking about 20 minutes of restoration (Juel et al.,
1990, PDF p. 70, printed p. 59). The vault's Verkhoshansky staging entry
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]], `proven`) treats
lactate as a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not a toxin, and states that blood
lactate returns to normal within about an hour of strenuous interval training; its `proven`
rating is scoped to two corrections, that lactate is not the cause of DOMS and that "oxygen
debt" is better described as recovery oxygen consumption. That entry does not say clearance
happens "regardless of cool-down activity"; that claim belongs to neither source and should
not be attributed to either. The two books' clearance-time figures are consistent with each
other (about 20 minutes after a 4-minute trial vs. within about an hour of a strenuous
interval session), and neither source ties lactate to DOMS: Issurin attributes DOMS to
strong eccentric ("plyometric") work instead (PDF pp. 69-70, printed pp. 58-59). The real
disagreement is terminology, Issurin's "acid metabolites and other waste products" (PDF p.
67, printed p. 56) against the Verkhoshansky entry's "normal byproduct and fuel." Keep this
book's clearance-time number and its active-recovery claim (slow locomotion speeds lactate
removal); do not repeat "waste product" as physiology, and do not attribute a "toxin" claim
or a "regardless of cool-down activity" claim to Issurin, since he states neither.

# A Structured Warm-Up/Cool-Down Program Cut Soccer Injuries Roughly Four-Fold Over Six Months

**What it is** — Ekstrand et al. (1983), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 58, printed p. 47,
Figure 2.1): **twelve** national-division soccer teams (**180 players**) were split into two
groups. The intervention group (six teams) used a modified program with carefully structured
warm-ups (ball exercises plus a stretching program) and cool-downs (jogging plus hold-relax
stretching), supervised by doctors and physiotherapists. The control group (six teams)
trained traditionally. Over a six-month follow-up, the intervention group showed "highly
significant superiority": a roughly **four-fold reduction in the number of injuries** and a
"drastic decrease" in workouts and games missed to musculoskeletal disorders. Issurin
separately cites supporting single-factor findings: stretching in warm-up increases lower
extremity range of motion in soccer players (Moller et al., 1985); active warm-up *without*
stretching does not affect flexibility (Zakas et al., 2006); and intense prior exercise
meaningfully stimulates aerobic metabolism in working muscles during subsequent strenuous
performance (Bangsbo et al., 2001). A related study (Moller et al., 1985, PDF p. 68, printed
p. 57) tracked 48 adult soccer players across three warm-up/cool-down protocols and found
that inserting a stretching series into the *cool-down* (not just the warm-up) produced range-
of-motion benefits both immediately after the session and 24 hours later, while stretching
only in the warm-up helped immediately but not at 24 hours.

**Why it works** — Issurin frames warm-up and cool-down as serving three functions each:
metabolic adjustment, technical/coordination adjustment, and mental readiness (warm-up,
Table 2.6, PDF p. 60, printed p. 49); and reduction of body temperature/HR/blood pressure,
removal of metabolic byproducts, endocrine-system recovery, and reduced emotional tension
(cool-down, Table 2.11, PDF p. 69, printed p. 58). **Contested — flag directly:** Issurin's
cool-down rationale explicitly frames blood lactate and "other acid metabolites" as "waste
products" to be "removed" from the muscles (PDF p. 68-69, printed pp. 57-58), citing a
specific clearance kinetic (blood lactate removal after a 4-minute exhausting time trial
takes about 20 minutes, Juel et al., 1990). This is in tension with a modern-physiology
claim already captured in this library's Verkhoshansky staging
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]], `proven`): lactate is
not a toxin causing soreness or requiring active "removal," and it clears from the blood on
its own within about an hour of strenuous exercise regardless of cool-down activity, with
current research attributing post-exercise soreness to muscle/connective-tissue microtrauma
rather than residual lactate. The specific clearance-time citation (20 minutes for a 4-minute
time trial) may still be a real kinetic fact — that is not itself disputed here — but
Issurin's *framing* of this as evidence that cool-down actively "removes" a harmful waste
product reflects the outdated "lactic acid as toxin" model the Verkhoshansky entry corrects.
Cite this book's clearance-time number without repeating its waste-product framing.

**When to apply** — The Ekstrand et al. (1983) result is directly relevant to Applied
Performance's collaboration with Athletic Medicine on injury reduction: a structured,
medically-supervised warm-up/cool-down protocol is associated with a large, measured
reduction in soft-tissue injury incidence in a team sport, over a real six-month season, not
an acute lab measure. The cool-down-stretching timing finding (Moller et al., 1985) suggests
cool-down, not just warm-up, is where a stretching series may do more for next-day range of
motion.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is an observational, non-randomized team-level
comparison (teams chose or were assigned to conditions; individual randomization is not
described), and the intervention bundled multiple changes at once (warm-up content, cool-down
content, and medical/physiotherapy supervision), so the four-fold injury reduction cannot be
attributed to warm-up or cool-down alone — Issurin himself flags this study as "atypical
because it refers to the complex effects of warming-up, cooling-down and medical supervision"
(PDF p. 58, printed p. 47). **Contested:** stretching's effect on preventing delayed-onset
muscle soreness specifically is described by Issurin himself as disputed within this same
chapter — "supported by several studies (Hartfield, 1985) and contradicted by others (High
et al., 1989)" (PDF p. 70, printed p. 59) — do not cite stretching-prevents-DOMS as settled.

**Example** — A Baylor position group's practice-ending routine that pairs light locomotion
with a stretching series (rather than stretching only in the pre-practice warm-up) has some
support here for next-day range-of-motion benefit, though the causal strength of the
underlying Moller et al. (1985) study for injury outcomes specifically (as opposed to ROM)
is not established by this citation.

**Related** — [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]] (staging;

add a reciprocal link back to this one once both are reviewed).

performance (Bangsbo et al., 2001). A related study (Moller et al., 1985, PDF p. 68, printed
p. 57) tracked 48 adult soccer players across three warm-up/cool-down protocols. The regular
soccer workout (no stretching) caused a significant decrease in all range-of-motion (ROM)
indices. A similar workout with a stretching series in the *warm-up* produced more favorable
ROM responses immediately after the session, with 24-hour ROM not reported for that arm. The
third version, with the stretching series inserted in the *cool-down*, produced significant
ROM benefits both immediately after the workout and 24 hours later.

**Why it works** — Issurin gives warm-up three stated functions: metabolic adjustment,
technical/coordination adjustment, and attainment of mental readiness (Table 2.6, PDF p. 60,
printed p. 49). Cool-down gets four stated objectives, given in prose rather than a table:
reduce body temperature, heart rate, and blood pressure to resting levels; remove acid
metabolites and other waste products from the muscles to the circulatory system for further
clearance; facilitate recovery of the endocrine system; and reduce emotional tension and
support positive mental recovery (PDF p. 67, printed p. 56).

**Contested, terminology only:** Issurin's cool-down rationale frames blood lactate and
"other acid metabolites" as "waste products" to be "removed" from the muscles (PDF pp.
67-69, printed pp. 56-58), and separately states that slow locomotion "causes faster lactate
removal" (Bonen & Belcastro, 1976, PDF p. 68, printed p. 57), with blood lactate removal
after a 4-minute exhausting time trial taking about 20 minutes of restoration (Juel et al.,
1990, PDF p. 70, printed p. 59). The vault's Verkhoshansky staging entry
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]], `proven`) treats
lactate as a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not a toxin, and states that blood
lactate returns to normal within about an hour of strenuous interval training; its `proven`
rating is scoped to two corrections, that lactate is not the cause of DOMS and that "oxygen
debt" is better described as recovery oxygen consumption. That entry does not say clearance
happens "regardless of cool-down activity"; that claim belongs to neither source and should
not be attributed to either. The two books' clearance-time figures are consistent with each
other (about 20 minutes after a 4-minute trial vs. within about an hour of a strenuous
interval session), and neither source ties lactate to DOMS: Issurin attributes DOMS to
strong eccentric ("plyometric") work instead (PDF pp. 69-70, printed pp. 58-59). The real
disagreement is terminology, Issurin's "acid metabolites and other waste products" (PDF p.
67, printed p. 56) against the Verkhoshansky entry's "normal byproduct and fuel." Keep this
book's clearance-time number and its active-recovery claim (slow locomotion speeds lactate
removal); do not repeat "waste product" as physiology, and do not attribute a "toxin" claim
or a "regardless of cool-down activity" claim to Issurin, since he states neither.

# A Structured Warm-Up/Cool-Down Program Cut Soccer Injuries Roughly Four-Fold Over Six Months

**What it is** — Ekstrand et al. (1983), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 58, printed p. 47,
Figure 2.1): **twelve** national-division soccer teams (**180 players**) were split into two
groups. The intervention group (six teams) used a modified program with carefully structured
warm-ups (ball exercises plus a stretching program) and cool-downs (jogging plus hold-relax
stretching), supervised by doctors and physiotherapists. The control group (six teams)
trained traditionally. Over a six-month follow-up, the intervention group showed "highly
significant superiority": a roughly **four-fold reduction in the number of injuries** and a
"drastic decrease" in workouts and games missed to musculoskeletal disorders. Issurin
separately cites supporting single-factor findings: stretching in warm-up increases lower
extremity range of motion in soccer players (Moller et al., 1985); active warm-up *without*
stretching does not affect flexibility (Zakas et al., 2006); and intense prior exercise
meaningfully stimulates aerobic metabolism in working muscles during subsequent strenuous
performance (Bangsbo et al., 2001). A related study (Moller et al., 1985, PDF p. 68, printed
p. 57) tracked 48 adult soccer players across three warm-up/cool-down protocols and found
that inserting a stretching series into the *cool-down* (not just the warm-up) produced range-
of-motion benefits both immediately after the session and 24 hours later, while stretching
only in the warm-up helped immediately but not at 24 hours.

**Why it works** — Issurin frames warm-up and cool-down as serving three functions each:
metabolic adjustment, technical/coordination adjustment, and mental readiness (warm-up,
Table 2.6, PDF p. 60, printed p. 49); and reduction of body temperature/HR/blood pressure,
removal of metabolic byproducts, endocrine-system recovery, and reduced emotional tension
(cool-down, Table 2.11, PDF p. 69, printed p. 58). **Contested — flag directly:** Issurin's
cool-down rationale explicitly frames blood lactate and "other acid metabolites" as "waste
products" to be "removed" from the muscles (PDF p. 68-69, printed pp. 57-58), citing a
specific clearance kinetic (blood lactate removal after a 4-minute exhausting time trial
takes about 20 minutes, Juel et al., 1990). This is in tension with a modern-physiology
claim already captured in this library's Verkhoshansky staging
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]], `proven`): lactate is
not a toxin causing soreness or requiring active "removal," and it clears from the blood on
its own within about an hour of strenuous exercise regardless of cool-down activity, with
current research attributing post-exercise soreness to muscle/connective-tissue microtrauma
rather than residual lactate. The specific clearance-time citation (20 minutes for a 4-minute
time trial) may still be a real kinetic fact — that is not itself disputed here — but
Issurin's *framing* of this as evidence that cool-down actively "removes" a harmful waste
product reflects the outdated "lactic acid as toxin" model the Verkhoshansky entry corrects.
Cite this book's clearance-time number without repeating its waste-product framing.

**When to apply** — The Ekstrand et al. (1983) result is directly relevant to Applied
Performance's collaboration with Athletic Medicine on injury reduction: a structured,
medically-supervised warm-up/cool-down protocol is associated with a large, measured
reduction in soft-tissue injury incidence in a team sport, over a real six-month season, not
an acute lab measure. The cool-down-stretching timing finding (Moller et al., 1985) suggests
cool-down, not just warm-up, is where a stretching series may do more for next-day range of
motion.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a controlled team-level trial (6 intervention
teams vs. 6 control teams; the method of allocating teams to condition is not described),
and the intervention bundled multiple changes at once (warm-up content, cool-down content,
and medical/physiotherapy supervision), so the four-fold injury reduction cannot be
attributed to warm-up or cool-down alone: Issurin himself flags this study as "atypical
because it refers to the complex effects of warming-up, cooling-down and medical supervision"
(PDF p. 58, printed p. 47). **Contested:** stretching's effect on preventing delayed-onset
muscle soreness specifically is described by Issurin himself as disputed within this same
chapter, "supported by several studies (Hartfield, 1985) and contradicted by others (High
et al., 1989)" (PDF p. 70, printed p. 59); do not cite stretching-prevents-DOMS as settled.

**Example** — **Inference:** a Baylor position group's practice-ending routine that pairs light locomotion
with a stretching series (rather than stretching only in the pre-practice warm-up) has some
support here for next-day range-of-motion benefit, though the causal strength of the
underlying Moller et al. (1985) study for injury outcomes specifically (as opposed to ROM)
is not established by this citation.

ROM benefits both immediately after the workout and 24 hours later.

**Why it works** — Issurin gives warm-up three stated functions: metabolic adjustment,
technical/coordination adjustment, and attainment of mental readiness (Table 2.6, PDF p. 60,
printed p. 49). Cool-down gets four stated objectives, given in prose rather than a table:
reduce body temperature, heart rate, and blood pressure to resting levels; remove acid
metabolites and other waste products from the muscles to the circulatory system for further
clearance; facilitate recovery of the endocrine system; and reduce emotional tension and
support positive mental recovery (PDF p. 67, printed p. 56).

**Contested, terminology only:** Issurin's cool-down rationale frames blood lactate and
"other acid metabolites" as "waste products" to be "removed" from the muscles (PDF pp.
67-69, printed pp. 56-58), and separately states that slow locomotion "causes faster lactate
removal" (Bonen & Belcastro, 1976, PDF p. 68, printed p. 57), with blood lactate removal
after a 4-minute exhausting time trial taking about 20 minutes of restoration (Juel et al.,
1990, PDF p. 70, printed p. 59). The vault's Verkhoshansky staging entry
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]], `proven`) treats
lactate as a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not a toxin, and states that blood
lactate returns to normal within about an hour of strenuous interval training; its `proven`
rating is scoped to two corrections, that lactate is not the cause of DOMS and that "oxygen
debt" is better described as recovery oxygen consumption. That entry does not say clearance
happens "regardless of cool-down activity"; that claim belongs to neither source and should
not be attributed to either. The two books' clearance-time figures are consistent with each
other (about 20 minutes after a 4-minute trial vs. within about an hour of a strenuous
interval session), and neither source ties lactate to DOMS: Issurin attributes DOMS to
strong eccentric ("plyometric") work instead (PDF pp. 69-70, printed pp. 58-59). The real
disagreement is terminology, Issurin's "acid metabolites and other waste products" (PDF p.
67, printed p. 56) against the Verkhoshansky entry's "normal byproduct and fuel." Keep this
book's clearance-time number and its active-recovery claim (slow locomotion speeds lactate
removal); do not repeat "waste product" as physiology, and do not attribute a "toxin" claim
or a "regardless of cool-down activity" claim to Issurin, since he states neither.

**When to apply** — The Ekstrand et al. (1983) result is directly relevant to Applied
Performance's collaboration with Athletic Medicine on injury reduction: a structured,
medically-supervised warm-up/cool-down protocol is associated with a large, measured
reduction in soft-tissue injury incidence in a team sport, over a real six-month season, not
an acute lab measure. The cool-down-stretching timing finding (Moller et al., 1985) suggests
cool-down, not just warm-up, is where a stretching series may do more for next-day range of
motion.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a controlled team-level trial (6 intervention
teams vs. 6 control teams; the method of allocating teams to condition is not described),
and the intervention bundled multiple changes at once (warm-up content, cool-down content,
and medical/physiotherapy supervision), so the four-fold injury reduction cannot be
attributed to warm-up or cool-down alone: Issurin himself flags this study as "atypical
because it refers to the complex effects of warming-up, cooling-down and medical supervision"
(PDF p. 58, printed p. 47). **Contested:** stretching's effect on preventing delayed-onset
muscle soreness specifically is described by Issurin himself as disputed within this same
chapter, "supported by several studies (Hartfield, 1985) and contradicted by others (High
et al., 1989)" (PDF p. 70, printed p. 59); do not cite stretching-prevents-DOMS as settled.

**Example** — **Inference:** a Baylor position group's practice-ending routine that pairs light locomotion
with a stretching series (rather than stretching only in the pre-practice warm-up) has some
support here for next-day range-of-motion benefit, though the causal strength of the
underlying Moller et al. (1985) study for injury outcomes specifically (as opposed to ROM)
is not established by this citation.

# Concentration of Training Workloads Is the Cornerstone Principle of Block Periodization

**What it is** — Issurin states the Block Periodization Concept (BPC) rests on one
foundational principle, concentration of training workloads, from which two others follow:
(1) a minimal number of targeted abilities per block, because highly concentrated loads
"only provide sufficient training stimuli to improve the targeted ability," and (2)
consecutive (not simultaneous) development of abilities, because "the number of decisive
abilities exceeds the number of abilities that can be developed simultaneously" (PDF p. 37,
printed p. 26, Figure 1.7). The rationale is laid out as a table of contradictions in the
traditional, simultaneous-development model for high-level athletes (Table 1.4, PDF p. 20,
printed p. 9): concurrent workloads compete for limited energy supply, differing
physiological-system restoration times leave athletes under-recovered for all targets at
once, workloads interact negatively (energy deficits, technical complexity, neuromuscular
fatigue), mental concentration cannot be split across many targets, and the training
stimulus needed for a high-level athlete's progress cannot be reached when it is divided
among many abilities.

**Why it works** — Issurin's own explanation is that above a threshold of athletic level,
a quality only responds to a training stimulus concentrated enough to exceed that
threshold; splitting the same total training time across many qualities keeps each one's
stimulus below that threshold. He does not give a quantitative mechanism for where that
threshold sits or how "concentrated enough" is defined for a given ability or athlete — the
principle is argued from coaches' and scientists' collective experience (Table 1.4) rather
than derived from a stated dose-response model.

**When to apply** — Designing training blocks for advanced, high-level athletes juggling
more qualities than can be trained well at once (the explicit target population, per
Issurin). **Eric's baseline:** this converges with the department's own compatibility rule,
"you can't ride two horses with one saddle" — incompatible qualities are not both trained at
full intensity in the same block (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29). It also converges with
[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]], which independently
describes concentrated, saturated loading on one quality with a delayed 4-12 week rebound.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin's own text (PDF p. 44, printed p. 33) states the
traditional, complex (simultaneous multi-ability) model "has visible benefits for the
preparation of low- and mid-level athletes": it is "more diversified, attractive and
lively," and medium-level concentration is "sufficient stimulation" at that level — the
concentration principle is explicitly scoped to high-performance athletes, not a universal
programming rule. **Contested:** Issurin's blanket claim elsewhere in the same chapter that
the traditional model "does not work well for high-performance athletes" (PDF p. 19,
printed p. 8) is disputed by this library's own Bompa & Haff 5th-edition material
(`periodization--bompa`), which is a current (not 1984-vintage) textbook still teaching and
defending a form of the traditional/complex periodization model for high-level athletes.
Issurin's critique in this chapter names Bompa's *1984* edition specifically (PDF p. 13,
printed p. 2) as one of the texts that propagated the traditional model he is arguing
against — it is not a critique of the Bompa & Haff 5th edition already in this library,
which incorporates concentrated-loading and conjugated-sequence ideas closer to Issurin's
own. **Inference:** Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review (2016, *Sports Medicine*,
"Benefits and Limitations of Block Periodized Training Approaches," Zotero item
`PT9QTQ2I`, not yet full-text-cached in this ingest) is titled around limitations as well as
benefits and likely narrows this 2008 book's confident framing; treat the frontmatter
`confidence: contested` as applying specifically to the universal "traditional doesn't work
for high performers" claim, not to the narrower, self-limited concentration principle.

**Example** — A collegiate football strength staff trying to develop max strength,
aerobic capacity, alactic power, and technical skill acquisition all at full intensity in
the same 4-week block, per Table 1.4's logic, risks under-stimulating all four rather than
meaningfully improving any one; concentrating the block on 1-2 of them (with the rest held
at a retention dose) is the alternative Issurin argues for.

**Related** — [[framework--block-periodization-mesocycle-taxonomy]] — the three-block
structure this principle produces. [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]
and [[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]] — converging concentrated-load
ideas already in this library. [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (staging) —
check for overlap on why generalized simultaneous training under-delivers for advanced
athletes.

# Concentration of Training Workloads Is the Cornerstone Principle of Block Periodization

**What it is** — Issurin states the Block Periodization Concept (BPC) rests on one
foundational principle, concentration of training workloads, from which two others follow:
(1) a minimal number of targeted abilities per block, because highly concentrated loads
"only provide sufficient training stimuli to improve the targeted ability," and (2)
consecutive (not simultaneous) development of abilities, because "the number of decisive
abilities exceeds the number of abilities that can be developed simultaneously" (PDF p. 37,
printed p. 26, Figure 1.7). The rationale is laid out as a table of contradictions in the
traditional, simultaneous-development model for high-level athletes (Table 1.4, PDF p. 20,
printed p. 9): concurrent workloads compete for limited energy supply, differing
physiological-system restoration times leave athletes under-recovered for all targets at
once, workloads interact negatively (energy deficits, technical complexity, neuromuscular
fatigue), mental concentration cannot be split across many targets, and the training
stimulus needed for a high-level athlete's progress cannot be reached when it is divided
among many abilities.

**Why it works** — Issurin's own explanation is that above a threshold of athletic level,
a quality only responds to a training stimulus concentrated enough to exceed that
threshold; splitting the same total training time across many qualities keeps each one's
stimulus below that threshold. He does not give a quantitative mechanism for where that
threshold sits or how "concentrated enough" is defined for a given ability or athlete — the
principle is argued from coaches' and scientists' collective experience (Table 1.4) rather
than derived from a stated dose-response model.

**When to apply** — Designing training blocks for advanced, high-level athletes juggling
more qualities than can be trained well at once (the explicit target population, per
Issurin). **Eric's baseline:** the course teaches this rule from Issurin directly
(week1-lecture.md marker pp.64, 67, which name "Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source
for block periodization and file "you can't ride 2 horses w/one saddle" under the same
section), not as an independent convergence: "you can't ride two horses with one saddle",
incompatible qualities are not both trained at full intensity in the same block
(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29). It also converges with
[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]], which independently
describes concentrated, saturated loading on one quality with a delayed 4-12 week rebound.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin's own text (PDF p. 44, printed p. 33) states the
traditional, complex (simultaneous multi-ability) model "has visible benefits for the
preparation of low- and mid-level athletes": it is "more diversified, attractive and
lively," and medium-level concentration is "sufficient stimulation" at that level — the
concentration principle is explicitly scoped to high-performance athletes, not a universal
programming rule. **Contested:** Issurin's blanket claim elsewhere in the same chapter that
the traditional model "does not work well for high-performance athletes" (PDF p. 19,
printed p. 8) is disputed by this library's own Bompa & Haff 5th-edition material
(`periodization--bompa`), which is a current (not 1984-vintage) textbook still teaching and
defending a form of the traditional/complex periodization model for high-level athletes.
Issurin's critique in this chapter names Bompa's *1984* edition specifically (PDF p. 13,
printed p. 2) as one of the texts that propagated the traditional model he is arguing
against — it is not a critique of the Bompa & Haff 5th edition already in this library,
which incorporates concentrated-loading and conjugated-sequence ideas closer to Issurin's
own. **Inference:** Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review (2016, *Sports Medicine*,
"Benefits and Limitations of Block Periodized Training Approaches," Zotero item
`PT9QTQ2I`, not yet full-text-cached in this ingest) is titled around limitations as well as
benefits and likely narrows this 2008 book's confident framing; treat the frontmatter
`confidence: contested` as applying specifically to the universal "traditional doesn't work
for high performers" claim, not to the narrower, self-limited concentration principle.

**Example** — A collegiate football strength staff trying to develop max strength,
aerobic capacity, alactic power, and technical skill acquisition all at full intensity in
the same 4-week block, per Table 1.4's logic, risks under-stimulating all four rather than
meaningfully improving any one; concentrating the block on 1-2 of them (with the rest held
at a retention dose) is the alternative Issurin argues for.

structure this principle produces. [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]
and [[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]] — converging concentrated-load
ideas already in this library. [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (staging) —
check for overlap on why generalized simultaneous training under-delivers for advanced
athletes.

# Concentration of Training Workloads Is the Cornerstone Principle of Block Periodization

**What it is** — Issurin states the Block Periodization Concept (BPC) rests on one
foundational principle, concentration of training workloads, from which two others follow:
(1) a minimal number of targeted abilities per block, because highly concentrated loads
"only provide sufficient training stimuli to improve the targeted ability," and (2)
consecutive (not simultaneous) development of abilities, because "the number of decisive
abilities exceeds the number of abilities that can be developed simultaneously" (PDF p. 37,
printed p. 26, Figure 1.7). The rationale is laid out as a table of contradictions in the
traditional, simultaneous-development model for high-level athletes (Table 1.4, PDF p. 20,
printed p. 9): concurrent workloads compete for limited energy supply, differing
physiological-system restoration times leave athletes under-recovered for all targets at
once, workloads interact negatively (energy deficits, technical complexity, neuromuscular
fatigue), mental concentration cannot be split across many targets, and the training
stimulus needed for a high-level athlete's progress cannot be reached when it is divided
among many abilities.

**Why it works** — Issurin's own explanation is that above a threshold of athletic level,
a quality only responds to a training stimulus concentrated enough to exceed that
threshold; splitting the same total training time across many qualities keeps each one's
stimulus below that threshold. He does not give a quantitative mechanism for where that
threshold sits or how "concentrated enough" is defined for a given ability or athlete — the
principle is argued from coaches' and scientists' collective experience (Table 1.4) rather
than derived from a stated dose-response model.

**When to apply** — Designing training blocks for advanced, high-level athletes juggling
more qualities than can be trained well at once (the explicit target population, per
Issurin). **Eric's baseline:** the course teaches this rule from Issurin directly
(week1-lecture.md marker pp.64, 67, which name "Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source
for block periodization and file "you can't ride 2 horses w/one saddle" under the same
section), not as an independent convergence: "you can't ride two horses with one saddle",
incompatible qualities are not both trained at full intensity in the same block
(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29). It also converges with
[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]], which independently
describes concentrated, saturated loading on one quality with a delayed 4-12 week rebound.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin's own text (PDF p. 44, printed p. 33) states the
traditional, complex (simultaneous multi-ability) model "has visible benefits for the
preparation of low- and mid-level athletes": it is "more diversified, attractive and
lively," and medium-level concentration is "sufficient stimulation" at that level — the
concentration principle is explicitly scoped to high-performance athletes, not a universal
programming rule. **Contested:** Issurin's blanket claim elsewhere in the same chapter that
the traditional model "does not work well for high-performance athletes" (PDF p. 19,
printed p. 8) is disputed by Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review (Issurin, 2016,
*Sports Medicine*, "Benefits and Limitations of Block Periodized Training Approaches to
Athletes' Preparation," Zotero item `PT9QTQ2I`, full text cached in this library at
`research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a.md`):
that review judges concentrated-unidirectional block programs' evidence insufficient for
broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation, and
frames the concentrated-unidirectional model as restricted when peak performance requires
many interacting abilities (its p.6, p.11) — a real narrowing of this 2008 book's confident
"does not work well for high-performance athletes" framing, for exactly the population this
principle targets. **Inference:** Bompa & Haff's 5th edition, already in this library, may
also bear on this claim, but only Bompa Ch1-2 has been ingested so far

traditional model he is arguing against; that is a different, narrower target than the 5th

# The Training Stage (A-T-R + Competition) Is the Annual Plan's Building Block, Enabling Multiple Peaks

**What it is** — Issurin's annual cycle is built from a sequence of **training stages**,
each one containing all three mesocycle-blocks (accumulation, transmutation, realization) in
order, ending in a competition (PDF p. 38, printed p. 27). Each training stage "gives the
appearance of an annual cycle in miniature" — a block resembling a preparatory period
(accumulation), one resembling a competition period (transmutation), and a tapering block
ending in competitive performance (realization) (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28). The duration of
a training stage is set by how long the constituent residual training effects can be
superimposed (Figure 1.8; see
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]) and "should be about two
months," though Issurin notes stages can run shorter near season's end or longer earlier in
the season, in which case "special measures should be used to prolong residual training
effects" (unspecified in this chapter — likely developed in Chapter 3, not yet ingested).
The number of training stages in a season "usually varies from four to seven," depending on
the sport's competition calendar (PDF p. 40, printed p. 29, Figure 1.9). Issurin lists five
claimed benefits of this design over the traditional model (PDF p. 40, printed p. 29, and
Table 1.8, PDF p. 42, printed p. 31): reduced total training volume without reducing workout
count; more purposeful monitoring (fewer targeted abilities per stage); improved
psychological focus and motivation; more targeted nutrition per block (e.g., higher protein
during strength-focused blocks); and — most relevant to the peaking question — "a
multi-stage annual plan creates more favorable conditions for peaking in time for the main
competition of the season," with intermediate peaks plannable mid-season or even early
season, not only at a single season-end date.

**Why it works** — Because each training stage runs its own compressed
accumulation-transmutation-realization cycle and ends in a real competitive test, the athlete
is brought to a peak (or near-peak) at the end of every stage rather than once per year;
stacking four to seven such stages across a season is what produces the multi-peak pattern.
Issurin's stated physiological contrast (Table 1.8) is that the traditional model relies on
adaptation to concurrent stimuli across a long period, while this model relies on
superimposing sequential residual effects from short, concentrated blocks — the same
mechanism underlying [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

**When to apply** — This is the entry most directly responsive to the strength-and-conditioning
miss-log gap ("peaking phase structure for collegiate football," logged 2026-09-03): for a
football program needing camp-readiness, then in-season week-to-week competitive readiness,
this framework suggests treating each significant test point (fall camp scrimmage, each
game week, or a defined in-season block) as a candidate training-stage boundary rather than
relying on a single annual peak, with the caveat below about untested claims. **Eric's
baseline** does not currently describe an explicit training-stage or multi-peak model for
football; the closest baseline material is the general macro/meso/microcycle planning
language and the in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Periodization and programming" and "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.17-18, 20-21) — this Issurin framework offers a
more explicit structural answer to "how do you actually sequence a season with more than one
peak" than anything currently captured in the baseline.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The "four to seven stages" and "about two months"
figures are stated without a derivation the reader can check — Issurin gives no worked
example of how stage count or duration is calculated for a specific sport's calendar in
this chapter. **Inference:** football's in-season structure (weekly games, not discrete
multi-week competition-free blocks) does not map cleanly onto a ~2-month training stage —
Issurin's model is built from and mainly evidenced by individual/dual sports with
discrete competitions (track and field, canoe-kayak, windsurfing), and Chapter 3's
microcycle-level material (not yet ingested; see `_book.md` for the recommended next batch)
is likely necessary before this framework can be translated into a week-by-week in-season
football plan. **Contested — flag as unqualified:** the "does not work well for
high-performance athletes" framing of the traditional alternative carries the same caveat as
in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] — Bompa & Haff's 5th edition, already
in this library, is a current high-level training text that does not abandon
period-based (as opposed to stage-based) annual planning. **Inference:** Issurin's own 2016
review (Zotero item `PT9QTQ2I`, not yet full-text-cached) is titled around benefits *and*
limitations of block periodization and likely qualifies the confident five-benefit list
above; this entry's claims should be revisited once that review is read.

**Example** — A five-stage football off-season/camp plan: Stage 1 (general
accumulation, ~8 weeks, winter conditioning); Stage 2 (strength/power transmutation into
spring ball, ending in the spring game as a "competition"); Stage 3 (summer accumulation);
Stage 4 (fall-camp transmutation, ending in the first scrimmage or game week as
realization); Stage 5+ (in-season stages keyed to bye weeks or rivalry-week peaks, pending
Chapter 3's in-season microcycle guidance).

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[claim--multi-peak-annual-preparation-elite-track-and-field]] (the empirical motivation for
needing a multi-peak model), [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]].
