-# Two Studies Issurin Cites Against Simultaneous Development: Swimmer Interference and Kayaker Decay
-**What it is** — Issurin presents two data-backed examples as motivation for abandoning
-simultaneous multi-ability training (traditional periodization) in favor of consecutive,
-concentrated blocks.
-**(1) Swimmer concurrent-training interference (PDF pp. 21-22, printed pp. 10-11, Figure
-1.3).** High-level male swimmers were studied over an 8-week early-season program combining
-extensive swimming with resistive/power dry-land work aimed at swim-specific strength
-(9-11 workouts/week; sample size not stated in this text). Measured: maximal force of
-tethered swimming (Ftsw), dry-land explosive strength (Fexp), and dry-land strength
-endurance (SE). Result: strength endurance improved markedly; swim-specific strength did not
-improve; explosive strength *decreased*, despite about 30% of dry-land program time devoted
-to maximal/explosive strength work. Issurin's mechanistic explanation has two separate
-parts: extensive endurance work captures the metabolic energy needed for post-exercise
-anabolism, which suppresses muscle hypertrophy; separately, coaches' and athletes'
-observations show that a strenuous, high-volume training program causes permanent fatigue,
-keeping central and peripheral neural factors far from the optimum needed for improving
-muscular contraction. Klausen (1990) is cited for a more general point about what conditions
-the neural mechanism (state of the CNS, sensitivity of the neuro-motor pool), not for the
-fatigue observation specifically.
-**(2) Kayaker decay under traditional periodization (PDF p. 25-26, printed pp. 14-15,
-Figure 1.4 — the in-text citation reads "Fig.1.3," which appears to be a labeling error in
-the source; the described variables match Figure 1.4's caption, not Figure 1.3's).** A group
-of highly qualified kayakers were tracked across a full annual cycle built on the classical
-model (Issurin et al., 1986). Measured: mean distance velocity (Vd), velocity at anaerobic
-threshold (V-AT), peak paddle force (PF), stroke rate (SR), muscle mass (MM). Result: the
-long general-preparatory period raised V-AT, muscle mass and peak force substantially; but
-during the extended, highly specialized competitive period, extensive aerobic workloads were
-replaced by more intense, event-specific exercises, and maximum-strength exercises were
-"reduced and even rejected as harmful for racing technique" (only maximum-strength work is
-called harmful in the source; the aerobic reduction is described as a substitution, not a
-harm judgment), and V-AT, peak force, and muscle mass all *declined* by the competitive
-period. Distance velocity
-still reached its season maximum, but only via increased stroke rate compensating for
-reduced force, i.e., technique/rate covered for a real loss in the underlying strength and
-aerobic qualities. Issurin's summary: "the timing pattern for developing different abilities
-was far from optimal."
-**Why it works** — For the swimmer case, Issurin gives two separate stated mechanisms (PDF
-p. 21, printed p. 10): extensive endurance work "captures the metabolic energy that is
-necessary for anabolism during post-exercise recovery," which "suppresses muscle
-hypertrophy"; and, separately, "the observations of coaches and athletes show that a
-strenuous high volume training program causes permanent fatigue," so "the central and
-peripheral neural factors are far from optimum." Klausen (1990) is cited for a different,
-more general point in between the two, that enhancement of the neural mechanism "is
-conditioned by the state of the central nervous system and the sensitivity of the
-neuro-motor pool," not specifically for the fatigue observation. For the kayaker case, Issurin
-gives no physiological mechanism for the decline beyond narration of what happened (reduced
-aerobic and strength work during the competitive period, PDF p. 25, printed p. 14); treat
-that case as a described pattern, not an explained one. **Inference:** labeling the two
-cases as "concurrent interference" versus "sequential decay" is this entry's own
-categorization for cross-referencing purposes, not language Issurin himself uses; both are
-offered by Issurin as evidence for the same underlying argument against simultaneous,
-non-block training (see [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]), which in turn
-motivates the consecutive block sequencing in
-[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] and
-[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]].
-**When to apply** — The swimmer study is the more detailed evidence of the two: it is an
-uncontrolled, single-group, uncited 8-week observation (no control group or reference given
-in this text, PDF p. 21, printed p. 10) with named outcome variables, giving concrete numbers
-useful for illustrating concurrent-training interference to Baylor strength staff
-programming for athletes who need both an aerobic base and explosive/max strength (e.g.,
-many football positions in a fall-camp conditioning window). The kayaker case is useful
-mainly as a cautionary illustration of "building a quality early in the year and then
-letting it decay unaddressed."
-**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The swimmer study's exact sample size is not given in
-this text (only workout frequency, 9-11/week), so its statistical strength cannot be judged
-from this source alone; treat the direction of the finding (interference occurred) as
-`supported` but the specific numeric changes in Figure 1.3 as unverifiable: the swimmer
-study carries no citation at all in this text, not even an author or year, so there is no
-underlying source to check the numbers against. **Untested:** the kayaker case is Issurin's
-own team's data (Issurin et al., 1986),
-observational across one season with no control group; it demonstrates a plausible pattern,
-not a controlled comparison against an alternative periodization model run on the same
-athletes. Neither study is football-specific; football's in-season structure (weekly
-competition, not one late-season peak) differs from both the swimmers' fixed 8-week block and
-the kayakers' single annual peak design.
-**Example** — **Inference:** a Baylor position group with both an in-season conditioning demand and a
-strength-maintenance demand should treat "just add more of both" as the swimmer study's
-failure mode: without deliberate sequencing or volume management, the concurrent aerobic
-load can blunt the intended strength/power adaptation even when strength work is
-programmed.
-**Related** — [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (Table 1.4's rationale,
-which these two studies are offered as concrete illustrations of),
-[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

+motivates the consecutive block sequencing in

+useful for illustrating concurrent-training interference to Baylor strength staff
+programming for athletes who need both an aerobic base and explosive/max strength (e.g.,

+mainly as a cautionary illustration of "building a quality early in the year and then
+letting it decay unaddressed."

+this text (only workout frequency, 9-11/week), so its statistical strength cannot be judged
+from this source alone; treat the direction of the finding (interference occurred) as
+`supported` but the specific numeric changes in Figure 1.3 as unverifiable: the swimmer

+athletes. Neither study is football-specific; football's in-season structure (weekly
+competition, not one late-season peak) differs from both the swimmers' fixed 8-week block and
+the kayakers' single annual peak design.

+strength-maintenance demand should treat "just add more of both" as the swimmer study's
+failure mode: without deliberate sequencing or volume management, the concurrent aerobic
+load can blunt the intended strength/power adaptation even when strength work is
+programmed.

-# Case Study: The USSR Canoe-Kayak Team and the Original Accumulation/Transmutation/Realization Design
-**What it is** — Issurin's own account of where his accumulation-transmutation-realization
-taxonomy came from (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22): in the early 1980s, elite USSR canoe-kayak
-paddlers were training an "enormous exercise volume." "The prevailing opinion was that this
-load level was excessive and that the training design could be made more effective." The
-block-and-mesocycle-sequencing idea was "conceptualized, implemented and proved in
-practice" with the national team, then published (Issurin & Kaverin, 1985). The duration of
-the mesocycles was set "according to physiological and biochemical prerequisites that
-usually allowed four weeks for the accumulation and transformation mesocycles, and two weeks
-for realization." The modified design allowed "about a 10-15% reduction in the annual
-training volume." Follow-up testing during preparation reportedly showed "considerable
-improvement in the main fitness components in all subgroups." The claimed competitive
-outcomes: three gold and three silver medals at the 1988 Seoul Olympics, and eight gold
-medals (1989) and nine gold medals (1990) at the World Championships.
-**Why it works — the author's own interpretation, not independently verified here** —
-Issurin attributes the improvement to reduced simultaneous multi-ability training and better
-volume management under the new block structure, consistent with the general BPC rationale
-in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]. No comparison data (e.g., what the
-same team's results looked like in prior Olympic/World Championship cycles under the old
-model, or what other nations' medal counts did over the same period) is presented in this
-chapter to isolate the training-design change from other factors (athlete development,
-equipment, competitor turnover).

-as the direct provenance of Issurin's own taxonomy (see

-national federation with centralized, well-resourced athlete monitoring implemented this
-design at scale (not just with one athlete).

-Kaverin (1985) but does not itself state what Issurin's own role on the national team was.
-**Inference:** reading this as the concept's inventor reporting on his own uncontrolled
-intervention with his own national team is a reasonable inference from the shared authorship
-and the book's framing, not something the text says outright. Either way, the account here

-Olympic and World Championship medal counts as a controlled test of the training design;
-1980s Soviet sport had structural advantages (centralized athlete development, resourcing)
-that are not present in most other training contexts, including a US college football
-program. The "10-15% volume reduction" figure has no comparison baseline stated (reduction
-from what specific prior volume, over what specific prior period) beyond "the annual
-training volume."
-**Example** — Citing "block periodization produced Olympic medals" should specify this is
-one 1980s Soviet national-team case reported by the method's own originator, not a
-controlled trial, and should be paired with the caveat already logged in
-[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]] about single-coach, single-program
-evidence.

-[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]].

-# Squat-First vs. Squat-After-Hang-Pull Changes Whether You Get More Reps or More Power
-**What it is** — Spreuwenberg et al. (2006), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62):
-**nine** resistance-trained male athletes performed the back squat (4 sets at 85% of 1RM) on
-two separate days under two protocols. Protocol A: squat performed during the initial part
-of the workout. Protocol B: squat performed after a whole-body resistance exercise (hang
-pull). Results: Protocol A produced significantly more repetitions per set (8.0 ± 1.9 vs.
-5.4 ± 2.7 in Protocol B), but average power per set was *higher* in Protocol B. The study
-authors attribute (Spreuwenberg et al., 2006, as cited by Issurin) the power difference to
-postactivation potentiation induced by the preceding whole-body power exercise.
-**Why it works** — Issurin reports only the study authors' own attribution for the power
-finding: they "attributed this phenomenon to postactivation potentiation induced by the
-preceding whole-body power exercise" (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62). **Inference:** the
-companion explanation for the rep-count finding, that fresh (unfatigued) muscle sustains
-more total repetitions at a given relative load than muscle that has just performed a
-preceding whole-body lift, is this entry's own reasoning to account for the Protocol A
-result; Issurin does not state that explanation for the rep-count difference in this
-passage.
-**When to apply** — Choosing exercise order based on the specific training goal for that
-session: Issurin's stated takeaway (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62) is that a coach wanting maximum
-hypertrophy stimulus should place the squat early in the session (more total volume/reps),
-while a coach targeting maximum power output should place it after appropriate whole-body
-resistance work, to exploit postactivation potentiation. Directly usable for Baylor
-strength-staff session design when max-effort lower-body power output (not volume) is the
-stated goal of a given lift.
-**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a small (n = 9), single published study;
-Issurin does not report effect sizes, statistical significance values, or the specific
-whole-body exercise's loading in this citation beyond "hang pull" — treat the direction of
-the finding as `supported` but do not treat the exact magnitude (8.0 vs. 5.4 reps) as
-something to replicate precisely without reading the original study. It is unclear from this
-text whether the postactivation-potentiation effect generalizes to different athlete
-populations (this sample was resistance-trained males), different preceding exercises, or
-different rest intervals between the potentiating exercise and the squat.
-**Example** — **Inference:** a power-focused lower-body day for football linemen might
-sequence a moderate-load hang pull or clean pull before back squats at 85% 1RM, accepting
-fewer total squat reps in exchange for higher power output per rep on the squats that
-follow; a hypertrophy-focused day for the same lift would instead put the squat first.
-**Related** — [[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
-[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]],
-[[research-papers/hanson-2007-acute-effects-of-heavy-and-light-load-squat-exercise-on-the-kinetic-measures-of-vertical-j]] (vault),
-[[research-papers/hirayama-2014-acute-effects-of-an-ascending-intensity-squat-protocol-on-vertical-jump-performance]] (vault),
-[[research-papers/seitz-2017-a-sled-push-stimulus-potentiates-subsequent-20-m-sprint-performance]] (vault).

-# A Structured Warm-Up/Cool-Down Program Cut Soccer Injuries Roughly Four-Fold Over Six Months
-**What it is** — Ekstrand et al. (1983), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 58, printed p. 47,
-Figure 2.1): **twelve** national-division soccer teams (**180 players**) were split into two
-groups. The intervention group (six teams) used a modified program with carefully structured
-warm-ups (ball exercises plus a stretching program) and cool-downs (jogging plus hold-relax
-stretching), supervised by doctors and physiotherapists. The control group (six teams)
-trained traditionally. Over a six-month follow-up, the intervention group showed "highly
-significant superiority": a roughly **four-fold reduction in the number of injuries** and a
-"drastic decrease" in workouts and games missed to musculoskeletal disorders. Issurin
-separately cites supporting single-factor findings: stretching in warm-up increases lower
-extremity range of motion in soccer players (Moller et al., 1985); active warm-up *without*
-stretching does not affect flexibility (Zakas et al., 2006); and intense prior exercise
-meaningfully stimulates aerobic metabolism in working muscles during subsequent strenuous
-performance (Bangsbo et al., 2001). A related study (Moller et al., 1985, PDF p. 68, printed
-p. 57) tracked 48 adult soccer players across three warm-up/cool-down protocols. The regular
-soccer workout (no stretching) caused a significant decrease in all range-of-motion (ROM)
-indices. A similar workout with a stretching series in the *warm-up* produced more favorable
-ROM responses immediately after the session, with 24-hour ROM not reported for that arm. The
-third version, with the stretching series inserted in the *cool-down*, produced significant
-ROM benefits both immediately after the workout and 24 hours later.
-**Why it works** — Issurin gives warm-up three stated functions: metabolic adjustment,
-technical/coordination adjustment, and attainment of mental readiness (Table 2.6, PDF p. 60,
-printed p. 49). Cool-down gets four stated objectives, given in prose rather than a table:
-reduce body temperature, heart rate, and blood pressure to resting levels; remove acid
-metabolites and other waste products from the muscles to the circulatory system for further
-clearance; facilitate recovery of the endocrine system; and reduce emotional tension and
-support positive mental recovery (PDF p. 67, printed p. 56).
-**Contested, terminology only:** Issurin's cool-down rationale frames blood lactate and
-"other acid metabolites" as "waste products" to be "removed" from the muscles (PDF pp.
-67-69, printed pp. 56-58), and separately states that slow locomotion "causes faster lactate
-removal" (Bonen & Belcastro, 1976, PDF p. 68, printed p. 57), with blood lactate removal
-after a 4-minute exhausting time trial taking about 20 minutes of restoration (Juel et al.,
-1990, PDF p. 70, printed p. 59). The vault's Verkhoshansky staging entry
-([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]], `proven`) treats
-lactate as a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not a toxin, and states that blood
-lactate returns to normal within about an hour of strenuous interval training; its `proven`
-rating is scoped to two corrections, that lactate is not the cause of DOMS and that "oxygen
-debt" is better described as recovery oxygen consumption. That entry does not say clearance
-happens "regardless of cool-down activity"; that claim belongs to neither source and should
-not be attributed to either. The two books' clearance-time figures are consistent with each
-other (about 20 minutes after a 4-minute trial vs. within about an hour of a strenuous
-interval session), and neither source ties lactate to DOMS: Issurin attributes DOMS to
-strong eccentric ("plyometric") work instead (PDF pp. 69-70, printed pp. 58-59). The real
-disagreement is terminology, Issurin's "acid metabolites and other waste products" (PDF p.
-67, printed p. 56) against the Verkhoshansky entry's "normal byproduct and fuel." Keep this
-book's clearance-time number and its active-recovery claim (slow locomotion speeds lactate
-removal); do not repeat "waste product" as physiology, and do not attribute a "toxin" claim
-or a "regardless of cool-down activity" claim to Issurin, since he states neither.
-**When to apply** — The Ekstrand et al. (1983) result is directly relevant to Applied
-Performance's collaboration with Athletic Medicine on injury reduction: a structured,
-medically-supervised warm-up/cool-down protocol is associated with a large, measured
-reduction in soft-tissue injury incidence in a team sport, over a real six-month season, not
-an acute lab measure. The cool-down-stretching timing finding (Moller et al., 1985) suggests
-cool-down, not just warm-up, is where a stretching series may do more for next-day range of
-motion.
-**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a controlled team-level trial (6 intervention
-teams vs. 6 control teams; the method of allocating teams to condition is not described),
-and the intervention bundled multiple changes at once (warm-up content, cool-down content,
-and medical/physiotherapy supervision), so the four-fold injury reduction cannot be
-attributed to warm-up or cool-down alone: Issurin himself flags this study as "atypical
-because it refers to the complex effects of warming-up, cooling-down and medical supervision"
-(PDF p. 58, printed p. 47). **Contested:** stretching's effect on preventing delayed-onset
-muscle soreness specifically is described by Issurin himself as disputed within this same
-chapter, "supported by several studies (Hartfield, 1985) and contradicted by others (High
-et al., 1989)" (PDF p. 70, printed p. 59); do not cite stretching-prevents-DOMS as settled.
-**Example** — **Inference:** a Baylor position group's practice-ending routine that pairs light locomotion
-with a stretching series (rather than stretching only in the pre-practice warm-up) has some
-support here for next-day range-of-motion benefit, though the causal strength of the
-underlying Moller et al. (1985) study for injury outcomes specifically (as opposed to ROM)
-is not established by this citation.
-**Related** — [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]] (staging;
-the direct source of the lactate-framing contest above, rewritten as terminology-only in this
-review pass; recommend the Verkhoshansky entry add a reciprocal link back to this one once
-both are reviewed).

+an acute lab measure. The cool-down-stretching timing finding (Moller et al., 1985) suggests
+cool-down, not just warm-up, is where a stretching series may do more for next-day range of
+motion.

+teams vs. 6 control teams; the method of allocating teams to condition is not described),
+and the intervention bundled multiple changes at once (warm-up content, cool-down content,
+and medical/physiotherapy supervision), so the four-fold injury reduction cannot be
+attributed to warm-up or cool-down alone: Issurin himself flags this study as "atypical
+because it refers to the complex effects of warming-up, cooling-down and medical supervision"
+(PDF p. 58, printed p. 47). **Contested:** stretching's effect on preventing delayed-onset
+muscle soreness specifically is described by Issurin himself as disputed within this same
+chapter, "supported by several studies (Hartfield, 1985) and contradicted by others (High
+et al., 1989)" (PDF p. 70, printed p. 59); do not cite stretching-prevents-DOMS as settled.
+**Example** — **Inference:** a Baylor position group's practice-ending routine that pairs light locomotion
+with a stretching series (rather than stretching only in the pre-practice warm-up) has some
+support here for next-day range-of-motion benefit, though the causal strength of the
+underlying Moller et al. (1985) study for injury outcomes specifically (as opposed to ROM)
+is not established by this citation.

# Concentration of Training Workloads Is the Cornerstone Principle of Block Periodization

**What it is** — Issurin states the Block Periodization Concept (BPC) rests on one
foundational principle, concentration of training workloads, from which two others follow:
(1) a minimal number of targeted abilities per block, because highly concentrated loads
"only provide sufficient training stimuli to improve the targeted ability," and (2)
consecutive (not simultaneous) development of abilities, because "the number of decisive
abilities exceeds the number of abilities that can be developed simultaneously" (PDF p. 37,
printed p. 26, Figure 1.7). The rationale is laid out as a table of contradictions in the
traditional, simultaneous-development model for high-level athletes (Table 1.4, PDF p. 20,
printed p. 9): energy supply gets spread across too many targets so the main one does not
get the attention it needs, differing physiological-system restoration times leave athletes
under-recovered for all targets at once, workloads interact negatively (energy deficits,
technical complexity, neuromuscular fatigue), mental concentration cannot be split across
many targets, and the training stimulus needed for a high-level athlete's progress cannot be
reached when it is divided among many abilities. **Locator note:** Table 1.4's
Contradictions column literally reads "There is sufficient energy supply for concurrent
performance of diversified workloads" (PDF p. 20, printed p. 9); its Consequences column
implies the opposite, "Energy is directed to many targets while the main target doesn't get
the appropriate attention." This reads as an apparent wording inconsistency in the source;
the table's overall point, that concentration protects the main target's stimulus, still
stands.

**Why it works** — Issurin's own explanation is that above a threshold of athletic level,
a quality only responds to a training stimulus concentrated enough to exceed that
threshold; splitting the same total training time across many qualities keeps each one's
stimulus below that threshold. He does not give a quantitative mechanism for where that
threshold sits or how "concentrated enough" is defined for a given ability or athlete, the
principle is argued from coaches' and scientists' collective experience (Table 1.4) rather
than derived from a stated dose-response model.

**When to apply** — Designing training blocks for advanced, high-level athletes juggling
more qualities than can be trained well at once (the explicit target population, per
Issurin). **Eric's baseline:** the course teaches this rule from Issurin directly
(week1-lecture.md marker pp.64, 67, which name "Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source
for block periodization and file "you can't ride 2 horses w/one saddle" under the same
section), not as an independent convergence: "you can't ride two horses with one saddle",
incompatible qualities are not both trained at full intensity in the same block
(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29). It also converges with
[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]], which independently
describes concentrated, saturated loading on one quality with a delayed 4-12 week rebound.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Issurin's own text (PDF p. 44, printed p. 33) states the
traditional, complex (simultaneous multi-ability) model "has visible benefits for the
preparation of low- and mid-level athletes": it is "more diversified, attractive and
lively," and medium-level concentration is "sufficient stimulation" at that level: the
concentration principle is explicitly scoped to high-performance athletes, not a universal
programming rule. **Contested:** Issurin's blanket claim elsewhere in the same chapter that
the traditional model "does not work well for high-performance athletes" (PDF p. 19,
printed p. 8) is disputed by Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review (Issurin, 2016,
*Sports Medicine*, "Benefits and Limitations of Block Periodized Training Approaches to
Athletes' Preparation," Zotero item `PT9QTQ2I`, full text cached in this library at
`research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a.md`):
that review judges concentrated-unidirectional block programs' evidence insufficient for
broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation, and
frames the concentrated-unidirectional model as restricted when peak performance requires
many interacting abilities (its p.6, p.11), a real narrowing of this 2008 book's confident
"does not work well for high-performance athletes" framing, for exactly the population this
principle targets. **Inference:** Bompa & Haff's 5th edition, already in this library, may
also bear on this claim, but only Bompa Ch1-2 has been ingested so far
(`periodization--bompa/_book.md`: Ch6 Annual Plan and Ch8 Training Cycles are pending); the
one relevant ingested entry, `principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching`, *converges*
with Issurin rather than disputing him, so it cannot be used to ground this contest. Check
whether Bompa & Haff Ch6-8 defend period-based annual planning for high-level athletes once
those chapters are ingested. Issurin's critique in this chapter also names Bompa's *1984*
edition specifically (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2) as one of the texts that propagated the
traditional model he is arguing against; that is a different, narrower target than the 5th
edition.

**Example** — **Inference:** a collegiate football strength staff trying to develop max strength,
aerobic capacity, alactic power, and technical skill acquisition all at full intensity in
the same 4-week block, per Table 1.4's logic, risks under-stimulating all four rather than
meaningfully improving any one; concentrating the block on 1-2 of them (with the rest held
at a retention dose) is the alternative Issurin argues for.

structure this principle produces. [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]
and [[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]], converging concentrated-load
ideas already in this library. [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (staging) —

athletes.

# Structuring Two-a-Day (and Denser) Training Days by Dominant Ability and Rest Interval

**What it is** — Issurin describes how high-performance programs structure multiple same-day
sessions. Two- and three-workout days are routine in camp practice; four, five, and even six
daily workouts are reported anecdotally by prominent coaches, with six an exception (PDF p.
76, printed p. 65). For a four-session aerobic-development day (Figure 2.5, PDF p. 77,
printed p. 66): **session 1** (6:40-7:20 AM, small load) is warm-up, calisthenics,
stretching, and sport-specific technical elements; **session 2** (10:20-11:30 AM, medium or
substantial load, after a multi-hour break) is anaerobic alactic bouts combined with
aerobic medium-intensity exercises; **session 3** (12:30-13:30 PM, medium or substantial
load, after a one-hour break) is aerobic interval series combined with technical tasks, with
velocity-resisted regimes allowed; **session 4** (16:40-18:10 PM, substantial load, after a
three-hour break) is aerobic continuous exercising, strength-endurance aerobic exercises, and
stretching/relaxation, with an emphasized, longer cool-down given accumulated fatigue. For
anaerobic-development days (Figure 2.6, PDF p. 78, printed p. 67): session 2 is substantial
load for anaerobic glycolytic power (fast lactate/oxygen-debt accumulation); the one-hour
break before session 3 allows roughly 70-80% of accumulated lactate to be oxidized (Volkov,
1986), so session 3's anaerobic glycolytic capacity work still starts with an
already-activated glycolytic/enzymatic system; session 4 (after a three-hour break, athletes
arriving fatigued) targets anaerobic strength endurance, deliberately sustaining progressive
fatigue. **Source inconsistency:** the body text calls session 2 "highly intense aerobic
power exercises," but the Figure 2.6 box for that same session reads "anaerobic glycolitic
power series" (PDF p. 78, printed p. 67); this entry follows the figure's label, since that
is where the load level and content are specified. For the more common two-a-day structure, Table
2.13 (PDF p. 79, printed p. 68) gives compatible first/second-workout pairings by dominant
ability: aerobic power/capacity, fartlek (10-15s sprint, 3-6min at anaerobic threshold)
first, aerobic interval series second; anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity, anaerobic power
interval series first, anaerobic capacity interval series second; maximal speed, anaerobic
alactic interval series first, anaerobic alactic plus explosive strength exercises second;
techno-tactical abilities, techno-tactical simulation/maximum speed first, match/scrimmage
second.

**Why it works** — Issurin states the purpose directly: subdividing the daily training into
three, four, or more workouts is meant to increase the quality of training (the intensity of
exercises and their partial volume), create more favorable conditions for restoration, and
let technique improvement benefit from a relatively better-restored athlete (PDF p. 77,
printed p. 66). **Inference:** the break length between sessions determines how much of the
prior session's fatigue and metabolic byproduct load has cleared before the next session
begins, and the daily plan appears to exploit this: shorter breaks (one hour) leave residual
glycolytic activation that helps a subsequent glycolytic-capacity session, while longer
breaks (three hours) still leave athletes fatigued enough that only fatigue-tolerant
modalities (strength endurance, continuous aerobic work) are appropriate for the day's final
session. This generalization is this entry's own reading of the pattern, not a mechanism
Issurin states in those terms.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** directly applicable to football fall-camp scheduling,
where two-a-day sessions are standard; check whether current NCAA Division I preseason rules
restrict multiple-practice days, and check Baylor's actual camp schedule, before applying.
**Eric's baseline** names a specific priority stack for fall camp —
"Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` pp.34, 39), and Table 2.13's
maximal-speed pairing (anaerobic alactic interval series both sessions, explosive strength
added to the second) is a directly relevant template for structuring a two-a-day built
around that same alactic/aerobic priority.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Issurin gives no controlled-study citation for the
specific figures in this section (session load levels, the four-session structure, the
70-80% lactate-oxidation-in-one-hour figure attributed to Volkov, 1986, is the one sourced
number; the rest of the daily-series structure reads as the author's own applied synthesis).
The four-session model is explicitly noted as less common in practice than the two-a-day.
**Inference:** none of this section's examples are football-specific (they are framed around
individual/endurance-and-power sports generally); the specific break lengths (one hour,
three hours) and load progressions should be treated as a template to adapt, not a
prescription to copy directly into a football fall-camp schedule without accounting for
football-specific factors (equipment, heat, practice structure, position-group differences)
not addressed in this chapter.

**Example** — **Inference:** a fall-camp two-a-day built around the department's stated
alactic/aerobic priority could pair a morning session of alactic interval sprint work with an
afternoon
session combining more alactic work and explosive strength (per Table 2.13's maximal-speed
row), rather than defaulting to a generic "conditioning AM, lift PM" split that does not
target a specific dominant ability across the two sessions.

**Related** — [[claim--morning-resistance-training-no-decrement-after-6hr-rest]],
[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

# World-Class Track and Field Athletes Compete and Peak Many Times Per Season, Not Once

**What it is** — Table 1.5 (PDF p. 24, printed p. 13, based on Suslov, 2001, with Issurin's
modifications) reports three world-class athletes' single-season competition patterns:
**Marion Jones** (100-200m, long jump; 1998 season) had **10 peaks** (8 in running, 2 in
long jump, all at personal-best level) across a **200-day** competitive span, with typical
19-22 day intervals between peaks. **Sergei Bubka** (pole vault; 1991 season) had **7
peaks** (all within 3% of his personal best, 595-612 cm) across a **265-day** span,
23-43 day intervals. **Stefka Kostadinova** (high jump; 1998 season) had **11 peaks** (all
within 3% of her personal best, 200-205 cm), 14-25 day intervals, across winter ~20 days and
spring/summer 135 days (**Inference:** 155 days combined; the table gives the two figures
separately, not a single summed span). Issurin's summary point, stated on the preceding page
(PDF p. 23, printed p. 12): these athletes' 5-8 month competitive spans "can not be
subdivided into traditional preparatory and competitive periods," yet their basic abilities
(max strength, aerobic regeneration capacity) still had to be maintained across that entire
span.

**Why it works: this is observational, not interventional** — These are real competition
records for three specific, historically documented elite athletes (Olympic/World
champions), not an experiment; the "why" is a report of what elite competition calendars
actually looked like by 1991/1998, cited to Suslov's (2001) analysis rather than derived
from a controlled study of periodization models.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** as direct evidence for the strength-and-conditioning
miss-log's "peaking phase structure" gap, this table is the empirical case Issurin uses to argue that a
single annual peak (or even a two-/three-peak model) does not describe how modern elite
individual-sport athletes actually compete, which motivates the multi-stage annual model in
[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]]. Useful for framing the *problem*
(competition calendars now demand many peaks) to Baylor coaches even before the
*solution* (Chapter 3's microcycle-level guidance, not yet ingested) is available.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — All three examples are individual, non-contact,
technique/power sports (sprinting/jumping, pole vault, high jump) where "peak" can be defined
by a single measurable performance (time, height, distance) on a given day. **Inference:**
this evidence does not directly transfer to football, where "peak" is not a single
measurable output and the competitive calendar is fixed by a weekly game schedule rather
than a chosen sequence of meets, the multi-peak *problem* generalizes (a football season
also demands repeated high-level performance, not one), but the specific 19-43 day
inter-peak intervals shown here are specific to how often these particular athletes chose to
compete, not a transferable spacing rule for football practice or game weeks. Data source is
single (Suslov, 2001, "with modifications" by Issurin) with no stated method for how "peak"
was defined or verified for each performance.

**Example** — **Inference:** when explaining to a Baylor position group why in-season
programming assumes more than one readiness peak per season, this table is a citable,
real-world existence proof that elite athletes routinely peak 7-11 times in a season; useful
for framing, not for directly copying an inter-peak interval into a football in-season plan.

**Related** — [[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]].

14	# No More Than Three Training Modalities Per Workout, With 65-70% of Time on One or Two
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin extends the concentration principle to single-session design
17	(Figure 2.4, PDF p. 74, printed p. 63; Table 2.12, PDF p. 76, printed p. 65) with five
18	stated rules (PDF p. 75, printed p. 64): (1) a workout should contain **no more than three
19	training modalities**, typically one dominant, one compatible with the main purpose, and
20	one for technique/tactics improvement or restoration; (2) **65-70% of total training time**
21	in a development workout should go to one or two selected modalities, to preserve workload
22	concentration; (3) the typical frequency of workouts in high-performance training (6-12 a
23	week) dictates certain conditions for the session after a key-workout: it should show a
24	significant load reduction, and running two consecutive key-workouts, while possible, risks
25	excessive load concentration; (4) hypertrophy-focused sessions require workload to be
26	"substantially reduced" for **at least 20 hours** afterward to protect the anabolic phase of
27	muscle restoration; (5) limiting modality count matters most in high-performance sport; the
28	daily program for juniors, for example, may be more diverse, multilateral, and therefore
29	more attractive. Figure 2.4 maps which modalities are compatible as secondary/tertiary
30	additions to five dominant ones: aerobic endurance pairs with alactic sprint,
31	strength-endurance-aerobic, and hypertrophy-strength (placed after); anaerobic glycolytic
32	endurance pairs with strength-endurance-anaerobic, aerobic restoration, and mixed
33	aerobic-anaerobic endurance; alactic sprint pairs with aerobic endurance, explosive
34	strength, hypertrophy-strength (after), and aerobic restoration; hypertrophy-strength pairs
35	with neural-strength, flexibility, and aerobic restoration; and, when learning new technical
36	elements is the dominant task, any kind of training modality may be added, but only *after*
37	the dominant, technical-learning task, not before it. Table 2.12 gives the
38	physiological/psychological rationale for
39	several of the strongest pairings (e.g., aerobic endurance + strength endurance: increased
40	oxidation supports the resistance work; alactic sprint + aerobic endurance: brief sprints
41	break monotony and keep a wide muscle-fiber pool activated for the subsequent aerobic work).

44	underlying logic is the same concentration principle from Chapter 1
45	([[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]): splitting a session across too many
46	modalities dilutes the stimulus for all of them. **Inference:** Issurin gives no stated
47	derivation for why the cutoff is exactly three modalities rather than two or four, why the
48	time-share threshold is 65-70% rather than some other range, or why 20 hours is the specific
49	reduced-load window after hypertrophy work (versus, e.g., 24 or 48 hours), these read as
50	the author's own practical rules of thumb built from coaching experience rather than
51	citations to a dose-response study.
52	
53	**When to apply** — Auditing whether a practice plan or lift is trying to do too much:
54	count distinct training modalities in a session and check whether one or two of them
55	actually receive the majority of training time, per the 65-70% rule. Use Figure 2.4/Table
56	2.12 to check whether a planned secondary modality is a known-compatible pairing or an
57	unaddressed combination. **Eric's baseline:** the class-1 lecture (transcript pp.28-29)

63	single-session level. This Issurin entry gives that instinct a specific numeric structure

75

77	conditioning, maximal-speed sprint work, and new-install technical work in one session would

14	# Accumulation, Transmutation (Transformation), and Realization: the Three Mesocycle-Blocks
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin's core structural unit is the mesocycle-block, one of three types
17	(Table 1.7, PDF p. 38, printed p. 27): **Accumulation** targets basic abilities (aerobic
18	endurance, muscular strength, basic coordination) with high volume/reduced intensity and
19	"reasonable restoration"; **Transmutation** targets sport-specific abilities (special
20	endurance, strength endurance, proper technique) with reduced volume/increased intensity,
21	and explicitly does *not* provide full restoration, fatigue accumulates; **Realization**
22	targets integrative, competition-ready preparedness (model performances, maximum speed,

# Accumulation, Transmutation (Transformation), and Realization: the Three Mesocycle-Blocks

**What it is** — Issurin's core structural unit is the mesocycle-block, one of three types
(Table 1.7, PDF p. 38, printed p. 27): **Accumulation** targets basic abilities (aerobic
endurance, muscular strength, basic coordination) with high volume/reduced intensity and
"reasonable restoration"; **Transmutation** targets sport-specific abilities (special
endurance, strength endurance, proper technique) with reduced volume/increased intensity,
and explicitly does *not* provide full restoration, fatigue accumulates; **Realization**
targets integrative, competition-ready preparedness (model performances, maximum speed,
event-specific tactics) at low-medium volume/high intensity, with full restoration required
going in. Each type has its own monitoring focus: basic-ability tests for accumulation,
sport-specific-ability tests for transmutation, and maximum speed/strategy checks for
realization. Original prescribed durations: about four weeks each for accumulation and
transformation, two weeks for realization (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22); more generally,
mesocycle-blocks run about 2-6 weeks, the time needed for morphological, organic, and
biochemical adaptation (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21). **Locator note:** the 1985 origin paper
(Issurin & Kaverin) and this book's 1.2.1 narrative (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22) use the term
**transformation**; from section 1.2.2 onward, starting at PDF p. 38, printed p. 27 (not
p.26 as the offset alone would suggest), and in the book's own tables, the term used is
**transmutation**. Both names refer to the same middle block; record both because a search
for either term should resolve to this entry.

**Why it works** — The sequencing is designed to exploit the fact that different motor
abilities have different **residual training effect** durations (see
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]): basic abilities (aerobic
endurance, max strength) decay slowest, so they can be built early and coast on their own
residual while transmutation and realization narrow the focus toward faster-decaying,
more specific and speed-dependent qualities close to competition. Issurin frames this as
superimposition of residual effects (Figure 1.8, PDF p. 39, printed p. 28) rather than
concurrent development of everything at once.

**When to apply** — Structuring a training stage (the accumulation-transmutation-realization
sequence, ending in competition) for advanced athletes who need multiple qualities peaked
together; see [[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]] for how these three
blocks compose into a full annual plan. **Eric's baseline:** the course teaches
accumulation/transmutation/realization directly from Issurin (week1-lecture.md marker p.65,
in the same slide block that names "Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source, marker
p.64). The department's own preparatory-period design, hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic
strength, then strength-to-power (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
citing week1-lecture.md pp.43-48), is a separate general-to-specific progression, not a
restatement of A-T-R; it is not explicitly framed with Issurin's residual-effect
superimposition logic or his restoration-status distinctions between blocks.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — This is a three-way classification built for advanced
athletes who can tolerate the fatigue-accumulating transmutation block (see
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] for the low-/mid-level-athlete
carve-out). It presumes a training stage that ends in a real competition or test date to
absorb the realization block's tapering logic; without a fixed target date, there is no
clear trigger for when accumulation should end and transmutation begin. **Inference (beyond
this review's scope, flagged during this fix pass since it repeats the same Bompa problem
found in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]):** the vault's Bompa & Haff
material (`periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching`) describes a
comparable saturated-load-then-restitution structure with a 4-12 week delayed rebound, a
longer and less rigidly three-staged model than Issurin's roughly two-month training stage
(below); the two should be read as convergent, not identical, prescriptions, and a program
note should say which model's timing a given plan follows.

**Example** — **Inference:** a training stage built for a mid-season peak using the book's
own prescribed durations (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22): about 4 weeks of accumulation (aerobic
base, general strength), about 4 weeks of transmutation (sport-specific conditioning,
strength-endurance, technique under fatigue), then 2 weeks of realization (tapered volume,
high-intensity model-speed work, full restoration) ending at the target competition or test
date.

15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin's annual cycle is built from a sequence of **training stages**,
17	each one containing all three mesocycle-blocks (accumulation, transmutation, realization) in
18	order, ending in a competition (PDF p. 38, printed p. 27). Each training stage "gives the
19	appearance of an annual cycle in miniature", a block resembling a preparatory period
20	(accumulation), one resembling a competition period (transmutation), and a tapering block
21	ending in competitive performance (realization) (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28). The duration of
22	a training stage is set by how long the constituent residual training effects can be
23	superimposed (Figure 1.8; see
24	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]) and "should be about two
25	months," though Issurin notes stages can run shorter near season's end or longer earlier in
26	the season, in which case "special measures should be used to prolong residual training
27	effects" (unspecified in this chapter, likely developed in Chapter 3, not yet ingested).
28	The number of training stages in a season "usually varies from four to seven," depending on
29	the sport's competition calendar (PDF p. 40, printed p. 29, Figure 1.9). Issurin lists four
30	benefits of this design over the traditional model at this point in the text (PDF p. 40,
31	printed p. 29): the model allows a reduction in total mileage and time spent training
32	without substantially changing the total number of workouts; monitoring of trainedness is
33	more purposeful and effective, because the reduced number of targeted abilities allows more
34	appropriate tests and an easier dose-effect analysis; psychological traits improve because
35	athletes can focus on fewer abilities, supporting mental concentration and motivation; and
36	nutritional aspects can be more carefully targeted (a high-protein diet to enhance strength
37	training's anabolic effect, and carbohydrates "particularly important in mesocycles for
38	specialized and strength-endurance" work). Table 1.8 (PDF p. 42, printed p. 31) is a
39	separate table contrasting the traditional and Block Periodization models' main differences,
40	not itself a benefits list. A second, five-item benefit summary appears later in the chapter
41	(PDF p. 44, printed p. 33), largely repeating the first four points and adding a fifth: "a
42	multi-stage annual plan creates more favorable conditions for peaking in time for the main
43	competition of the season," with intermediate peaks plannable mid-season or even early
44	season, not only at a single season-end date.
45	
46	**Why it works** — Because each training stage runs its own compressed
47	accumulation-transmutation-realization cycle and ends in a real competitive test, the athlete
48	is brought to a peak (or near-peak) at the end of every stage rather than once per year;
49	stacking four to seven such stages across a season is what produces the multi-peak pattern.
50	Issurin's stated physiological contrast (Table 1.8) is that the traditional model relies on
51	adaptation to concurrent stimuli across a long period, while this model relies on
52	superimposing sequential residual effects from short, concentrated blocks, the same
53	mechanism underlying [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].
54	
55	**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the entry most directly responsive to the strength-and-conditioning
56	miss-log gap ("peaking phase structure for collegiate football," logged 2026-09-03): for a
57	football program needing camp-readiness, then in-season week-to-week competitive readiness,
58	this framework suggests treating each significant test point (fall camp scrimmage, each
59	game week, or a defined in-season block) as a candidate training-stage boundary rather than
60	relying on a single annual peak, with the caveat below about untested claims. **Eric's
61	baseline** does not currently describe an explicit training-stage or multi-peak model for
62	football; the closest baseline material is the general macro/meso/microcycle planning
63	language and the in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (`method-baseline.md`,
64	"Periodization and programming" and "Strength and power," citing
65	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.17-18, 20-21), this Issurin framework offers a
66	more explicit structural answer to "how do you actually sequence a season with more than one
67	peak" than anything currently captured in the baseline.
68	
69	**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — The "four to seven stages" and "about two months"
70	figures are stated without a derivation the reader can check: Issurin gives no worked
71	example of how stage count or duration is calculated for a specific sport's calendar in
72	this chapter. **Inference:** football's in-season structure (weekly games, not discrete
73	multi-week competition-free blocks) does not map cleanly onto a ~2-month training stage.
74	Issurin's model is built from and mainly evidenced by individual/dual sports with discrete
75	competitions (track and field, canoe-kayak, windsurfing); Chapter 3's microcycle-level
76	material (now ingested; see `_book.md`) is a necessary next read before this framework can
77	be translated into a week-by-week in-season football plan. **Contested:** Issurin's "does
78	not work well for high-performance athletes" framing of the traditional alternative (PDF p.

83	cached in this library at
84	`research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a.md`).
85	That review reports that concentrated-unidirectional programs in team and combat sports
86	improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team
87	practice or competitive performance (its p.6): a direct qualification of the confident
88	five-benefit list above, for exactly the team-sport context football sits in. **Inference:**

90	well" claim, but only Bompa Ch1-2 has been ingested so far (`periodization--bompa/_book.md`:

92	check once those chapters are ingested.

# Concentration of Training Workloads Is the Cornerstone Principle of Block Periodization

**What it is** — Issurin states the Block Periodization Concept (BPC) rests on one
foundational principle, concentration of training workloads, from which two others follow:
(1) a minimal number of targeted abilities per block, because highly concentrated loads
"only provide sufficient training stimuli to improve the targeted ability," and (2)
consecutive (not simultaneous) development of abilities, because "the number of decisive
abilities exceeds the number of abilities that can be developed simultaneously" (PDF p. 37,
printed p. 26, Figure 1.7). The rationale is laid out as a table of contradictions in the
traditional, simultaneous-development model for high-level athletes (Table 1.4, PDF p. 20,
printed p. 9): energy supply gets spread across too many targets so the main one does not
get the attention it needs, differing physiological-system restoration times leave athletes
under-recovered for all targets at once, workloads interact negatively (energy deficits,
technical complexity, neuromuscular fatigue), mental concentration cannot be split across
many targets, and the training stimulus needed for a high-level athlete's progress cannot be
reached when it is divided among many abilities. **Locator note:** Table 1.4's
Contradictions column literally reads "There is sufficient energy supply for concurrent
performance of diversified workloads" (PDF p. 20, printed p. 9); its Consequences column
implies the opposite, "Energy is directed to many targets while the main target doesn't get
the appropriate attention." This reads as an apparent wording inconsistency in the source;
the table's overall point, that concentration protects the main target's stimulus, still
stands.

**Why it works** — Issurin's own explanation is that above a threshold of athletic level,
a quality only responds to a training stimulus concentrated enough to exceed that
threshold; splitting the same total training time across many qualities keeps each one's
stimulus below that threshold. He does not give a quantitative mechanism for where that
threshold sits or how "concentrated enough" is defined for a given ability or athlete, the
principle is argued from coaches' and scientists' collective experience (Table 1.4) rather
than derived from a stated dose-response model.

**When to apply** — Designing training blocks for advanced, high-level athletes juggling
more qualities than can be trained well at once (the explicit target population, per
Issurin). **Eric's baseline:** the course teaches this rule from Issurin directly
(week1-lecture.md marker pp.64, 67, which name "Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source
for block periodization and file "you can't ride 2 horses w/one saddle" under the same
section), not as an independent convergence: "you can't ride two horses with one saddle",
incompatible qualities are not both trained at full intensity in the same block
(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29). It also converges with
[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]], which independently
describes concentrated, saturated loading on one quality with a delayed 4-12 week rebound.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Issurin's own text (PDF p. 44, printed p. 33) states the
traditional, complex (simultaneous multi-ability) model "has visible benefits for the
preparation of low- and mid-level athletes": it is "more diversified, attractive and
lively," and medium-level concentration is "sufficient stimulation" at that level: the
concentration principle is explicitly scoped to high-performance athletes, not a universal
programming rule. **Contested:** Issurin's blanket claim elsewhere in the same chapter that
the traditional model "does not work well for high-performance athletes" (PDF p. 19,
printed p. 8) is disputed by Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review (Issurin, 2016,
*Sports Medicine*, "Benefits and Limitations of Block Periodized Training Approaches to
Athletes' Preparation," Zotero item `PT9QTQ2I`, full text cached in this library at
`research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a.md`):
that review judges concentrated-unidirectional block programs' evidence insufficient for
broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation, and
frames the concentrated-unidirectional model as restricted when peak performance requires
many interacting abilities (its p.6, p.11), a real narrowing of this 2008 book's confident
"does not work well for high-performance athletes" framing, for exactly the population this
principle targets. **Inference:** Bompa & Haff's 5th edition, already in this library, may
also bear on this claim, but only Bompa Ch1-2 has been ingested so far
(`periodization--bompa/_book.md`: Ch6 Annual Plan and Ch8 Training Cycles are pending); the
one relevant ingested entry, `principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching`, *converges*
with Issurin rather than disputing him, so it cannot be used to ground this contest. Check
whether Bompa & Haff Ch6-8 defend period-based annual planning for high-level athletes once
those chapters are ingested. Issurin's critique in this chapter also names Bompa's *1984*
edition specifically (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2) as one of the texts that propagated the
traditional model he is arguing against; that is a different, narrower target than the 5th
edition.

**Example** — **Inference:** a collegiate football strength staff trying to develop max strength,
aerobic capacity, alactic power, and technical skill acquisition all at full intensity in
the same 4-week block, per Table 1.4's logic, risks under-stimulating all four rather than
meaningfully improving any one; concentrating the block on 1-2 of them (with the rest held
at a retention dose) is the alternative Issurin argues for.

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]], the three-block
structure this principle produces. [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]
and [[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]], converging concentrated-load
ideas already in this library. [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (staging):
check for overlap on why generalized simultaneous training under-delivers for advanced
athletes.

# No More Than Three Training Modalities Per Workout, With 65-70% of Time on One or Two

**What it is** — Issurin extends the concentration principle to single-session design
(Figure 2.4, PDF p. 74, printed p. 63; Table 2.12, PDF p. 76, printed p. 65) with five
stated rules (PDF p. 75, printed p. 64): (1) a workout should contain **no more than three
training modalities**, typically one dominant, one compatible with the main purpose, and
one for technique/tactics improvement or restoration; (2) **65-70% of total training time**
in a development workout should go to one or two selected modalities, to preserve workload
concentration; (3) the typical frequency of workouts in high-performance training (6-12 a
week) dictates certain conditions for the session after a key-workout: it should show a
significant load reduction, and running two consecutive key-workouts, while possible, risks
excessive load concentration; (4) hypertrophy-focused sessions require workload to be
"substantially reduced" for **at least 20 hours** afterward to protect the anabolic phase of
muscle restoration; (5) limiting modality count matters most in high-performance sport; the
daily program for juniors, for example, may be more diverse, multilateral, and therefore
more attractive. Figure 2.4 maps which modalities are compatible as secondary/tertiary
additions to five dominant ones: aerobic endurance pairs with alactic sprint,
strength-endurance-aerobic, and hypertrophy-strength (placed after); anaerobic glycolytic
endurance pairs with strength-endurance-anaerobic, aerobic restoration, and mixed
aerobic-anaerobic endurance; alactic sprint pairs with aerobic endurance, explosive
strength, hypertrophy-strength (after), and aerobic restoration; hypertrophy-strength pairs
with neural-strength, flexibility, and aerobic restoration; and, when learning new technical
elements is the dominant task, any kind of training modality may be added, but only *after*
the dominant, technical-learning task, not before it. Table 2.12 gives the
physiological/psychological rationale for
several of the strongest pairings (e.g., aerobic endurance + strength endurance: increased
oxidation supports the resistance work; alactic sprint + aerobic endurance: brief sprints
break monotony and keep a wide muscle-fiber pool activated for the subsequent aerobic work).

**Why it works: the specific numeric thresholds are asserted, not derived** — The
underlying logic is the same concentration principle from Chapter 1
([[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]): splitting a session across too many
modalities dilutes the stimulus for all of them. **Inference:** Issurin gives no stated
derivation for why the cutoff is exactly three modalities rather than two or four, why the
time-share threshold is 65-70% rather than some other range, or why 20 hours is the specific
reduced-load window after hypertrophy work (versus, e.g., 24 or 48 hours), these read as
the author's own practical rules of thumb built from coaching experience rather than
citations to a dose-response study.

**When to apply** — Auditing whether a practice plan or lift is trying to do too much:
count distinct training modalities in a session and check whether one or two of them
actually receive the majority of training time, per the 65-70% rule. Use Figure 2.4/Table
2.12 to check whether a planned secondary modality is a known-compatible pairing or an
unaddressed combination. **Eric's baseline:** the class-1 lecture (transcript pp.28-29)
presents this same Figure 2.4 chart, and the course attributes its block-periodization
material to Issurin (week1-lecture.md marker p.64); "incompatible qualities... are not both
targeted at full intensity in the same block" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29, "you can't ride two
horses with one saddle") is the same instinct at the block level rather than the
single-session level. This Issurin entry gives that instinct a specific numeric structure
(≤3 modalities, 65-70% time-share) that the baseline material does not itself repeat at the
session level.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Treat the ≤3-modality, 65-70%, and 20-hour figures as
Issurin's own heuristics rather than established constants: no citation or underlying data
is given for any of the three in this chapter. Issurin explicitly narrows the number
constraints to high-performance training; junior/developmental programming is stated to
reasonably need more variety, not fewer modalities. Figure 2.4's compatibility map is not
exhaustive (it covers five dominant modalities, not every possible combination); an
untested pairing should not be assumed incompatible or compatible by default; Issurin gives
no guidance for modalities not shown in the figure.

**Example** — **Inference:** a practice plan combining strength-endurance, aerobic-anaerobic
conditioning, maximal-speed sprint work, and new-install technical work in one session would
have four distinct modalities, exceeding the stated ≤3 rule. Per Figure 2.4, glycolytic
endurance pairs well with strength-endurance-anaerobic and aerobic restoration; new-install
technical work, if it is the priority for the day, should stay the dominant, first task of
its own session (per Figure 2.3, new-skill acquisition needs a well-rested or only slightly
fatigued athlete), with strength-endurance or conditioning work added afterward, or moved to
a separate session entirely, rather than demoted to a secondary slot after glycolytic work.

**Related** — [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]],
[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]].

# Accumulation, Transmutation (Transformation), and Realization: the Three Mesocycle-Blocks

**What it is** — Issurin's core structural unit is the mesocycle-block, one of three types
(Table 1.7, PDF p. 38, printed p. 27): **Accumulation** targets basic abilities (aerobic
endurance, muscular strength, basic coordination) with high volume/reduced intensity and
"reasonable restoration"; **Transmutation** targets sport-specific abilities (special
endurance, strength endurance, proper technique) with reduced volume/increased intensity,
and explicitly does *not* provide full restoration, fatigue accumulates; **Realization**
targets integrative, competition-ready preparedness (model performances, maximum speed,
event-specific tactics) at low-medium volume/high intensity, with full restoration required
going in. Each type has its own monitoring focus: basic-ability tests for accumulation,
sport-specific-ability tests for transmutation, and maximum speed/strategy checks for
realization. Original prescribed durations: about four weeks each for accumulation and
transformation, two weeks for realization (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22); more generally,
mesocycle-blocks run about 2-6 weeks, the time needed for morphological, organic, and
biochemical adaptation (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21). **Locator note:** the 1985 origin paper
(Issurin & Kaverin) and this book's 1.2.1 narrative (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22) use the term
**transformation**; from section 1.2.2 onward, starting at PDF p. 38, printed p. 27 (not
p.26 as the offset alone would suggest), and in the book's own tables, the term used is
**transmutation**. Both names refer to the same middle block; record both because a search
for either term should resolve to this entry.

**Why it works** — The sequencing is designed to exploit the fact that different motor
abilities have different **residual training effect** durations (see
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]): basic abilities (aerobic
endurance, max strength) decay slowest, so they can be built early and coast on their own
residual while transmutation and realization narrow the focus toward faster-decaying,
more specific and speed-dependent qualities close to competition. Issurin frames this as
superimposition of residual effects (Figure 1.8, PDF p. 39, printed p. 28) rather than
concurrent development of everything at once.

**When to apply** — Structuring a training stage (the accumulation-transmutation-realization
sequence, ending in competition) for advanced athletes who need multiple qualities peaked
together; see [[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]] for how these three
blocks compose into a full annual plan. **Eric's baseline:** the course teaches
accumulation/transmutation/realization directly from Issurin (week1-lecture.md marker p.65,
in the same slide block that names "Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source, marker
p.64). The department's own preparatory-period design, hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic
strength, then strength-to-power (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
citing week1-lecture.md pp.43-48), is a separate general-to-specific progression, not a
restatement of A-T-R; it is not explicitly framed with Issurin's residual-effect
superimposition logic or his restoration-status distinctions between blocks.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — This is a three-way classification built for advanced
athletes who can tolerate the fatigue-accumulating transmutation block (see
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] for the low-/mid-level-athlete
carve-out). It presumes a training stage that ends in a real competition or test date to
absorb the realization block's tapering logic; without a fixed target date, there is no
clear trigger for when accumulation should end and transmutation begin. **Inference (beyond
this review's scope, flagged during this fix pass since it repeats the same Bompa problem
found in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]):** the vault's Bompa & Haff
material (`periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching`) describes a
comparable saturated-load-then-restitution structure with a 4-12 week delayed rebound, a
longer and less rigidly three-staged model than Issurin's roughly two-month training stage
(below); the two should be read as convergent, not identical, prescriptions, and a program
note should say which model's timing a given plan follows.

**Example** — **Inference:** a training stage built for a mid-season peak using the book's
own prescribed durations (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22): about 4 weeks of accumulation (aerobic
base, general strength), about 4 weeks of transmutation (sport-specific conditioning,
strength-endurance, technique under fatigue), then 2 weeks of realization (tapered volume,
high-intensity model-speed work, full restoration) ending at the target competition or test
date.

# The Training Stage (A-T-R + Competition) Is the Annual Plan's Building Block, Enabling Multiple Peaks

**What it is** — Issurin's annual cycle is built from a sequence of **training stages**,
each one containing all three mesocycle-blocks (accumulation, transmutation, realization) in
order, ending in a competition (PDF p. 38, printed p. 27). Each training stage "gives the
appearance of an annual cycle in miniature", a block resembling a preparatory period
(accumulation), one resembling a competition period (transmutation), and a tapering block
ending in competitive performance (realization) (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28). The duration of
a training stage is set by how long the constituent residual training effects can be
superimposed (Figure 1.8; see
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]) and "should be about two
months," though Issurin notes stages can run shorter near season's end or longer earlier in
the season, in which case "special measures should be used to prolong residual training
effects" (unspecified in this chapter, likely developed in Chapter 3, not yet ingested).
The number of training stages in a season "usually varies from four to seven," depending on
the sport's competition calendar (PDF p. 40, printed p. 29, Figure 1.9). Issurin lists four
benefits of this design over the traditional model at this point in the text (PDF p. 40,
printed p. 29): the model allows a reduction in total mileage and time spent training
without substantially changing the total number of workouts; monitoring of trainedness is
more purposeful and effective, because the reduced number of targeted abilities allows more
appropriate tests and an easier dose-effect analysis; psychological traits improve because
athletes can focus on fewer abilities, supporting mental concentration and motivation; and
nutritional aspects can be more carefully targeted (a high-protein diet to enhance strength
training's anabolic effect, and carbohydrates "particularly important in mesocycles for
specialized and strength-endurance" work). Table 1.8 (PDF p. 42, printed p. 31) is a
separate table contrasting the traditional and Block Periodization models' main differences,
not itself a benefits list. A second, five-item benefit summary appears later in the chapter
(PDF p. 44, printed p. 33), largely repeating the first four points and adding a fifth: "a
multi-stage annual plan creates more favorable conditions for peaking in time for the main
competition of the season," with intermediate peaks plannable mid-season or even early
season, not only at a single season-end date.

**Why it works** — Because each training stage runs its own compressed
accumulation-transmutation-realization cycle and ends in a real competitive test, the athlete
is brought to a peak (or near-peak) at the end of every stage rather than once per year;
stacking four to seven such stages across a season is what produces the multi-peak pattern.
Issurin's stated physiological contrast (Table 1.8) is that the traditional model relies on
adaptation to concurrent stimuli across a long period, while this model relies on
superimposing sequential residual effects from short, concentrated blocks, the same
mechanism underlying [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the entry most directly responsive to the strength-and-conditioning
miss-log gap ("peaking phase structure for collegiate football," logged 2026-09-03): for a
football program needing camp-readiness, then in-season week-to-week competitive readiness,
this framework suggests treating each significant test point (fall camp scrimmage, each
game week, or a defined in-season block) as a candidate training-stage boundary rather than
relying on a single annual peak, with the caveat below about untested claims. **Eric's
baseline** does not currently describe an explicit training-stage or multi-peak model for
football; the closest baseline material is the general macro/meso/microcycle planning
language and the in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Periodization and programming" and "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.17-18, 20-21), this Issurin framework offers a
more explicit structural answer to "how do you actually sequence a season with more than one
peak" than anything currently captured in the baseline.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — The "four to seven stages" and "about two months"
figures are stated without a derivation the reader can check: Issurin gives no worked
example of how stage count or duration is calculated for a specific sport's calendar in
this chapter. **Inference:** football's in-season structure (weekly games, not discrete
multi-week competition-free blocks) does not map cleanly onto a ~2-month training stage.
Issurin's model is built from and mainly evidenced by individual/dual sports with discrete
competitions (track and field, canoe-kayak, windsurfing); Chapter 3's microcycle-level
material (now ingested; see `_book.md`) is a necessary next read before this framework can
be translated into a week-by-week in-season football plan. **Contested:** Issurin's "does
not work well for high-performance athletes" framing of the traditional alternative (PDF p.
19, printed p. 8, the same claim flagged in
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]) is disputed by Issurin's own later
peer-reviewed review (Issurin, 2016, *Sports Medicine*, "Benefits and Limitations of Block
Periodized Training Approaches to Athletes' Preparation," Zotero item `PT9QTQ2I`, full text
cached in this library at
`research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a.md`).
That review reports that concentrated-unidirectional programs in team and combat sports
improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team
practice or competitive performance (its p.6): a direct qualification of the confident
five-benefit list above, for exactly the team-sport context football sits in. **Inference:**
Bompa & Haff's 5th edition, already in this library, may also bear on the "does not work
well" claim, but only Bompa Ch1-2 has been ingested so far (`periodization--bompa/_book.md`:
Ch6 Annual Plan and Ch8 Training Cycles are pending), so it cannot ground this contest yet;
check once those chapters are ingested.

**Example** — **Inference:** a five-stage football off-season/camp plan: Stage 1 (general
accumulation, ~8 weeks, winter conditioning); Stage 2 (strength/power transmutation into
spring ball, ending in the spring game as a "competition"); Stage 3 (summer accumulation);
Stage 4 (fall-camp transmutation, ending in the first scrimmage or game week as
realization); Stage 5+ (in-season stages keyed to bye weeks or rivalry-week peaks, pending
Chapter 3's in-season microcycle guidance).
