# The Training Stage (A-T-R + Competition) Is the Annual Plan's Building Block, Enabling Multiple Peaks

**What it is** — Issurin's annual cycle is built from a sequence of **training stages**,
each one containing all three mesocycle-blocks (accumulation, transmutation, realization) in
order, ending in a competition (PDF p. 38, printed p. 27). Each training stage "gives the
appearance of an annual cycle in miniature", a block resembling a preparatory period
(accumulation), one resembling a competition period (transmutation), and a tapering block
ending in competitive performance (realization) (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28). The duration of
a training stage is set by how long the constituent residual training effects can be
superimposed (Figure 1.8; see
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]) and "should be about two
months," though Issurin notes stages can run shorter near season's end or longer earlier in
the season, in which case "special measures should be used to prolong residual training
effects" (unspecified in this chapter; developed in Chapter 3, now ingested, see `_book.md`).
The number of training stages in a season "usually varies from four to seven," depending on
the sport's competition calendar (PDF p. 40, printed p. 29, Figure 1.9). Issurin lists four
benefits of this design over the traditional model at this point in the text (PDF p. 40,
printed p. 29): the model allows a reduction in total mileage and time spent training
without substantially changing the total number of workouts; monitoring of trainedness is
more purposeful and effective, because the reduced number of targeted abilities allows more
appropriate tests and an easier dose-effect analysis; psychological traits improve because
athletes can focus on fewer abilities, supporting mental concentration and motivation; and
nutritional aspects can be more carefully targeted (a high-protein diet to enhance strength
training's anabolic effect, and carbohydrates "particularly important in mesocycles for
specialized and strength-endurance" work). Table 1.8 (PDF p. 42, printed p. 31) is a
separate table contrasting the traditional and Block Periodization models' main differences,
not itself a benefits list. A second, five-item benefit summary appears later in the chapter
(PDF p. 44, printed p. 33), largely repeating the first four points and adding a fifth: "a
multi-stage annual plan creates more favorable conditions for peaking in time for the main
competition of the season," with intermediate peaks plannable mid-season or even early
season, not only at a single season-end date.

**Why it works** — Because each training stage runs its own compressed
accumulation-transmutation-realization cycle and ends in a real competitive test, the athlete
is brought to a peak (or near-peak) at the end of every stage rather than once per year;
stacking four to seven such stages across a season is what produces the multi-peak pattern.
Issurin's stated physiological contrast (Table 1.8) is that the traditional model relies on
adaptation to concurrent stimuli across a long period, while this model relies on
superimposing sequential residual effects from short, concentrated blocks, the same
mechanism underlying [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the entry most directly responsive to the strength-and-conditioning
miss-log gap ("peaking phase structure for collegiate football," logged 2026-09-03): for a
football program needing camp-readiness, then in-season week-to-week competitive readiness,
this framework suggests treating each significant test point (fall camp scrimmage, each
game week, or a defined in-season block) as a candidate training-stage boundary rather than
relying on a single annual peak, with the caveat below about untested claims. **Eric's
baseline** does not currently describe an explicit training-stage or multi-peak model for
football; the closest baseline material is the general macro/meso/microcycle planning
language and the in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Periodization and programming" and "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.17-18, 20-21), this Issurin framework offers a
more explicit structural answer to "how do you actually sequence a season with more than one
peak" than anything currently captured in the baseline.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — The "four to seven stages" and "about two months"
figures are stated without a derivation the reader can check: Issurin gives no worked
example of how stage count or duration is calculated for a specific sport's calendar in
this chapter. **Inference:** football's in-season structure (weekly games, not discrete
multi-week competition-free blocks) does not map cleanly onto a ~2-month training stage.
Issurin's model is built from and mainly evidenced by individual/dual sports with discrete
competitions (track and field, canoe-kayak, windsurfing); Chapter 3's microcycle-level
material (now ingested; see `_book.md`) is a necessary next read before this framework can
be translated into a week-by-week in-season football plan. **Contested:** Issurin's "does
not work well for high-performance athletes" framing of the traditional alternative (PDF p.
19, printed p. 8, the same claim flagged in
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]) is disputed by Issurin's own later
peer-reviewed review (Issurin, 2016, *Sports Medicine*, "Benefits and Limitations of Block
Periodized Training Approaches to Athletes' Preparation," Zotero item `PT9QTQ2I`, full text
cached in this library at
`research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a.md`).
That review reports that concentrated-unidirectional programs in team and combat sports
improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team
practice or competitive performance (its p.6): a direct qualification of the confident
five-benefit list above, for exactly the team-sport context football sits in. **Inference:**
Bompa & Haff's 5th edition, already in this library, may also bear on the "does not work
well" claim, but only Bompa Ch1-2 has been ingested so far (`periodization--bompa/_book.md`:
Ch6 Annual Plan and Ch8 Training Cycles are pending), so it cannot ground this contest yet;
check once those chapters are ingested.

**Example** — **Inference:** a five-stage football off-season/camp plan: Stage 1 (general
accumulation, ~8 weeks, winter conditioning); Stage 2 (strength/power transmutation into
spring ball, ending in the spring game as a "competition"); Stage 3 (summer accumulation);
Stage 4 (fall-camp transmutation, ending in the first scrimmage or game week as
realization); Stage 5+ (in-season stages keyed to bye weeks or rivalry-week peaks, pending
Chapter 3's in-season microcycle guidance).

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[claim--multi-peak-annual-preparation-elite-track-and-field]] (the empirical motivation for
needing a multi-peak model), [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]].

14	# Residual Training Effects Last Different Numbers of Days for Different Motor Abilities
15	
16	**What it is** — The residual training effect is defined as "the retention of changes
17	induced by systematic workloads beyond a certain time period after the cessation of
18	training," a term Issurin attributes to Brian and James Counsilman (1991) (PDF p. 33,
19	printed p. 22). Issurin & Lustig (2004) is cited as the source of Table 1.6 (PDF p. 35,
20	printed p. 24), giving residual duration ± SD in days after cessation of training for each
21	motor ability: **aerobic endurance 30 ± 5 days**, **maximum strength 30 ± 5 days**,
22	**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
23	**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. Table 1.6's own physiological-background column
24	lists aerobic endurance's residual as resting on increased aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
25	muscle capillaries, hemoglobin capacity, glycogen storage, and fat-metabolism rate, and
26	maximum strength's on improved neural mechanism and muscle hypertrophy from fiber
27	enlargement, with no percentages attached in the table itself. Later in the text (PDF p. 35,
28	printed p. 24), Issurin gives a specific figure for one of those table items: aerobic
29	enzymes increase by 40-90% with training (Volkov, 1986; Fox et al., 1993; Wilmore & Costill,
30	1993). He contrasts this with much smaller local adaptations from sprint training:
31	phosphocreatine storage (+2-5%), peak lactate accumulation (+10-20%), and anaerobic enzymes
32	(+2-20%), given without a citation on that page. On the following page (PDF p. 36, printed
33	p. 25), Thorstensson (1988) is cited specifically for "relatively small increases" in
34	quickly available energy sources, ATP and phosphocreatine, and enzymes such as creatine
35	kinase, from highly concentrated sprint training.
36	
37	**Why it works** — Issurin states the mechanism directly (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp. 24-25):
38	aerobic ability, supported by pronounced morphological and biochemical changes, is retained
39	"for a number of weeks at near-peak level," while anaerobic abilities, particularly maximum
40	sprint speed, "retain near-peak levels for much shorter periods" because peak speed's gains
41	are smaller and rest on "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions, which
42	are relatively unstable and cannot be maintained at the highest level without specially
43	organized training." Maximum strength's comparably long residual is attributed to pronounced
44	morphological, biochemical, and neural changes: enlargement of muscle-fiber cross-sectional
45	area, hyperplasia, recruitment of previously inactive motor units, synchronization of their
46	activity, and increased motor-neuron discharge frequency (Zatsiorsky, 1995). Strength
47	endurance's residual is stated to depend on event duration and the degree of
48	anaerobic-resource mobilization; longer-duration strength endurance has a relatively longer
49	residual thanks to aerobic adaptation.
50	
51	**When to apply** — Sequencing which ability to develop first in a training stage (see
52	[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]): an ability with a long
53	residual (aerobic endurance, max strength) can be built early in accumulation and largely
54	coast through transmutation/realization without a maintenance dose, while an ability with a
55	short residual (max speed) needs re-exposure close to competition or its gain will be lost
56	before it is used. **Eric's baseline directly echoes half of this table:** "Training
57	residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need
58	re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue
59	readiness for max-velocity work degrades" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
60	programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` p.27), this 30/30/5-day
61	pattern matches Issurin's 30±5 / 30±5 / 5±3 figures because it is this table:
62	week1-lecture.md (marker p.66) reproduces Table 1.6 directly, under a slide block that names
63	"Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source (marker p.64), and gives strength endurance as
64	~12 days against Issurin's 15±5, the one value where the course departs from the book.
65	
66	**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Treat the numbers as a synthesized rule of thumb
67	(±5, ±4, ±5, ±3 day spreads are themselves wide relative to the means), not a precise
68	per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig
69	(2004) in this text, so the table's evidentiary base cannot be checked further from this
70	source alone. Issurin's own surrounding text also notes limits on how far residual-effect
71	thinking travels: maximum oxygen uptake in highly trained endurance athletes falls when
72	weekly training volume drops below a certain level (Steinacker, 1993; Steinacker et al.,
73	1998), and large volumes of highly intense exercise do not prevent detraining and loss of
74	aerobic endurance during a taper (Mujika, 1999) (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23).
75	
76	**Contested, flag this directly to Eric:** a *different* part of the same baseline corpus
77	states the opposite ordering for detraining rate: "the traits easiest to build (aerobic) are
78	lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest"
79	(`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` p.47).
80	This conflicts with Table 1.6 (aerobic residual is the *longest*, tied with strength, at
81	30±5 days, while alactic speed is the *shortest* at 5±3 days). The class-1 transcript is
82	not a third, independent data point against class-4-2026.md: it also states that aerobic
83	capacity is gained and lost very quickly (marker pp.25, 28), gives its 30-day retention
84	windows as conditional on "a small retention load" continuing during that window (marker
85	p.28), a different construct from Issurin's residual *after cessation* of training, and
86	ties its 5-day speed figure to connective-tissue and nervous-system readiness ("otherwise
87	the nervous system doesn't change a whole lot," marker p.28) rather than to speed itself
88	decaying in 5 days. The course's own numbers come directly from this table (week1-lecture.md
89	marker pp.64, 66, strength endurance given there as ~12 days against Issurin's 15±5). Resolve
90	with Eric: this may be residual effect after cessation (Issurin, Table 1.6) versus rate of
91	loss without any retention dose (class-4-2026.md), two different constructs the corpus does
92	not itself reconcile. Do not harmonize these; record all three with their locators and keep
93	`contested`, with this as the stated reason.
94	
95	**Inference:** this table also converges with, but is not identical to, the vault's
96	Verkhoshansky-staging entry on heterochronic adaptation
97	([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]],
98	staging), which describes a *different* mechanism (order of biochemical sub-processes
99	gained/lost) rather than absolute day-counts per motor ability, both describe
100	heterochronicity in de-training, but at different levels of description; do not treat them
101	as restating the same specific claim.
102	
103	**Example** — **Inference:** in a training stage that opens with 4 weeks of accumulation
104	(building aerobic base and max strength) followed by 3 weeks of transmutation and 2 weeks of
105	realization, competition falls 35 days after accumulation ends: at the outer edge of the
106	aerobic and strength residuals' 30 ± 5-day window, not safely inside it. A coach relying on
107	this table would want a maintenance dose of both qualities somewhere in transmutation, not
108	an assumption that accumulation-phase gains are still fully in hand. Maximum speed work
109	needs re-introduction within about 5 days of the target competition, or its residual will
110	have decayed well below peak by competition day.
111	
112	**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
113	[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]] (a ratio-based rule for
114	fatigue-vs-fitness decay, distinct from this table's absolute per-ability day counts —
115	cross-reference, do not conflate),
116	[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] (staging),
117	[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]] (staging).

re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue
readiness for max-velocity work degrades" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` p.27), this 30/30/5-day
pattern matches Issurin's 30±5 / 30±5 / 5±3 figures because it is this table:
week1-lecture.md (marker p.66) reproduces Table 1.6 directly, under a slide block that names
"Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source (marker p.64), and gives strength endurance as
~12 days against Issurin's 15±5, the one value where the course departs from the book.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Treat the numbers as a synthesized rule of thumb
(±5, ±4, ±5, ±3 day spreads are themselves wide relative to the means), not a precise
per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig
(2004) in this text, so the table's evidentiary base cannot be checked further from this
source alone. Issurin's own surrounding text also notes limits on how far residual-effect
thinking travels: maximum oxygen uptake in highly trained endurance athletes falls when
weekly training volume drops below a certain level (Steinacker, 1993; Steinacker et al.,
1998), and large volumes of highly intense exercise do not prevent detraining and loss of
aerobic endurance during a taper (Mujika, 1999) (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23).

**Contested, flag this directly to Eric:** a *different* part of the same baseline corpus
states the opposite ordering for detraining rate: "the traits easiest to build (aerobic) are
lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` p.47).
This conflicts with Table 1.6 (aerobic residual is the *longest*, tied with strength, at
30±5 days, while alactic speed is the *shortest* at 5±3 days). The class-1 transcript is
not a third, independent data point against class-4-2026.md: it also states that aerobic
capacity is gained and lost very quickly (marker pp.25, 28), gives its 30-day retention
windows as conditional on "a small retention load" continuing during that window (marker
p.28), a different construct from Issurin's residual *after cessation* of training, and
ties its 5-day speed figure to connective-tissue and nervous-system readiness ("otherwise
the nervous system doesn't change a whole lot," marker p.28) rather than to speed itself
decaying in 5 days. The course's own numbers come directly from this table (week1-lecture.md
marker pp.64, 66, strength endurance given there as ~12 days against Issurin's 15±5). Resolve
with Eric: this may be residual effect after cessation (Issurin, Table 1.6) versus rate of
loss without any retention dose (class-4-2026.md), two different constructs the corpus does
not itself reconcile. Do not harmonize these; record all three with their locators and keep
`contested`, with this as the stated reason.

**Inference:** this table also converges with, but is not identical to, the vault's
Verkhoshansky-staging entry on heterochronic adaptation
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]],
staging), which describes a *different* mechanism (order of biochemical sub-processes
gained/lost) rather than absolute day-counts per motor ability, both describe
heterochronicity in de-training, but at different levels of description; do not treat them
as restating the same specific claim.

**Example** — **Inference:** in a training stage that opens with 4 weeks of accumulation
(building aerobic base and max strength) followed by 3 weeks of transmutation and 2 weeks of
realization, competition falls 35 days after accumulation ends: at the outer edge of the
aerobic and strength residuals' 30 ± 5-day window, not safely inside it. A coach relying on
this table would want a maintenance dose of both qualities somewhere in transmutation, not
an assumption that accumulation-phase gains are still fully in hand. Maximum speed work
needs re-introduction within about 5 days of the target competition, or its residual will
have decayed well below peak by competition day.

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]] (a ratio-based rule for
fatigue-vs-fitness decay, distinct from this table's absolute per-ability day counts —
cross-reference, do not conflate),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] (staging),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]] (staging).

15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin presents two data-backed examples as motivation for abandoning
17	simultaneous multi-ability training (traditional periodization) in favor of consecutive,
18	concentrated blocks.
19	
20	**(1) Swimmer concurrent-training interference (PDF pp. 21-22, printed pp. 10-11, Figure
21	1.3).** High-level male swimmers were studied over an 8-week early-season program combining
22	extensive swimming with resistive/power dry-land work aimed at swim-specific strength
23	(9-11 workouts/week; sample size not stated in this text). Measured: maximal force of
24	tethered swimming (Ftsw), dry-land explosive strength (Fexp), and dry-land strength
25	endurance (SE). Result: strength endurance improved markedly; swim-specific strength did not
26	improve; explosive strength *decreased*, despite about 30% of dry-land program time devoted
27	to maximal/explosive strength work. Issurin's mechanistic explanation has two separate
28	parts: extensive endurance work captures the metabolic energy needed for post-exercise
29	anabolism, which suppresses muscle hypertrophy; separately, coaches' and athletes'
30	observations show that a strenuous, high-volume training program causes permanent fatigue,
31	keeping central and peripheral neural factors far from the optimum needed for improving
32	muscular contraction. Klausen (1990) is cited for a more general point about what conditions
33	the neural mechanism (state of the CNS, sensitivity of the neuro-motor pool), not for the
34	fatigue observation specifically.
35	
36	**(2) Kayaker decay under traditional periodization (PDF p. 25-26, printed pp. 14-15,
37	Figure 1.4, the in-text citation reads "Fig.1.3," which appears to be a labeling error in
38	the source; the described variables match Figure 1.4's caption, not Figure 1.3's).** A group
39	of highly qualified kayakers were tracked across a full annual cycle built on the classical
40	model (Issurin et al., 1986). Measured: mean distance velocity (Vd), velocity at anaerobic
41	threshold (V-AT), peak paddle force (PF), stroke rate (SR), muscle mass (MM). Result: the
42	long general-preparatory period raised V-AT, muscle mass and peak force substantially; but
43	during the extended, highly specialized competitive period, extensive aerobic workloads were
44	replaced by more intense, event-specific exercises, and maximum-strength exercises were
45	"reduced and even rejected as harmful for racing technique" (only maximum-strength work is
46	called harmful in the source; the aerobic reduction is described as a substitution, not a
47	harm judgment), and V-AT, peak force, and muscle mass all *declined* by the competitive
48	period. Distance velocity
49	still reached its season maximum, but only via increased stroke rate compensating for
50	reduced force, i.e., technique/rate covered for a real loss in the underlying strength and
51	aerobic qualities. Issurin's summary: "the timing pattern for developing different abilities
52	was far from optimal."
53	
54	**Why it works** — For the swimmer case, Issurin gives two separate stated mechanisms (PDF
55	p. 21, printed p. 10): extensive endurance work "captures the metabolic energy that is
56	necessary for anabolism during post-exercise recovery," which "suppresses muscle
57	hypertrophy"; and, separately, "the observations of coaches and athletes show that a
58	strenuous high volume training program causes permanent fatigue," so "the central and
59	peripheral neural factors are far from optimum." Klausen (1990) is cited for a different,
60	more general point in between the two, that enhancement of the neural mechanism "is
61	conditioned by the state of the central nervous system and the sensitivity of the
62	neuro-motor pool," not specifically for the fatigue observation. For the kayaker case, Issurin
63	gives no physiological mechanism for the decline beyond narration of what happened (reduced
64	aerobic and strength work during the competitive period, PDF p. 25, printed p. 14); treat
65	that case as a described pattern, not an explained one. **Inference:** labeling the two
66	cases as "concurrent interference" versus "sequential decay" is this entry's own
67	categorization for cross-referencing purposes, not language Issurin himself uses; both are
68	offered by Issurin as evidence for the same underlying argument against simultaneous,
69	non-block training (see [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]), which in turn
70	motivates the consecutive block sequencing in
71	[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] and
72	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]].
73	
74	**When to apply** — The swimmer study is the more detailed evidence of the two: it is an
75	uncontrolled, single-group, uncited 8-week observation (no control group or reference given
76	in this text, PDF p. 21, printed p. 10) with named outcome variables, giving concrete numbers
77	useful for illustrating concurrent-training interference to Baylor strength staff
78	programming for athletes who need both an aerobic base and explosive/max strength (e.g.,
79	many football positions in a fall-camp conditioning window). The kayaker case is useful
80	mainly as a cautionary illustration of "building a quality early in the year and then
81	letting it decay unaddressed."
82	
83	**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — The swimmer study's exact sample size is not given in
84	this text (only workout frequency, 9-11/week), so its statistical strength cannot be judged
85	from this source alone; treat the direction of the finding (interference occurred) as
86	`supported` but the specific numeric changes in Figure 1.3 as unverifiable: the swimmer
87	study carries no citation at all in this text, not even an author or year, so there is no
88	underlying source to check the numbers against. **Untested:** the kayaker case is Issurin's
89	own team's data (Issurin et al., 1986),
90	observational across one season with no control group; it demonstrates a plausible pattern,
91	not a controlled comparison against an alternative periodization model run on the same
92	athletes. Neither study is football-specific; football's in-season structure (weekly
93	competition, not one late-season peak) differs from both the swimmers' fixed 8-week block and
94	the kayakers' single annual peak design.
95	
96	**Example** — **Inference:** a Baylor position group with both an in-season conditioning demand and a
97	strength-maintenance demand should treat "just add more of both" as the swimmer study's
98	failure mode: without deliberate sequencing or volume management, the concurrent aerobic
99	load can blunt the intended strength/power adaptation even when strength work is
100	programmed.

103	which these two studies are offered as concrete illustrations of),

14	# Case Study: The USSR Canoe-Kayak Team and the Original Accumulation/Transmutation/Realization Design
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin's own account of where his accumulation-transmutation-realization
17	taxonomy came from (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22): in the early 1980s, elite USSR canoe-kayak
18	paddlers were training an "enormous exercise volume." "The prevailing opinion was that this
19	load level was excessive and that the training design could be made more effective." The
20	block-and-mesocycle-sequencing idea was "conceptualized, implemented and proved in
21	practice" with the national team, then published (Issurin & Kaverin, 1985). The duration of
22	the mesocycles was set "according to physiological and biochemical prerequisites that
23	usually allowed four weeks for the accumulation and transformation mesocycles, and two weeks
24	for realization." The modified design allowed "about a 10-15% reduction in the annual
25	training volume." Follow-up testing during preparation reportedly showed "considerable
26	improvement in the main fitness components in all subgroups." The claimed competitive
27	outcomes: three gold and three silver medals at the 1988 Seoul Olympics, and eight gold
28	medals (1989) and nine gold medals (1990) at the World Championships.
29	
30	**Why it works: the author's own interpretation, not independently verified here** —
31	Issurin attributes the improvement to reduced simultaneous multi-ability training and better
32	volume management under the new block structure, consistent with the general BPC rationale
33	in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]. No comparison data (e.g., what the
34	same team's results looked like in prior Olympic/World Championship cycles under the old
35	model, or what other nations' medal counts did over the same period) is presented in this
36	chapter to isolate the training-design change from other factors (athlete development,
37	equipment, competitor turnover).
38	
39	**When to apply: untested, treat as the concept's origin story, not as proof** — Useful
40	as the direct provenance of Issurin's own taxonomy (see
41	[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]) and as a data point that a
42	national federation with centralized, well-resourced athlete monitoring implemented this
43	design at scale (not just with one athlete).
44	
45	**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — The book gives the source publication as Issurin &
46	Kaverin (1985) but does not itself state what Issurin's own role on the national team was.
47	**Inference:** reading this as the concept's inventor reporting on his own uncontrolled
48	intervention with his own national team is a reasonable inference from the shared authorship
49	and the book's framing, not something the text says outright. Either way, the account here
50	(2008 book) is a secondary retelling with no cited independent replication or outcome audit. As with the Bondarchuk case, do not treat the
51	Olympic and World Championship medal counts as a controlled test of the training design;
52	1980s Soviet sport had structural advantages (centralized athlete development, resourcing)
53	that are not present in most other training contexts, including a US college football
54	program. The "10-15% volume reduction" figure has no comparison baseline stated (reduction
55	from what specific prior volume, over what specific prior period) beyond "the annual
56	training volume."
57	
58	**Example** — Citing "block periodization produced Olympic medals" should specify this is
59	one 1980s Soviet national-team case reported by the method's own originator, not a
60	controlled trial, and should be paired with the caveat already logged in
61	[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]] about single-coach, single-program
62	evidence.
63	
64	**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
65	[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]].

practice" with the national team, then published (Issurin & Kaverin, 1985). The duration of

usually allowed four weeks for the accumulation and transformation mesocycles, and two weeks
for realization." The modified design allowed "about a 10-15% reduction in the annual
training volume." Follow-up testing during preparation reportedly showed "considerable

14	# Case Study: Bondarchuk's Developmental/Competitive/Restorative Blocks and the 1988 Hammer Throw Podium
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin credits Anatoly Bondarchuk, hammer-throw coach, with one of the
17	precursor systems to Block Periodization (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21). Based on his own
18	athletic career (1972 Olympic hammer-throw champion) and doctoral research on throwers'
19	training programs (1988), Bondarchuk built a periodization chart using three types of
20	specialized mesocycle-blocks: **developmental** (workload gradually increases to maximum),
21	**competitive** (load stabilizes, athletes focus on competitive performance), and
22	**restorative** (active recovery, preparing for the next developmental block). Stated
23	durations: developmental and competitive blocks are "usually four weeks," restorative "can
24	be shortened to two weeks." Sequencing depends on the competition schedule and individual
25	athlete response. The book also gives what it calls Bondarchuk's design's outstanding
26	characteristic: alternation and repetition of the exercise repertory in each mesocycle-block
27	(every four weeks); the traditional period names, preparatory, competitive, and transitory,
28	were kept, but Issurin notes "their essence is very different" in Bondarchuk's concept (PDF
29	p. 32, printed p. 21). The claimed outcome: Bondarchuk coached the gold, silver, and bronze
30	medalists in hammer throw at the 1988 and other Olympic Games, "the entire Olympic podium
31	occupied by athletes of the same coach" (Bondarchuk, 1986 and 1988, as cited by Issurin).
32	
33	**Why it works: the author gives no mechanism beyond the general BPC rationale** — Issurin
34	does not describe Bondarchuk's own stated reasoning for why these particular block lengths
35	(4/4/2 weeks) were chosen. **Inference:** the entry's characterization of the three-way split
36	as organized "by competitive readiness rather than by ability type" is this entry's own
37	reading, not language Issurin uses; the mechanism Issurin offers is the same general BPC
38	logic (concentrated, sequenced blocks beat simultaneous multi-ability training) applied
39	retroactively to Bondarchuk's design.
40	
41	**When to apply: untested, use as a historical precedent, not as evidence** — Useful for
42	explaining the lineage of block-periodization thinking. Issurin presents Bondarchuk's system
43	as a parallel reform, not a source he built on: it appears in the text alongside "Issurin &
44	Kaverin, 1985, Bondarchuk, 1986, 1988" as one of the era's several reforms away from
45	traditional periodization (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23), and Issurin & Kaverin's own 1985
46	publication predates Bondarchuk's cited 1986 and 1988 works. Useful as an alternative
47	three-block naming scheme organized around competitive readiness
48	(developmental/competitive/restorative) rather than ability type
49	(accumulation/transmutation/realization); worth distinguishing the two schemes explicitly
50	when citing "Bondarchuk's blocks" versus "Issurin's blocks."
51	
52	**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Population: elite (Olympic-level) Soviet male hammer

# Case Study: Bondarchuk's Developmental/Competitive/Restorative Blocks and the 1988 Hammer Throw Podium

**What it is** — Issurin credits Anatoly Bondarchuk, hammer-throw coach, with one of the
precursor systems to Block Periodization (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21). Based on his own
athletic career (1972 Olympic hammer-throw champion) and doctoral research on throwers'
training programs (1988), Bondarchuk built a periodization chart using three types of
specialized mesocycle-blocks: **developmental** (workload gradually increases to maximum),
**competitive** (load stabilizes, athletes focus on competitive performance), and
**restorative** (active recovery, preparing for the next developmental block). Stated
durations: developmental and competitive blocks are "usually four weeks," restorative "can
be shortened to two weeks." Sequencing depends on the competition schedule and individual
athlete response. The book also gives what it calls Bondarchuk's design's outstanding
characteristic: alternation and repetition of the exercise repertory in each mesocycle-block
(every four weeks); the traditional period names, preparatory, competitive, and transitory,
were kept, but Issurin notes "their essence is very different" in Bondarchuk's concept (PDF
p. 32, printed p. 21). The claimed outcome: Bondarchuk coached the gold, silver, and bronze
medalists in hammer throw at the 1988 and other Olympic Games, "the entire Olympic podium
occupied by athletes of the same coach" (Bondarchuk, 1986 and 1988, as cited by Issurin).

**Why it works: the author gives no mechanism beyond the general BPC rationale** — Issurin
does not describe Bondarchuk's own stated reasoning for why these particular block lengths
(4/4/2 weeks) were chosen. **Inference:** the entry's characterization of the three-way split
as organized "by competitive readiness rather than by ability type" is this entry's own
reading, not language Issurin uses; the mechanism Issurin offers is the same general BPC
logic (concentrated, sequenced blocks beat simultaneous multi-ability training) applied
retroactively to Bondarchuk's design.

**When to apply: untested, use as a historical precedent, not as evidence** — Useful for
explaining the lineage of block-periodization thinking. Issurin presents Bondarchuk's system
as a parallel reform, not a source he built on: it appears in the text alongside "Issurin &
Kaverin, 1985, Bondarchuk, 1986, 1988" as one of the era's several reforms away from
traditional periodization (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23), and Issurin & Kaverin's own 1985
publication predates Bondarchuk's cited 1986 and 1988 works. Useful as an alternative
three-block naming scheme organized around competitive readiness
(developmental/competitive/restorative) rather than ability type
(accumulation/transmutation/realization); worth distinguishing the two schemes explicitly
when citing "Bondarchuk's blocks" versus "Issurin's blocks."

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Population: elite (Olympic-level) Soviet male hammer
throwers training under one coach; one Olympic final's podium (plus unspecified "other
Olympic Games" results). This is a single coach's outcome with no comparison group, no
report of what other finalists' training looked like, and total reliance on the coach's and
Issurin's own secondary account rather than an independent case audit. A three-medal sweep at one Olympics
is a striking result but cannot isolate the training design's contribution from athlete
talent, competitor variance on the day, or other coaching factors. Do not cite this as
evidence that a 4/4/2-week block cadence "works" for hammer throw or any other event; it
illustrates a design, not a validated dose-response finding. This is distinct from and
should not be merged with Issurin's own accumulation/transmutation/realization taxonomy, see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] for that separate, though
historically related, three-block system.

**Example** — **Inference:** a coach citing "block periodization has a track record" should
specify which system (Bondarchuk's competitive-readiness blocks or Issurin's ability-type
blocks) and should not present the 1988 podium sweep as generalizable evidence beyond "one
documented historical instance this concept coincided with a strong outcome."

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[case-study--issurin-kaverin-canoe-kayak-block-periodization]], a comparable single-coach
case from the same era; consider also cross-referencing
`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault), the *same* coach (Bondarchuk), but a completely different, unrelated framework
of his (an exercise-classification taxonomy by movement similarity, not a mesocycle-timing
system). The two should never be conflated when either is cited.

# Residual Training Effects Last Different Numbers of Days for Different Motor Abilities

**What it is** — The residual training effect is defined as "the retention of changes
induced by systematic workloads beyond a certain time period after the cessation of
training," a term Issurin attributes to Brian and James Counsilman (1991) (PDF p. 33,
printed p. 22). Issurin & Lustig (2004) is cited as the source of Table 1.6 (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), giving residual duration ± SD in days after cessation of training for each
motor ability: **aerobic endurance 30 ± 5 days**, **maximum strength 30 ± 5 days**,
**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. Table 1.6's own physiological-background column
lists aerobic endurance's residual as resting on increased aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
muscle capillaries, hemoglobin capacity, glycogen storage, and fat-metabolism rate, and
maximum strength's on improved neural mechanism and muscle hypertrophy from fiber
enlargement, with no percentages attached in the table itself. Later in the text (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), Issurin gives a specific figure for one of those table items: aerobic
enzymes increase by 40-90% with training (Volkov, 1986; Fox et al., 1993; Wilmore & Costill,
1993). He contrasts this with much smaller local adaptations from sprint training:
phosphocreatine storage (+2-5%), peak lactate accumulation (+10-20%), and anaerobic enzymes
(+2-20%), given without a citation on that page. On the following page (PDF p. 36, printed
p. 25), Thorstensson (1988) is cited specifically for "relatively small increases" in
quickly available energy sources, ATP and phosphocreatine, and enzymes such as creatine
kinase, from highly concentrated sprint training.

**Why it works** — Issurin states the mechanism directly (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp. 24-25):
aerobic ability, supported by pronounced morphological and biochemical changes, is retained
"for a number of weeks at near-peak level," while anaerobic abilities, particularly maximum
sprint speed, "retain near-peak levels for much shorter periods" because peak speed's gains
are smaller and rest on "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions, which
are relatively unstable and cannot be maintained at the highest level without specially
organized training." Maximum strength's comparably long residual is attributed to pronounced
morphological, biochemical, and neural changes: enlargement of muscle-fiber cross-sectional
area, hyperplasia, recruitment of previously inactive motor units, synchronization of their
activity, and increased motor-neuron discharge frequency (Zatsiorsky, 1995). Strength
endurance's residual is stated to depend on event duration and the degree of
anaerobic-resource mobilization; longer-duration strength endurance has a relatively longer
residual thanks to aerobic adaptation.

**When to apply** — Sequencing which ability to develop first in a training stage (see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]): an ability with a long
residual (aerobic endurance, max strength) can be built early in accumulation and largely
coast through transmutation/realization without a maintenance dose, while an ability with a
short residual (max speed) needs re-exposure close to competition or its gain will be lost
before it is used. **Eric's baseline directly echoes half of this table:** "Training
residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need
re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue
readiness for max-velocity work degrades" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` p.27), this 30/30/5-day
pattern matches Issurin's 30±5 / 30±5 / 5±3 figures because it is this table:
week1-lecture.md (marker p.66) reproduces Table 1.6 directly, under a slide block that names
"Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source (marker p.64), and gives strength endurance as
~12 days against Issurin's 15±5, the one value where the course departs from the book.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Treat the numbers as a synthesized rule of thumb
(±5, ±4, ±5, ±3 day spreads are themselves wide relative to the means), not a precise
per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig
(2004) in this text, so the table's evidentiary base cannot be checked further from this
source alone. Issurin's own surrounding text also notes limits on how far residual-effect
thinking travels: maximum oxygen uptake in highly trained endurance athletes falls when
weekly training volume drops below a certain level (Steinacker, 1993; Steinacker et al.,
1998), and large volumes of highly intense exercise do not prevent detraining and loss of
aerobic endurance during a taper (Mujika, 1999) (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23).

**Contested, flag this directly to Eric:** a *different* part of the same baseline corpus
states the opposite ordering for detraining rate: "the traits easiest to build (aerobic) are
lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` p.47).
This conflicts with Table 1.6 (aerobic residual is the *longest*, tied with strength, at
30±5 days, while alactic speed is the *shortest* at 5±3 days). The class-1 transcript is
not a third, independent data point against class-4-2026.md: it also states that aerobic
capacity is gained and lost very quickly (marker pp.25, 28), gives its 30-day retention
windows as conditional on "a small retention load" continuing during that window (marker
p.28), a different construct from Issurin's residual *after cessation* of training, and
ties its 5-day speed figure to connective-tissue and nervous-system readiness ("otherwise
the nervous system doesn't change a whole lot," marker p.28) rather than to speed itself
decaying in 5 days. The course's own numbers come directly from this table (week1-lecture.md
marker pp.64, 66, strength endurance given there as ~12 days against Issurin's 15±5). Resolve
with Eric: this may be residual effect after cessation (Issurin, Table 1.6) versus rate of
loss without any retention dose (class-4-2026.md), two different constructs the corpus does
not itself reconcile. Do not harmonize these; record all three with their locators and keep
`contested`, with this as the stated reason.

**Inference:** this table also converges with, but is not identical to, the vault's
Verkhoshansky-staging entry on heterochronic adaptation
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]],
staging), which describes a *different* mechanism (order of biochemical sub-processes
gained/lost) rather than absolute day-counts per motor ability, both describe
heterochronicity in de-training, but at different levels of description; do not treat them
as restating the same specific claim.

**Example** — **Inference:** in a training stage that opens with 4 weeks of accumulation
(building aerobic base and max strength) followed by 3 weeks of transmutation and 2 weeks of
realization, competition falls 35 days after accumulation ends: at the outer edge of the
aerobic and strength residuals' 30 ± 5-day window, not safely inside it. A coach relying on
this table would want a maintenance dose of both qualities somewhere in transmutation, not
an assumption that accumulation-phase gains are still fully in hand. Maximum speed work
needs re-introduction within about 5 days of the target competition, or its residual will
have decayed well below peak by competition day.

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]] (a ratio-based rule for
fatigue-vs-fitness decay, distinct from this table's absolute per-ability day counts —
cross-reference, do not conflate),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] (staging),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]] (staging).

# Residual Training Effects Last Different Numbers of Days for Different Motor Abilities

**What it is** — The residual training effect is defined as "the retention of changes
induced by systematic workloads beyond a certain time period after the cessation of
training," a term Issurin attributes to Brian and James Counsilman (1991) (PDF p. 33,
printed p. 22). Issurin & Lustig (2004) is cited as the source of Table 1.6 (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), giving residual duration ± SD in days after cessation of training for each
motor ability: **aerobic endurance 30 ± 5 days**, **maximum strength 30 ± 5 days**,
**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. Table 1.6's own physiological-background column
lists aerobic endurance's residual as resting on increased aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
muscle capillaries, hemoglobin capacity, glycogen storage, and fat-metabolism rate, and
maximum strength's on improved neural mechanism and muscle hypertrophy from fiber
enlargement, with no percentages attached in the table itself. Later in the text (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), Issurin gives a specific figure for one of those table items: aerobic
enzymes increase by 40-90% with training (Volkov, 1986; Fox et al., 1993; Wilmore & Costill,
1993). He contrasts this with much smaller local adaptations from sprint training:
phosphocreatine storage (+2-5%), peak lactate accumulation (+10-20%), and anaerobic enzymes
(+2-20%), given without a citation on that page. On the following page (PDF p. 36, printed
p. 25), Thorstensson (1988) is cited specifically for "relatively small increases" in
quickly available energy sources, ATP and phosphocreatine, and enzymes such as creatine
kinase, from highly concentrated sprint training.

**Why it works** — Issurin states the mechanism directly (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp. 24-25):
aerobic ability, supported by pronounced morphological and biochemical changes, is retained
"for a number of weeks at near-peak level," while anaerobic abilities, particularly maximum
sprint speed, "retain near-peak levels for much shorter periods" because peak speed's gains
are smaller and rest on "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions, which
are relatively unstable and cannot be maintained at the highest level without specially
organized training." Maximum strength's comparably long residual is attributed to pronounced
morphological, biochemical, and neural changes: enlargement of muscle-fiber cross-sectional
area, hyperplasia, recruitment of previously inactive motor units, synchronization of their
activity, and increased motor-neuron discharge frequency (Zatsiorsky, 1995). Strength
endurance's residual is stated to depend on event duration and the degree of
anaerobic-resource mobilization; longer-duration strength endurance has a relatively longer
residual thanks to aerobic adaptation.

**When to apply** — Sequencing which ability to develop first in a training stage (see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]): an ability with a long
residual (aerobic endurance, max strength) can be built early in accumulation and largely
coast through transmutation/realization without a maintenance dose, while an ability with a
short residual (max speed) needs re-exposure close to competition or its gain will be lost
before it is used. **Eric's baseline directly echoes half of this table:** "Training
residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need
re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue
readiness for max-velocity work degrades" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` p.27). This 30/30/5-day
pattern matches Issurin's 30±5 / 30±5 / 5±3 figures because it is this table:
week1-lecture.md (marker p.66) reproduces Table 1.6 directly, under a slide block that names
"Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source (marker p.64), and gives strength endurance as
~12 days against Issurin's 15±5, the one value where the course departs from the book.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Treat the numbers as a synthesized rule of thumb
(±5, ±4, ±5, ±3 day spreads are themselves wide relative to the means), not a precise
per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig
(2004) in this text, so the table's evidentiary base cannot be checked further from this
source alone. Issurin's own surrounding text also notes limits on how far residual-effect
thinking travels: maximum oxygen uptake in highly trained endurance athletes falls when
weekly training volume drops below a certain level (Steinacker, 1993; Steinacker et al.,
1998), and large volumes of highly intense exercise do not prevent detraining and loss of
aerobic endurance during a taper (Mujika, 1999) (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23).

**Contested, flag this directly to Eric:** a *different* part of the same baseline corpus
states the opposite ordering for detraining rate: "the traits easiest to build (aerobic) are
lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` p.47).
This conflicts with Table 1.6 (aerobic residual is the *longest*, tied with strength, at

not a third, independent data point against class-4-2026.md: it also states that aerobic
capacity is gained and lost very quickly (marker pp.25, 28), gives its 30-day retention
windows as conditional on "a small retention load" continuing during that window (marker
p.28), a different construct from Issurin's residual *after cessation* of training, and
ties its 5-day speed figure to connective-tissue and nervous-system readiness ("otherwise
the nervous system doesn't change a whole lot," marker p.28) rather than to speed itself
decaying in 5 days. The course's own numbers come directly from this table (week1-lecture.md
marker pp.64, 66, strength endurance given there as ~12 days against Issurin's 15±5). Resolve
with Eric: this may be residual effect after cessation (Issurin, Table 1.6) versus rate of
loss without any retention dose (class-4-2026.md), two different constructs the corpus does
not itself reconcile. Do not harmonize these; record all three with their locators and keep
`contested`, with this as the stated reason.

# Case Study: Bondarchuk's Developmental/Competitive/Restorative Blocks and the 1988 Hammer Throw Podium

**What it is** — Issurin credits Anatoly Bondarchuk, hammer-throw coach, with one of the
precursor systems to Block Periodization (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21). Based on his own
athletic career (1972 Olympic hammer-throw champion) and doctoral research on throwers'
training programs (1988), Bondarchuk built a periodization chart using three types of
specialized mesocycle-blocks: **developmental** (workload gradually increases to maximum),
**competitive** (load stabilizes, athletes focus on competitive performance), and
**restorative** (active recovery, preparing for the next developmental block). Stated
durations: developmental and competitive blocks are "usually four weeks," restorative "can
be shortened to two weeks." Sequencing depends on the competition schedule and individual
athlete response. The book also gives what it calls Bondarchuk's design's outstanding
characteristic: alternation and repetition of the exercise repertory in each mesocycle-block
(every four weeks); the traditional period names, preparatory, competitive, and transitory,
were kept, but Issurin notes "their essence is very different" in Bondarchuk's concept (PDF
p. 32, printed p. 21). The claimed outcome: Bondarchuk coached the gold, silver, and bronze
medalists in hammer throw at the 1988 and other Olympic Games, "the entire Olympic podium
occupied by athletes of the same coach" (Bondarchuk, 1986 and 1988, as cited by Issurin).

**Why it works: the author gives no mechanism beyond the general BPC rationale** — Issurin
does not describe Bondarchuk's own stated reasoning for why these particular block lengths
(4/4/2 weeks) were chosen. **Inference:** the entry's characterization of the three-way split
as organized "by competitive readiness rather than by ability type" is this entry's own
reading, not language Issurin uses; the mechanism Issurin offers is the same general BPC
logic (concentrated, sequenced blocks beat simultaneous multi-ability training) applied
retroactively to Bondarchuk's design.

**When to apply: untested, use as a historical precedent, not as evidence** — Useful for
explaining the lineage of block-periodization thinking. Issurin presents Bondarchuk's system
as a parallel reform, not a source he built on: it appears in the text alongside "Issurin &
Kaverin, 1985, Bondarchuk, 1986, 1988" as one of the era's several reforms away from
traditional periodization (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23), and Issurin & Kaverin's own 1985
publication predates Bondarchuk's cited 1986 and 1988 works. Useful as an alternative
three-block naming scheme organized around competitive readiness
(developmental/competitive/restorative) rather than ability type
(accumulation/transmutation/realization); worth distinguishing the two schemes explicitly
when citing "Bondarchuk's blocks" versus "Issurin's blocks."

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Population: elite (Olympic-level) Soviet male hammer
throwers training under one coach; one Olympic final's podium (plus unspecified "other
Olympic Games" results). This is a single coach's outcome with no comparison group, no
report of what other finalists' training looked like, and total reliance on the coach's and
Issurin's own secondary account rather than an independent case audit. A three-medal sweep at one Olympics
is a striking result but cannot isolate the training design's contribution from athlete
talent, competitor variance on the day, or other coaching factors. Do not cite this as
evidence that a 4/4/2-week block cadence "works" for hammer throw or any other event; it
illustrates a design, not a validated dose-response finding. This is distinct from and
should not be merged with Issurin's own accumulation/transmutation/realization taxonomy, see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] for that separate, though
historically related, three-block system.

**Example** — **Inference:** a coach citing "block periodization has a track record" should
specify which system (Bondarchuk's competitive-readiness blocks or Issurin's ability-type
blocks) and should not present the 1988 podium sweep as generalizable evidence beyond "one
documented historical instance this concept coincided with a strong outcome."

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[case-study--issurin-kaverin-canoe-kayak-block-periodization]], a comparable single-coach
case from the same era; consider also cross-referencing
`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault), the *same* coach (Bondarchuk), but a completely different, unrelated framework
of his (an exercise-classification taxonomy by movement similarity, not a mesocycle-timing
system). The two should never be conflated when either is cited.

# Case Study: The USSR Canoe-Kayak Team and the Original Accumulation/Transmutation/Realization Design

**What it is** — Issurin's own account of where his accumulation-transmutation-realization
taxonomy came from (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22): in the early 1980s, elite USSR canoe-kayak
paddlers were training an "enormous exercise volume." "The prevailing opinion was that this
load level was excessive and that the training design could be made more effective." The
block-and-mesocycle-sequencing idea was "conceptualized, implemented and proved in
practice" with the national team, then published (Issurin & Kaverin, 1985). The duration of
the mesocycles was set "according to physiological and biochemical prerequisites that
usually allowed four weeks for the accumulation and transformation mesocycles, and two weeks
for realization." The modified design allowed "about a 10-15% reduction in the annual
training volume." Follow-up testing during preparation reportedly showed "considerable
improvement in the main fitness components in all subgroups." The claimed competitive
outcomes: three gold and three silver medals at the 1988 Seoul Olympics, and eight gold
medals (1989) and nine gold medals (1990) at the World Championships.

**Why it works: the author's own interpretation, not independently verified here** —
Issurin attributes the improvement to reduced simultaneous multi-ability training and better
volume management under the new block structure, consistent with the general BPC rationale
in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]. No comparison data (e.g., what the
same team's results looked like in prior Olympic/World Championship cycles under the old
model, or what other nations' medal counts did over the same period) is presented in this
chapter to isolate the training-design change from other factors (athlete development,
equipment, competitor turnover).

**When to apply: untested, treat as the concept's origin story, not as proof** — Useful
as the direct provenance of Issurin's own taxonomy (see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]) and as a data point that a
national federation with centralized, well-resourced athlete monitoring implemented this
design at scale (not just with one athlete).

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — The book gives the source publication as Issurin &
Kaverin (1985) but does not itself state what Issurin's own role on the national team was.
**Inference:** reading this as the concept's inventor reporting on his own uncontrolled
intervention with his own national team is a reasonable inference from the shared authorship
and the book's framing, not something the text says outright. Either way, the account here
(2008 book) is a secondary retelling with no cited independent replication or outcome audit. As with the Bondarchuk case, do not treat the
Olympic and World Championship medal counts as a controlled test of the training design;
1980s Soviet sport had structural advantages (centralized athlete development, resourcing)
that are not present in most other training contexts, including a US college football
program. The "10-15% volume reduction" figure has no comparison baseline stated (reduction
from what specific prior volume, over what specific prior period) beyond "the annual
training volume."

**Example** — Citing "block periodization produced Olympic medals" should specify this is
one 1980s Soviet national-team case reported by the method's own originator, not a
controlled trial, and should be paired with the caveat already logged in
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]] about single-coach, single-program
evidence.

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]].

14	# Quantifying Workout Load on a 1-5 Scale, Mapped to Borg RPE Bands
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin presents a load-related workout classification built around three
17	functions: **development**, **retention**, and **restoration** (PDF p. 52, printed p. 41).
18	Table 2.3 (PDF p. 53, printed p. 42, based on Zatsiorsky 1995, modified by Issurin 2003)
19	quantifies this on a 1-5 scale using restoration time as the objective marker: restoration
20	level 1 (< 12 hours), retention level 2 (12-24 hours), development-substantial level 3
21	(24-48 hours), development-large level 4 (48-72 hours), development-extreme level 5
22	(> 72 hours). Because restoration-time-based classification does not fit every training type
23	well (Issurin notes coordination/neuro-emotional-stress workouts need less restoration time
24	than the scale implies), Table 2.4 (PDF p. 54, printed p. 43), Issurin's own adaptation of
25	Borg's scale to workout load levels, not a direct reproduction of Borg 1973, offers a
26	parallel mapping using Borg's Rate of Perceived Exertion scale (Borg, 1973): RPE 6-11 (very-very-easy to
27	fairly-easy) = restoration; RPE 12-14 (slightly difficult) = retention; RPE 15-16
28	(difficult) = development-substantial; RPE 17-18 (very difficult) = development-large; RPE
29	19-20 (very-very difficult) = development-extreme.
30	
31	**Why it works: inference on the underlying logic** — Restoration time and perceived
32	exertion are both proxies for how disruptive a session was to homeostasis; using either (or
33	both together) lets a coach assign every workout a comparable numeric load value even in
34	non-measurable sports (team sports, gymnastics), which Issurin identifies as the practical
35	payoff: "the load level of each workout can be quantified and expressed numerically" (PDF
36	p. 54, printed p. 43), enabling load-dependent categorization (development vs. retention vs.
37	restoration) across an entire training plan, not just isolated hard/easy labeling.
38	
39	**When to apply** — Building a simple, athlete-reportable RPE-based load log for sports or
40	settings where objective physiological monitoring (HR, blood lactate) is not available for
41	every session; classifying a completed week of training after the fact into
42	development/retention/restoration proportions to check whether the intended block emphasis
43	(see [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]) was actually
44	delivered. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name Borg's RPE scale specifically, though
45	session-level subjective load tracking is philosophically consistent with the department's
46	general preference for practical, staff-sustainable monitoring tools over burdensome ones
47	(`method-baseline.md`, "Load monitoring and GPS," on why daily wellness surveys were
48	abandoned when athletes learned to game them). Session-RPE load tracking has its own gaming
49	and reliability considerations documented in team-sport settings (Comyns & Flanagan, 2013,
50	`research-papers/comyns-2013-applications-of-the-session-rating-of-perceived-exertion-system-in-professional-rugby-unio.md`;
51	McLaren et al., 2017,
52	`research-papers/mclaren-2017-a-detailed-quantification-of-differential-ratings-of-perceived-exertion-during-team-sport.md`)
53	that is not addressed anywhere in this Issurin chapter and should be treated as an open
54	question, not assumed solved.
55	
56	**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — **The author gives no mechanism** for why these
57	specific RPE cut-points (11/12, 14/15, 16/17, 18/19) map to these specific restoration-time
58	bands rather than some other set of cut-points; both tables are presented as ready-made
59	scales without a validation study cited in this chapter. RPE is a subjective, athlete-reported
60	measure and is vulnerable to the same reporting-fatigue and gaming dynamics documented
61	elsewhere for subjective wellness tools; do not treat it as equivalent in reliability to the
62	objective HR/blood-lactate markers used in Table 2.10's key-exercise prescriptions
63	(see [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]]). The scale also does not
64	distinguish RPE driven by physical load from RPE driven by psychological/technical/cognitive
65	demand (e.g., a technically difficult but physically light session). Issurin notes the
66	restoration-time scale itself overstates load for high-level coordination training and
67	workouts that induce heightened neuro-emotional stress, which "usually require less time for
68	full restoration" than the scale would suggest (PDF p. 53, printed p. 42); this is a
69	comparison to the restoration-time scale, not to RPE.
70

72	players self-report session RPE and multiply by session duration, the session-RPE method
73	used widely in team sports (an approach not itself stated in this Issurin chapter; see
74	Comyns & Flanagan, 2013,
75	`research-papers/comyns-2013-applications-of-the-session-rating-of-perceived-exertion-system-in-professional-rugby-unio.md`,
76	noted here as an inference, not something Issurin describes), and classify the week's
77	development vs. retention vs. restoration balance against the intended training-stage
78	emphasis.

14	# A Morning Full-Body Resistance Workout Did Not Hurt Jump, Anaerobic Power, or Shooting Accuracy Six Hours Later
15	
16	**What it is** — Woolstenhulme et al. (2004), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 80, printed p. 69):
17	highly trained female basketball players (ages 18-22; exact sample size not stated in this
18	text) completed a within-subject comparison on two separate days. On the experimental day,
19	they performed a full-body morning resistance workout (7 exercises, 3-6 sets, 5-12RM loads),
20	then after **six hours of rest** were tested on vertical jump, a 30-second Wingate anaerobic
21	cycling test, and a 60-second shooting-accuracy trial. On the control day, the same test
22	battery was completed without the preceding resistance workout. Statistical analysis found
23	no differences between the athletes' results on the experimental vs. control days. Issurin's
24	stated conclusion: "a high-resistance full-body workout of moderate intensity has no negative
25	impact on the manifestation of sport-specific athletic abilities of trained basketball
26	players after six hours of rest."
27	
28	**Why it works: inference, not stated in the cited passage** — Six hours appears to be
29	sufficient for the acute neuromuscular fatigue from a moderate-intensity, moderate-volume
30	resistance session (5-12RM, 7 exercises) to resolve enough that it does not measurably
31	degrade jump, anaerobic power, or a skill-accuracy task; Issurin does not present the
32	physiological recovery mechanism in this passage beyond citing the outcome.
33	
34	**When to apply** — Issurin frames this as an additional comment on sequencing resistance
35	workouts and game practice "in dual and team sports," where "regular strength training is an
36	indispensable part of in-season preparation on professional and semi-professional teams"
37	(PDF p. 79, printed p. 68); he does not name football specifically. **Inference:** this
38	applies to football, a team sport with a long competitive season, whether morning hours can
39	be used for resistance training on a day with afternoon practice or competition,
40	given that in-season strength training is described elsewhere in this chapter as necessary
41	to offset the "dramatic losses of lean body mass, and maximum and explosive strength" a long
42	20-35 week competitive season can otherwise cause (Baker, 2001; Gamble, 2006, as cited by
43	Issurin, PDF pp. 79-80). This gives a specific, citable data point (six hours, moderate
44	5-12RM loading) supporting a same-day AM-lift/PM-practice-or-game model, consistent with
45	Eric's baseline's general in-season rule to "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than
46	avoid lifting in-season (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
47	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.20-21).
48	
49	**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — The cited sample is female basketball players; exact
50	sample size, loading specifics beyond "5-12RM," and effect-size/statistical detail are not
51	given in this text, so the finding should be treated as a directional result, not a precise
52	dosing guarantee. **Inference:** football involves substantially higher-impact,
53	higher-volume, and often heavier absolute loading than a 5-12RM "moderate intensity"
54	basketball-focused protocol, and involves collision-based rather than jump/shoot-accuracy
55	outcome measures, do not assume this six-hour window transfers unchanged to a heavier
56	football-specific lift or to contact-sport performance measures without independent
57	verification. The study also does not address multi-day accumulated fatigue from repeated
58	same-day lift-then-compete scheduling across a full season, only a single isolated
59	comparison day.
60	
61	**Example** — **Inference:** a football program considering morning lifts on game day or heavy-practice
62	days has a citable data point that a moderate-intensity, moderate-volume full-body session
63	six hours before performance testing did not degrade jump, anaerobic power, or a
64	skill-accuracy measure in one studied population, but should treat football-specific
65	validation (heavier loads, contact-sport outcome measures) as a separate, unanswered
66	question.

# Key-Workouts and Key-Exercises Apply the Concentration Principle Inside a Single Session

**What it is** — Issurin extends the BPC concentration principle (see
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]) down to the level of a single session.
A **key-workout** is the most important development session in a training cycle, focused on
the current main training emphasis (Table 2.5, PDF p. 56, printed p. 45): it targets the
cycle's most relevant abilities (usually one motor-fitness and one technique/tactics
target), demands focused athlete motivation and coach support, is timed for the athlete's
"best time" (adjusted to prior load but not overly fatigued), is loaded at a
substantial/large/extreme level, favors partnership/team-spirit organizational forms, and
requires thorough objective monitoring (chronometry, HR, blood lactate, video). New,
unfamiliar training means should *not* be introduced during a key-workout, since novelty
diverts attention and motivation from load-specific execution. Within a workout, the
analogous concept is the **key-exercise** (or **key-task** in team/combat sports where a
scrimmage or sparring session plays the role), the single most important exercise, given
priority placement, maximal self-motivation and support, "prime-time" timing, and careful
monitoring (Table 2.9, PDF p. 64, printed p. 53). Issurin gives typical prescriptive ranges
for key-exercises by targeted ability (Table 2.10, PDF p. 66, printed p. 55, based on Fox &
Mathews 1981 and Viru 1995, "with author's modification"): maximal speed, 7-15s work at a
1:10 work/rest ratio, maximal intensity, 5-8 reps, 2-5 series; anaerobic glycolytic power,
30-50s, 1:(4-5), submaximal, 4-6 reps, 2-4 series, blood lactate >8 mmol/L and HR >180;
anaerobic glycolytic endurance, 1-1.5 min, 1:3, high intensity, 8-12 reps, 1-3 series,
maximal lactate >8 and HR >180; aerobic power, 1-2 min, 1:(1-0.5), intermediate, 5-8 reps,
1-3 series, lactate 4-8 and HR 160-180; aerobic endurance, 1-8 min, 1:0.3, medium intensity,
4-16 reps, 1-3 series, lactate 2.5-4(5) and HR 140-160; restoration/fat oxidation, 20-90 min,
low intensity, 1-3 reps, lactate 1-2.5 and HR 100-140.

**Why it works** — Issurin states this connection directly, not just by analogy: "From the
viewpoint of block training, the emphasis on key-function exercises/drills is very
characteristic. Following the principle of training workload concentration (1.2.2) the
accentuation of a specially selected exercise is logical and desirable" (PDF p. 64, printed
p. 53). **Inference:** the further claim that this concentration "protects" the stimulus
from being diluted by fatigue or divided attention is this entry's own restatement of that
logic, not a sentence Issurin himself writes in those terms.

**When to apply** — Programming a training cycle's hardest, most important session so it
actually gets the recovery state, attention, and monitoring it needs to produce the intended
adaptation, rather than treating every practice/lift as interchangeable. Table 2.10's
intervals give a concrete starting point for designing a key-exercise once the targeted
ability is chosen. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name an equivalent "key-workout"
concept explicitly. **Inference:** the department's own metric-selection discipline (pick 1-2
output metrics per force-plate report, per the Hawkin Dynamics ODSF framework,
`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring") reflects a similar
instinct toward concentrating monitoring attention rather than tracking everything equally;
this is this entry's own comparison, not a link Issurin or the baseline material states.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Issurin's own cautionary example (PDF p. 66, printed
p. 55) is that selecting the correct key-exercise is harder than it looks: at a national
coaching seminar of Olympic/World/Continental medalist-producing coaches, "more than 50%"
of proposed workouts confused exercises for maximal speed with exercises for speed endurance
(anaerobic glycolytic capacity), or aerobic endurance with aerobic power, i.e., experienced
coaches routinely mis-assign an exercise to the wrong physiological bucket. Table 2.10's
numeric ranges are themselves secondary citations (Fox & Mathews 1981; Viru 1995) filtered
through "author's modification", the specific modification is not described, so treat the
exact numbers as Issurin's own adapted synthesis rather than a directly-reproduced published
table. **Inference:** this system also assumes a coach has the staff capacity for thorough,
per-workout objective monitoring (HR, blood lactate, video), which is not always feasible
outside individual/dual sports with small rosters; Issurin does not state this limitation
himself.

**Example** — **Inference:** for a football skill player whose training cycle emphasizes maximal speed,
the key-exercise might be 6-8 reps of 7-15s maximal-intensity sprints at roughly a 1:10
work-rest ratio (per Table 2.10), placed early in the week's most-rested session, with
sprint times or GPS max-velocity data as the monitored variable, while other exercises in
that same session are deliberately treated as secondary, not co-equal priorities.

**Related** — [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]],
[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
[[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]].
