# Squat-First vs. Squat-After-Hang-Pull Changes Whether You Get More Reps or More Power

**What it is** — Spreuwenberg et al. (2006), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62):
**nine** resistance-trained male athletes performed the back squat (4 sets at 85% of 1RM) on
two separate days under two protocols. Protocol A: squat performed during the initial part
of the workout. Protocol B: squat performed after a whole-body resistance exercise (hang
pull). Results: Protocol A produced significantly more repetitions per set (8.0 ± 1.9 vs.
5.4 ± 2.7 in Protocol B), but average power per set was *higher* in Protocol B. The study
authors attribute (Spreuwenberg et al., 2006, as cited by Issurin) the power difference to
postactivation potentiation induced by the preceding whole-body power exercise.

**Why it works** — Issurin reports only the study authors' own attribution for the power
finding: they "attributed this phenomenon to postactivation potentiation induced by the
preceding whole-body power exercise" (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62). **Inference:** the
companion explanation for the rep-count finding, that fresh (unfatigued) muscle sustains
more total repetitions at a given relative load than muscle that has just performed a
preceding whole-body lift, is this entry's own reasoning to account for the Protocol A
result; Issurin does not state that explanation for the rep-count difference in this
passage.

**When to apply** — Choosing exercise order based on the specific training goal for that
session: Issurin's stated takeaway (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62) is that a coach wanting maximum
hypertrophy stimulus should place the squat early in the session (more total volume/reps),
while a coach targeting maximum power output should place it after appropriate whole-body
resistance work, to exploit postactivation potentiation. Directly usable for Baylor
strength-staff session design when max-effort lower-body power output (not volume) is the
stated goal of a given lift.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — This is a small (n = 9), single published study;
Issurin does not report effect sizes, statistical significance values, or the specific
whole-body exercise's loading in this citation beyond "hang pull", treat the direction of
the finding as `supported` but do not treat the exact magnitude (8.0 vs. 5.4 reps) as
something to replicate precisely without reading the original study. It is unclear from this
text whether the postactivation-potentiation effect generalizes to different athlete
populations (this sample was resistance-trained males), different preceding exercises, or
different rest intervals between the potentiating exercise and the squat.

**Example** — **Inference:** a power-focused lower-body day for football linemen might
sequence a moderate-load hang pull or clean pull before back squats at 85% 1RM, accepting
fewer total squat reps in exchange for higher power output per rep on the squats that
follow; a hypertrophy-focused day for the same lift would instead put the squat first.

15	
16	**What it is** — Ekstrand et al. (1983), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 58, printed p. 47,
17	Figure 2.1): **twelve** national-division soccer teams (**180 players**) were split into two
18	groups. The intervention group (six teams) used a modified program with carefully structured
19	warm-ups (ball exercises plus a stretching program) and cool-downs (jogging plus hold-relax
20	stretching), supervised by doctors and physiotherapists. The control group (six teams)
21	trained traditionally. Over a six-month follow-up, the intervention group showed "highly
22	significant superiority": a roughly **four-fold reduction in the number of injuries** and a
23	"drastic decrease" in workouts and games missed to musculoskeletal disorders. Issurin
24	separately cites supporting single-factor findings: stretching in warm-up increases lower
25	extremity range of motion in soccer players (Moller et al., 1985); active warm-up *without*
26	stretching does not affect flexibility (Zakas et al., 2006); and intense prior exercise
27	meaningfully stimulates aerobic metabolism in working muscles during subsequent strenuous
28	performance (Bangsbo et al., 2001). A related study (Moller et al., 1985, PDF p. 68, printed
29	p. 57) tracked 48 adult soccer players across three warm-up/cool-down protocols. The regular
30	soccer workout (no stretching) caused a significant decrease in all range-of-motion (ROM)
31	indices. A similar workout with a stretching series in the *warm-up* produced more favorable
32	ROM responses immediately after the session, with 24-hour ROM not reported for that arm. The
33	third version, with the stretching series inserted in the *cool-down*, produced significant
34	ROM benefits both immediately after the workout and 24 hours later.
35	
36	**Why it works** — Issurin gives warm-up three stated functions: metabolic adjustment,
37	technical/coordination adjustment, and attainment of mental readiness (Table 2.6, PDF p. 60,
38	printed p. 49). Cool-down gets four stated objectives, given in prose rather than a table:
39	reduce body temperature, heart rate, and blood pressure to resting levels; remove acid
40	metabolites and other waste products from the muscles to the circulatory system for further
41	clearance; facilitate recovery of the endocrine system; and reduce emotional tension and
42	support positive mental recovery (PDF p. 67, printed p. 56).
43	
44	**Contested, terminology only:** Issurin's cool-down rationale frames blood lactate and
45	"other acid metabolites" as "waste products" to be "removed" from the muscles (PDF pp.
46	67-69, printed pp. 56-58), and separately states that slow locomotion "causes faster lactate
47	removal" (Bonen & Belcastro, 1976, PDF p. 68, printed p. 57), with blood lactate removal
48	after a 4-minute exhausting time trial taking about 20 minutes of restoration (Juel et al.,
49	1990, PDF p. 70, printed p. 59). The vault's Verkhoshansky staging entry
50	([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]], `proven`) treats
51	lactate as a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not a toxin, and states that blood
52	lactate returns to normal within about an hour of strenuous interval training; its `proven`
53	rating is scoped to two corrections, that lactate is not the cause of DOMS and that "oxygen
54	debt" is better described as recovery oxygen consumption. That entry does not say clearance
55	happens "regardless of cool-down activity"; that claim belongs to neither source and should
56	not be attributed to either. The two books' clearance-time figures are consistent with each
57	other (about 20 minutes after a 4-minute trial vs. within about an hour of a strenuous
58	interval session), and neither source ties lactate to DOMS: Issurin attributes DOMS to
59	strong eccentric ("plyometric") work instead (PDF pp. 69-70, printed pp. 58-59). The real
60	disagreement is terminology, Issurin's "acid metabolites and other waste products" (PDF p.
61	67, printed p. 56) against the Verkhoshansky entry's "normal byproduct and fuel." Keep this
62	book's clearance-time number and its active-recovery claim (slow locomotion speeds lactate
63	removal); do not repeat "waste product" as physiology, and do not attribute a "toxin" claim
64	or a "regardless of cool-down activity" claim to Issurin, since he states neither.
65	
66	**When to apply** — The Ekstrand et al. (1983) result is directly relevant to Applied
67	Performance's collaboration with Athletic Medicine on injury reduction: a structured,
68	medically-supervised warm-up/cool-down protocol is associated with a large, measured
69	reduction in soft-tissue injury incidence in a team sport, over a real six-month season, not
70	an acute lab measure. The cool-down-stretching timing finding (Moller et al., 1985) suggests
71	cool-down, not just warm-up, is where a stretching series may do more for next-day range of
72	motion.
73	
74	**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — This is a controlled team-level trial (6 intervention
75	teams vs. 6 control teams; the method of allocating teams to condition is not described),
76	and the intervention bundled multiple changes at once (warm-up content, cool-down content,
77	and medical/physiotherapy supervision), so the four-fold injury reduction cannot be
78	attributed to warm-up or cool-down alone: Issurin himself flags this study as "atypical
79	because it refers to the complex effects of warming-up, cooling-down and medical supervision"
80	(PDF p. 58, printed p. 47). **Contested:** stretching's effect on preventing delayed-onset
81	muscle soreness specifically is described by Issurin himself as disputed within this same
82	chapter, "supported by several studies (Hartfield, 1985) and contradicted by others (High
83	et al., 1989)" (PDF p. 70, printed p. 59); do not cite stretching-prevents-DOMS as settled.
84	
85	**Example** — **Inference:** a Baylor position group's practice-ending routine that pairs light locomotion
86	with a stretching series (rather than stretching only in the pre-practice warm-up) has some
87	support here for next-day range-of-motion benefit, though the causal strength of the
88	underlying Moller et al. (1985) study for injury outcomes specifically (as opposed to ROM)
89	is not established by this citation.
90	
91	**Related** — [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]] (staging;
92	the direct source of the lactate-framing contest above, rewritten as terminology-only in this
93	review pass; recommend the Verkhoshansky entry add a reciprocal link back to this one once
94	both are reviewed).

14	# Which Training Modalities Tolerate Fatigue, and Which Need a Fresh Athlete
15	
16	**What it is** — Figure 2.3 (PDF p. 71, printed p. 60) ranks twelve training modalities by
17	how much athlete fatigue they can tolerate before the acute training effect is compromised,
18	from "well rested" through "slightly fatigued," "moderately fatigued," to "fatigued":
19	**well rested only**, maximal speed (least fatigue-tolerant of all); **well rested to
20	slightly fatigued**, maximal strength (neural mechanism, e.g. 1-3RM), explosive strength,
21	acquisition of new technical skills, anaerobic glycolytic power; **up to moderately
22	fatigued**, anaerobic glycolytic capacity, aerobic power, maximal strength (hypertrophy,
23	e.g. 8-10RM); **through to fatigued, end of session (most fatigue-tolerant)**, aerobic
24	endurance (long duration), strength endurance, technique perfection, flexibility. Issurin's
25	stated reasoning (PDF pp. 71-73, printed pp. 60-62): exercises needing precise excitatory
26	neural output (max speed, explosive strength, technical skill acquisition, neural-mechanism
27	strength) are blocked by inhibitory CNS output in fatigued athletes, so they belong early;
28	anaerobic glycolytic power needs available energy reserves that are depleted in fatigued
29	athletes; aerobic power's acute effect depends on the total duration of exercise performed
30	close to maximum oxygen uptake, a metabolic level moderately fatigued athletes can still
31	sustain (PDF p. 72, printed p. 61); hypertrophy-strength work depends on total mechanical
32	work and post-exercise recovery conditions, not the athlete's pre-exercise freshness, so it
33	can be placed later, even after an endurance session; anaerobic glycolytic capacity,
34	technique perfection, and strength/aerobic endurance work are defined by sustained effort
35	*despite* accumulating fatigue ("some part of technique perfection can be performed by
36	fatigued athletes," PDF p. 73, printed p. 62), so some fatigue is expected and even required
37	for the intended stimulus.
38	
39	**Why it works** — CNS-dependent, high-precision, high-velocity qualities are limited by
40	inhibitory neural output and available energy stores that both degrade with fatigue, while
41	volume/duration-dependent qualities (hypertrophy, strength/aerobic endurance, technique
42	perfection late in a session) depend on total accumulated work or post-session recovery
43	rather than the athlete's moment-to-moment freshness. Sequencing exists to protect the
44	fatigue-sensitive qualities' window, not because "harder exercises always go first."
45	
46	**When to apply** — Ordering exercises within a single practice or lift: place max-speed
47	work, new skill acquisition, explosive strength, and low-rep neural-strength work at the
48	start of a session (or after only light warm-up fatigue); place hypertrophy work, technical
49	perfection under fatigue, and long-duration aerobic/strength-endurance work later, when some
50	accumulated fatigue is acceptable or even intended. Issurin gives a worked example (PDF
51	p. 72, printed p. 61): an endurance athlete needing to preserve muscle mass can have a
52	hypertrophy-focused strength session (8-10RM) placed *after* a medium-load endurance
53	session, because hypertrophy's driver is total mechanical work and post-workout recovery
54	conditions, not pre-workout freshness; this would be the wrong sequencing choice for a
55	neural-strength (1-3RM) session, which does need "prime time."
56	
57	**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — The author gives no primary citation for Figure 2.3
58	itself: it reads as the author's own synthesized ranking rather than a reproduced,
59	independently-sourced scale; treat the ordinal ranking (which modality is more or less
60	fatigue-tolerant than its neighbor) as a reasonable but unvalidated synthesis, not a measured
61	result. The figure gives no guidance on *how much* fatigue is "slight" vs. "moderate" in
62	objective terms (RPE, HR, or specific fatigue markers), so applying it requires a coach's own
63	judgment call about where an athlete currently sits on that continuum. It also does not
64	address multi-session days directly: see [[heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability]]
65	for cross-session sequencing.
66	
67	**Example** — **Inference:** a football practice combining new install (technical skill
68	acquisition) with conditioning: install work belongs at the start of practice when players
69	are fresh and can attend to technical detail; conditioning work belongs at the end, where
70	sustained effort under fatigue is the intended stimulus rather than a limitation.
71	
72	**Related** — [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]],
73	[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].
74

2.13 (PDF p. 79, printed p. 68) gives compatible first/second-workout pairings by dominant
ability: aerobic power/capacity, fartlek (10-15s sprint, 3-6min at anaerobic threshold)
first, aerobic interval series second; anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity, anaerobic power
interval series first, anaerobic capacity interval series second; maximal speed, anaerobic
alactic interval series first, anaerobic alactic plus explosive strength exercises second;
techno-tactical abilities, techno-tactical simulation/maximum speed first, match/scrimmage
second.

# Which Training Modalities Tolerate Fatigue, and Which Need a Fresh Athlete

**What it is** — Figure 2.3 (PDF p. 71, printed p. 60) ranks twelve training modalities by
how much athlete fatigue they can tolerate before the acute training effect is compromised,
from "well rested" through "slightly fatigued," "moderately fatigued," to "fatigued":
**well rested only**, maximal speed (least fatigue-tolerant of all); **well rested to
slightly fatigued**, maximal strength (neural mechanism, e.g. 1-3RM), explosive strength,
acquisition of new technical skills, anaerobic glycolytic power; **up to moderately
fatigued**, anaerobic glycolytic capacity, aerobic power, maximal strength (hypertrophy,
e.g. 8-10RM); **through to fatigued, end of session (most fatigue-tolerant)**, aerobic
endurance (long duration), strength endurance, technique perfection, flexibility. Issurin's
stated reasoning (PDF pp. 71-73, printed pp. 60-62): exercises needing precise excitatory
neural output (max speed, explosive strength, technical skill acquisition, neural-mechanism
strength) are blocked by inhibitory CNS output in fatigued athletes, so they belong early;
anaerobic glycolytic power needs available energy reserves that are depleted in fatigued
athletes; aerobic power's acute effect depends on the total duration of exercise performed
close to maximum oxygen uptake, a metabolic level moderately fatigued athletes can still
sustain (PDF p. 72, printed p. 61); hypertrophy-strength work depends on total mechanical
work and post-exercise recovery conditions, not the athlete's pre-exercise freshness, so it
can be placed later, even after an endurance session; anaerobic glycolytic capacity,
technique perfection, and strength/aerobic endurance work are defined by sustained effort
*despite* accumulating fatigue ("some part of technique perfection can be performed by
fatigued athletes," PDF p. 73, printed p. 62), so some fatigue is expected and even required
for the intended stimulus.

**Why it works** — CNS-dependent, high-precision, high-velocity qualities are limited by
inhibitory neural output and available energy stores that both degrade with fatigue, while
volume/duration-dependent qualities (hypertrophy, strength/aerobic endurance, technique
perfection late in a session) depend on total accumulated work or post-session recovery
rather than the athlete's moment-to-moment freshness. Sequencing exists to protect the
fatigue-sensitive qualities' window, not because "harder exercises always go first."

**When to apply** — Ordering exercises within a single practice or lift: place max-speed
work, new skill acquisition, explosive strength, and low-rep neural-strength work at the
start of a session (or after only light warm-up fatigue); place hypertrophy work, technical
perfection under fatigue, and long-duration aerobic/strength-endurance work later, when some
accumulated fatigue is acceptable or even intended. Issurin gives a worked example (PDF
p. 72, printed p. 61): an endurance athlete needing to preserve muscle mass can have a
hypertrophy-focused strength session (8-10RM) placed *after* a medium-load endurance
session, because hypertrophy's driver is total mechanical work and post-workout recovery
conditions, not pre-workout freshness; this would be the wrong sequencing choice for a
neural-strength (1-3RM) session, which does need "prime time."

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — The author gives no primary citation for Figure 2.3
itself: it reads as the author's own synthesized ranking rather than a reproduced,
independently-sourced scale; treat the ordinal ranking (which modality is more or less
fatigue-tolerant than its neighbor) as a reasonable but unvalidated synthesis, not a measured
result. The figure gives no guidance on *how much* fatigue is "slight" vs. "moderate" in
objective terms (RPE, HR, or specific fatigue markers), so applying it requires a coach's own
judgment call about where an athlete currently sits on that continuum. It also does not
address multi-session days directly: see [[heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability]]
for cross-session sequencing.

**Example** — **Inference:** a football practice combining new install (technical skill
acquisition) with conditioning: install work belongs at the start of practice when players
are fresh and can attend to technical detail; conditioning work belongs at the end, where
sustained effort under fatigue is the intended stimulus rather than a limitation.

**Related** — [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]],
[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

# A Structured Warm-Up/Cool-Down Program Cut Soccer Injuries Roughly Four-Fold Over Six Months

**What it is** — Ekstrand et al. (1983), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 58, printed p. 47,
Figure 2.1): **twelve** national-division soccer teams (**180 players**) were split into two
groups. The intervention group (six teams) used a modified program with carefully structured
warm-ups (ball exercises plus a stretching program) and cool-downs (jogging plus hold-relax
stretching), supervised by doctors and physiotherapists. The control group (six teams)
trained traditionally. Over a six-month follow-up, the intervention group showed "highly
significant superiority": a roughly **four-fold reduction in the number of injuries** and a
"drastic decrease" in workouts and games missed to musculoskeletal disorders. Issurin
separately cites supporting single-factor findings: stretching in warm-up increases lower
extremity range of motion in soccer players (Moller et al., 1985); active warm-up *without*
stretching does not affect flexibility (Zakas et al., 2006); and intense prior exercise
meaningfully stimulates aerobic metabolism in working muscles during subsequent strenuous
performance (Bangsbo et al., 2001). A related study (Moller et al., 1985, PDF p. 68, printed
p. 57) tracked 48 adult soccer players across three warm-up/cool-down protocols. The regular
soccer workout (no stretching) caused a significant decrease in all range-of-motion (ROM)
indices. A similar workout with a stretching series in the *warm-up* produced more favorable
ROM responses immediately after the session, with 24-hour ROM not reported for that arm. The
third version, with the stretching series inserted in the *cool-down*, produced significant
ROM benefits both immediately after the workout and 24 hours later.

**Why it works** — Issurin gives warm-up three stated functions: metabolic adjustment,
technical/coordination adjustment, and attainment of mental readiness (Table 2.6, PDF p. 60,
printed p. 49). Cool-down gets four stated objectives, given in prose rather than a table:
reduce body temperature, heart rate, and blood pressure to resting levels; remove acid
metabolites and other waste products from the muscles to the circulatory system for further
clearance; facilitate recovery of the endocrine system; and reduce emotional tension and
support positive mental recovery (PDF p. 67, printed p. 56).

**Contested, terminology only:** Issurin's cool-down rationale frames blood lactate and
"other acid metabolites" as "waste products" to be "removed" from the muscles (PDF pp.
67-69, printed pp. 56-58), and separately states that slow locomotion "causes faster lactate
removal" (Bonen & Belcastro, 1976, PDF p. 68, printed p. 57), with blood lactate removal
after a 4-minute exhausting time trial taking about 20 minutes of restoration (Juel et al.,
1990, PDF p. 70, printed p. 59). The vault's Verkhoshansky staging entry
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]], `proven`) treats
lactate as a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not a toxin, and states that blood
lactate returns to normal within about an hour of strenuous interval training; its `proven`
rating is scoped to two corrections, that lactate is not the cause of DOMS and that "oxygen
debt" is better described as recovery oxygen consumption. That entry does not say clearance
happens "regardless of cool-down activity"; that claim belongs to neither source and should
not be attributed to either. The two books' clearance-time figures are consistent with each
other (about 20 minutes after a 4-minute trial vs. within about an hour of a strenuous
interval session), and neither source ties lactate to DOMS: Issurin attributes DOMS to
strong eccentric ("plyometric") work instead (PDF pp. 69-70, printed pp. 58-59). The real
disagreement is terminology, Issurin's "acid metabolites and other waste products" (PDF p.
67, printed p. 56) against the Verkhoshansky entry's "normal byproduct and fuel." Keep this
book's clearance-time number and its active-recovery claim (slow locomotion speeds lactate
removal); do not repeat "waste product" as physiology, and do not attribute a "toxin" claim
or a "regardless of cool-down activity" claim to Issurin, since he states neither.

**When to apply** — The Ekstrand et al. (1983) result is directly relevant to Applied
Performance's collaboration with Athletic Medicine on injury reduction: a structured,
medically-supervised warm-up/cool-down protocol is associated with a large, measured
reduction in soft-tissue injury incidence in a team sport, over a real six-month season, not
an acute lab measure. The cool-down-stretching timing finding (Moller et al., 1985) suggests
cool-down, not just warm-up, is where a stretching series may do more for next-day range of
motion.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — This is a controlled team-level trial (6 intervention
teams vs. 6 control teams; the method of allocating teams to condition is not described),
and the intervention bundled multiple changes at once (warm-up content, cool-down content,
and medical/physiotherapy supervision), so the four-fold injury reduction cannot be
attributed to warm-up or cool-down alone: Issurin himself flags this study as "atypical
because it refers to the complex effects of warming-up, cooling-down and medical supervision"
(PDF p. 58, printed p. 47). **Contested:** stretching's effect on preventing delayed-onset
muscle soreness specifically is described by Issurin himself as disputed within this same
chapter, "supported by several studies (Hartfield, 1985) and contradicted by others (High
et al., 1989)" (PDF p. 70, printed p. 59); do not cite stretching-prevents-DOMS as settled.

**Example** — **Inference:** a Baylor position group's practice-ending routine that pairs light locomotion
with a stretching series (rather than stretching only in the pre-practice warm-up) has some
support here for next-day range-of-motion benefit, though the causal strength of the
underlying Moller et al. (1985) study for injury outcomes specifically (as opposed to ROM)
is not established by this citation.

review pass; recommend the Verkhoshansky entry add a reciprocal link back to this one once
both are reviewed).

lines: **Why it works** — For the Case 4 frequency cut, Harries states the reason directly: reducing running frequency let him "make a more significant volume increase in those individual sessions" so there was "a nice little progression into" the larger, match-comparable session planned for the following week (~37:26-37:55). For the broader practice of shaping rehab-week structure around the team's rhythm, his only stated reason is the week-7 mid-week session "aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season" (~38:20-38:22); he gives no further explicit rationale for the general practice. Inference (entry writer's): tying rehab-session load to the team's own hard/light day pattern lets the returning athlete's tolerance build in step with what full training will actually demand in the week he returns, rather than on a schedule disconnected from it.

-**When to apply** — When designing a returning athlete's week once he is off an isolated running-only schedule and beginning to overlap with team sessions (typically mid-to-late rehab, alongside modified/partial training participation). Eric's review: Applied Performance "already undulate[s] load across the team week," and this pattern is proposed as "the same logic applied to one returning player, anchored to the team's Tue/Wed high, Thu low pattern" (Review and Plan, line 75) - i.e. the existing team-week undulation is the natural anchor for this on-field-rehab pattern, not a separate structure to invent.

+**When to apply** — When designing a returning athlete's week once he is off an isolated running-only schedule and beginning to overlap with team sessions (typically mid-to-late rehab, alongside modified/partial training participation). Eric's review (Review and Plan line 75, "Linear → undulating" row): "You already undulate load across the team week"; the gap it fills is "the same logic applied to one returning player, anchored to the team's Tue/Wed high, Thu low pattern." That remark is about linear-then-undulating MV progression (see [[heuristic--linear-then-undulating-mv-progression]]), not this week-shaping pattern directly. Inference: the same anchor fits the week-shape pattern in this entry.

-**When NOT to apply** — Harries never states this as a fixed template; no claim is made that a "high-moderate-high" week or a captain's-run walkthrough is required, and the specific weekly shapes differ across all three cases that show them, tracking each athlete's own timeline and injury type. None of it is validated against outcome data beyond what happened in each case being reported without a stated recurrence. Do not import a specific case's weekly pattern wholesale as a template; use the underlying idea, build the rehab week around the team's actual week, and rebuild the specific days for each returning athlete.

Case outcomes only (n=3), no outcome data.
